president of the council. mr president, mr poettering, mr president of the commission, mr barroso, ladies and gentlemen, i am speaking as a representative of a national parliament, almost as a colleague. i am pleased to be addressing you today for the first time as president of the council in this european parliament, a parliament with members from 27 member states. i would therefore like to extend a very warm welcome to the romanian and bulgarian members. (applause from the centre) the treaties of rome are almost 50 years old. we are celebrating this anniversary on 24 and 25 march in berlin, a city which symbolizes the reunification of europe after the end of the cold war like no other. but let's face it, 50 years is basically a blink of an eye in history. but in that short time, europe has achieved an unimaginable amount! so this is europe from the outside. but even from the inside, the european union is a wonderful house. i find it experienced from the inside - that's my experience of the last 17 years - even more beautiful than from the outside. i would never want to leave this house again: there is - that is my conviction - no better place for us to live in europe than our common european home! (applause from the centre) today we're going to expand it. we're expanding it. we're renewing it in some places. i sometimes think that if we are so busy building and renovating the building that today almost half a billion europeans are living in, then we can easily overlook the greatness, the uniqueness, of the building. then sometimes we can't quite grasp what this building really is, where its core is. ladies and gentlemen, many people in europe - you can feel it when you are at home - are going through exactly the same thing today. they ask themselves: what is europe supposed to be? what do we need europe for? what is it that holds europe together at its core? what is this european union? some people think that trying to define the nature of europe is a waste of time. i don't see it that way, to be honest. i remember jacques delors. he was a great man. he famously said: 'we must give europe a soul'. i would add that we must find the soul of europe. we do not need to give it to europe, because we already have it. is diversity that soul? few have put it more beautifully than the writer karel čapek, a great european from prague: 'the creator of europe made it small and even divided it into tiny pieces, so that our hearts rejoice not in its size but in its diversity.' what about diversity? it is certainly true to say that europe lives on its diversity. we want to preserve the differences between our nations, between the regions of europe, the diversity of languages and mentalities. we cannot and will not harmonize everything that can be harmonized. it is true that europe lives on its diversity. but it 's also true: the diversity as such cannot be the universal european principle which helps us to understand what holds europe together at its core, what constitutes its soul. but with the recognition of the diversity of nations and people, we create something different. that is how we get to the real question we have to answer. it is: what does europe's diversity make possible? i think the answer to that question is clear: freedom allows us to be diverse. (applause from the centre) freedom is the prerequisite for our diversity. freedom in all its forms: the freedom to express one's opinion publicly, even if it offends others. freedom to believe or not to believe, freedom of enterprise. the freedom of the artist to shape his work as he sees fit. europe needs this freedom like it needs air to breathe. where it is restricted, we wither. it is vital for europe to be aware that freedom is not won once and for all. freedom must be won anew almost every day. (applause from the centre) and freedom is not without obligations. it is inseparable from responsibility. so when we talk about true freedom, we are actually always talking about the freedom of the other. or to put it in the famous words of voltaire, i quote: "i may hate what you say, but i will stake my life on your right to say it". i think voltaire was the soul of europe. (applause from the centre) the european union is not a political union, but a political union of the peoples of europe. we europeans have learned in our history to make the most of diversity. and the quality that enables us to do that, that enables us to be free in responsibility for the other, that is a precious asset: it is tolerance. the soul of europe is tolerance. europe is the continent of tolerance. it took us centuries to learn that. on our way to tolerance, we had to suffer through disasters. we've hunted each other down and destroyed each other. we have devastated our home. we have compromised what is sacred to us. the worst period of hatred, devastation and destruction is not yet over. it was done in the name of my people. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to play a full part in the development of the european union. but from this centuries-long history, we in europe are obliged to promote tolerance everywhere in europe and throughout the world, and to help everyone to practice tolerance. (applause from the centre) yes, ladies and gentlemen, tolerance is a demanding virtue. she needs the heart and the mind. she's charging us. but it is not to be confused with arbitrariness and lack of a point of view. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. there is a simple way to the soul of europe, to tolerance: one must also see with the eyes of the other. try it once! it is a fascinating adventure to discover, through the eyes of the many peoples of europe, the diversity of our continent, that is, our wealth. but while we may be fascinated by it, we must not forget that tolerance is constantly being challenged. i therefore say clearly: europe must never have the slightest understanding of intolerance. (applause from the centre) europe must never have the slightest tolerance for violence by right-wing and left-wing extremism, for violence in the name of religion. tolerance is its own grave-digger if it does not guard against intolerance. or, in the words of thomas mann, "tolerance becomes a crime when it is applied to evil". tolerance without understanding intolerance - that's what makes a man human. in lessing's famous ring parable, nathan the wise tells of a quarrel between three brothers. it's about who is the true heir to the father's ring and therefore to religious truth. this heritage can only be shown by good deeds. that's what the brothers should excel at. i believe that this is where we find the soul of europe again, in our peaceful coexistence, in our search for the best for each other. for me, as a christian who expressly professes the christian foundations of europe, the most beautiful part of the play is a wish of the sultan to nathan. across all the religious divides, the muslim asks the jew, "be my friend". the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe in the past, and it is a great help to us in the present. that was and is the great aim of european unification. (applause from the centre) this was the starting point of the first european steps after 1945: the treaty on the european coal and steel community, the treaties of rome, have not yet dealt with our culture, or have done so only very little, and the maastricht treaty does not deal with it at all. but without a vision of a common europe, of what europe is at its heart, all these treaties would not have been possible. the treaties have already addressed important questions of european coexistence and have provided some wonderful answers. and so, on this basis, i can commit myself today to the tasks of today, to a europe of the equal participation of all member states, large and small, old and new. europe will only succeed if we work together. and that is precisely the motto of our presidency: europe succeeds together. and i would add that europe can only succeed if we work together. i am in favour of a europe that focuses on what is best managed at european level, but does so with the necessary commitment and efficiency. i am in favour of a europe which, on the other hand, deliberately leaves to the member states, their regions and their local authorities policy areas where european regulation would be more of an obstacle. (applause from the centre) i am committed to a europe that explicitly relies on european solutions, where it wants and must act together to meet the challenges of the 21st century: globalisation, the threat to peace and security posed by new threats such as terrorism. i believe that we can only meet all these challenges on the basis of our understanding of tolerance. the draft constitutional treaty is the first time that a european treaty text expressly speaks of the tolerance which characterizes the member states of the european union and which will help us to create the basis on which the future europe can develop new, sensible rules, rules which are appropriate to the new size of the european union and the challenges ahead, rules which must enable us to act. we know that the european union cannot be enlarged under the present rules, nor is it able to take the necessary decisions. we have to overcome this condition. we therefore need clear descriptions of the competences of the european union and the national states. rules of procedure must be more clearly defined than before. in other words, the treaty bases we have must be adapted to the changing conditions if the european union is to survive in the world of tomorrow. this is the background against which i am consulting with all the member states, the european commission and parliament on behalf of the european council on a way out of the ratification crisis of the constitutional treaty. the thinking phase is over. the time has now come to work out new decisions by june. i am working to ensure that at the end of the german presidency a roadmap for the further process of the constitutional treaty can be adopted. president of romania. dear mr president,honourable members of the european parliament,your excellences,ladies and gentlemen,it is an honour for me to be the first president of romania to address this distinguished parliamentary forum and, through you, all european citizens, since our accession to the european union. the privilege is all the greater as the outstanding work of the parliament in the service of european construction is known. by its position as a firm and committed promoter of the enlargement process, the parliamentary forum has sent romania a message of support and partnership from the outset. many members of parliament have become our closest friends over the years, and i thank them for that. i would also like to convey my congratulations to mr hans-gert pöttering on his election as president of the european parliament and to wish him every success in his future work. i also congratulate all of you who have been appointed to the european parliament's leadership structure and wish you every success in your task. at the same time, i thank and congratulate mr josep borrell on his impressive work as president of the european parliament. mr borrell's term of office coincided with important moments in our european journey, and for this we are grateful to him. i also wish the romanian meps who are at the beginning of the road success. their duty as representatives of the european citizens is both honourable and difficult. i have full confidence in the ability of the romanian parliamentarians to respond properly to the expectations of european citizens, which now include the citizens of romania. ladies and gentlemen, ever since they were able to express themselves freely after december 1989, romanians have been unequivocally in favour of returning to the european family. the main message of our accession was: 'we are back in europe!' romanians saw the european union as a model of cooperation that had succeeded in facilitating the fulfillment of the potential of every european citizen. romania's accession to the european union coincides with the approach of a landmark anniversary for community building. it is about marking, on 25 march, half a century of solidarity action around common ideals: peace, freedom, tolerance, pluralism, respect for the law, unity in diversity, economic prosperity, social cohesion. all these values define the european union and have given it the permanent strength to go further. in a globalised world, the union must be stronger, more efficient, and the resources it needs to do so must come from solidarity, from the political, economic and social strength of our member states. with each new state, the union becomes stronger, more dynamic, richer. from this perspective, a union of 27 member states can only be a win for both the newcomers and the union as a whole. distinguished members of the european parliament,even though we have become a member state of the european union, we understand from our own experience of the internal preparation process that accession is not synonymous with integration itself. i might even say that the real challenge is now beginning. a new perspective has been opened to us, it is up to us to capitalize on it and turn it into a success for both romania and the european project. i assure you that after 1 january 2007 we have not fallen into the trap of relaxation and we are aware that the real process of our integration is only just beginning. it's a long-term effort, which must be done at home, not only by the state institutions, but also by each romanian. our integration must come, first of all, from the capacity to generate economic growth, from effective institutions, a credible, independent judiciary capable of delivering justice to the people, non-corrupt officials, infrastructure of european standards, a clean environment. in short, a standard of living for romanian citizens compatible with that of european citizens. equally, romania's integration must also come from our capacity to be in solidarity with the general interest of the union. the integration of romania also means our ability to harmonize the national interest with the general interest of the union, but also our ability to make a real contribution to the competitiveness, security and internal cohesion of the european union. if we go back to the beginning, the early 1990s, the results are important. in today's romania, judges are independent, and ministers are accountable for their actions in office. the situation of institutionalized or disabled children has improved considerably. a major effort has been made to integrate the roma, a problem that is still not resolved to satisfactory parameters. romania has today the toughest laws for declarations of wealth and interests for public officials; romania has eliminated the practice of rescheduling corporate debts, introduced transparency in the allocation of public funds and strengthened criminal sanctions for tax evasion. however, romania still has a long way to go to catch up with the advanced member states, even compared to the current european average. the average income per economy is only 328 euros. the transportation infrastructure is way behind. rural development and the elimination of subsistence farming remain a major challenge. the percentage of the population employed in agriculture is still very high. the middle class is not strong enough to become a powerful engine of society. and the list doesn't end there. your natural question might be: what guarantees are there that romania will continue the reforms started and that it will eliminate these shortcomings? the guarantee is the support of the romanian people and the political will of the leaders. remember that no other political objective, other than joining the european union, has succeeded in uniting the entire romanian society around it with the same force and in coalition the entire political spectrum, rising above any party interests or individual interests. i'm counting on the same mobilization for the integration process itself. i personally, within the limits of my constitutional powers, assure you that this objective will be achieved. we have this political and moral duty first of all to the citizens of romania. we will continue this effort with the romanians and for the romanians. we will find more time and more patience to debate at home the direct implications of this effort on the daily lives of our citizens. we will make them more familiar with european institutions and themes. we'll talk about the benefits, but at the same time, we'll have to explain things that seem hard to explain. for example, why romanians cannot access the labour market in some member states, even though most of them are honest workers. and as i speak from the highest tribune of european democracy, i would like to confess to you a personal concern on this subject: the union has succeeded, formally and institutionally, in overcoming the old east-west divisions. it's a historic achievement, an achievement of this century. however, a lack of awareness and hesitation among citizens in some member states to accept eastern europeans as full partners and members of the same family persists. i do not want to generalize, but the phenomenon exists and has effects on the union as a whole. we, the politicians, directly elected by the citizens, have a duty to promote together ways of improving mutual knowledge between our citizens. the result will enhance the union's internal cohesion, diminish ultra-nationalist or extremist tendencies and strengthen our union of 27 member states. let us learn from the experience of politicians in those member states who have paid a heavy political price for not giving due weight to communication with their citizens and for leaving room for doubt and misunderstanding about some european developments. and here we need your support. we need your will to understand that our eastern european nations have reasons for pride, have exceptional people, often have a rich european history, have advantages that they offer to the union as a whole. ladies and gentlemen,we are convinced that ensuring the internal cohesion of the european union is an essential prerequisite, including for equipping the union with the capacity to play an external role commensurate with its potential. this will enable us to respond to today's broader security challenges, whether it is energy security, illegal migration, or hotbeds of conflict and instability in neighbouring areas. romania will contribute to the european union's increasingly strong assertion as a global actor. especially where it can add real value. and here, i am thinking of relations with the western balkans and the eastern neighbourhood of the european union. in the western balkans, 2007 will be the 'year of truth' in a way. it is the year in which the international community will have to demonstrate that it can propose a viable solution for the province of kosovo. you are of course aware of the reservations we have about imposing a solution from outside. i believe that the sensitive problems of the balkans - kosovo, the prospects for bosnia and herzegovina, the republic of montenegro, the commitment of serbia to the european orbit, but also the fight against crime and extremist groups - will be solved only by a unified approach at regional level. the difficulties in the western balkans area require an integrated solution, including the provision of a clear european perspective. the european perspective offered to the republic of moldova should be similar to that for the western balkans. romania intends to explain, support and find support within the european union for the republic of moldova to return to europe, where it left in 1940 without its will. both the people of romania and the people of the republic of moldova have the same history, speak the same language, have the same culture, the same traditions and the same european aspirations. certainly, it is a moral and political obligation of romania and romanians to fight for our families from east of the prut to return home to europe. another area that is increasingly focusing our attention is the black sea basin, considering that this is not only an area of great prospects but also one of multiple risks and challenges. i think we are all convinced that the vast black sea area offers many of the possible answers to the big questions of european and global energy security. we want to equip the region with tools and mechanisms to control illicit trafficking of any kind, to combat terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction. we want 2007 to bring real progress in resolving the various frozen conflicts in the region and we are open to dialogue with any partner that can contribute to this. we will support the involvement of the european union in the processes of resolving frozen conflicts, including under the umbrella of the european security and defence policy. we hope that together with the neighbouring states, we can transform this region into a model of peaceful coexistence. romania aims to continue to be an active contributor to strengthening international security. we will remain engaged in projects promoted by beneficial for us, but also entails responsibilities and solidarity. and since i am often asked what is the added value that romania brings to the european union, let me address a few aspects: the european union is a key player in the european union's economic growth and global competitiveness, offering the second largest market among the new member states after poland and important investment opportunities. romania entered its seventh consecutive year of economic growth, with a rate of 8.4% for 2006, well above the union's average. this gives us confidence that we are on the right track, even if some reforms still need to be continued and strengthened. foreign direct investment in romania in 2006 amounted to €8.5 billion, and in the 17 years of reforms the dramatic transformations that have taken place have allowed romanians who embraced change to approach the standards for joining the european union. another argument is that romanians are a christian people, of latin origin, with a strong european culture, a people who have preserved their traditions and customs. we are a country with important connections both in south-eastern europe and east of the external border of the union. the black sea is directly adjacent to the european union. it is a geostrategic gain, but also an additional guarantee that romania gives to secure the european space. since joining nato, romania has become a security provider rather than a security consumer. we come with an important political and social tradition of tolerance and diversity, of protection of national minorities, of respect and participation of them in the political, social and cultural life of the country. this experience has prepared us for the culture of dialogue and partnership that is so much a part of solidarity in the union of 27. last but not least, romania brings a fresh, invigorating breath of support for the political objectives of the european agenda at a time when the mood is relatively skeptical. today, 67% of romanians say they have confidence in the european union. in addition, by the fact that the accession process was longer and perhaps more difficult, we are a clear example part. at european level, we will join the effort to strengthen political union with strong and effective institutions capable of further promoting the process of european integration. in our view, in developments at home and abroad and that provide the answers that european citizens expect. i am thinking of: ensuring the area of freedom and security, energy security, combating illegal immigration. member of the commission. madam president, i congratulate you, first of all, on your election to the office of vice-president and i am confident that you will fully meet the demands and expectations of the distinguished colleagues who supported you with their votes. mr president, never before has climate change been so prominent on the political agenda. the message from science is clear: climate change is happening. citizens expect european union leadership on this issue. the standard review and the commission's communication on post-2012 make the economic case for action. the risks of climate change far outweigh the costs of doing something about it. following several natural events, notably the warm winter we are experiencing this year, there is a lively public debate about the threat of climate change. the european union must use this political momentum to act. now is the time for decisions on how to put europe and the world on the path to a more energy-secure, low-carbon future. the urgency and scale of the climate change challenge requires europe to further reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and convince its partners around the globe to do the same. the european union has the objective of limiting global warming to two degrees celsius above pre-industrial levels. the climate change and energy package that the commission put on the table on 10 january provides a blueprint for a european union strategy to meet this objective. it outlines the basic elements of a global climate agreement post-2012 and gives a clear signal on the necessary level of ambition. this will encourage the start of negotiation on a post-2012 deal. the strength of this fully integrated package is that it demonstrates that further reducing the european union's greenhouse gas emissions goes hand in hand with strengthening our competitiveness and the security of our energy supply. the credibility of the package is further underlined by the combination of concrete policy proposals to be adopted in 2007 or later. we had the approval of our targets, which are very important. i can just remind you that about a year ago, we didn't even talk about targets. we did not even think about unilateral commitments. about 15 months ago, the european council had used the language "explore" when giving the commission the mandate: the mandate was to explore reduction pathways of 15 to 30% with other developed countries. now we have a target to negotiate and we are asking the european council to give us the mandate to negotiate a 30% target with other developed countries. on top of that we have a unilateral commitment, irrespective of the agreement and until such an agreement is reached, to reduce by 20%, which will enable us to achieve the other targets which we have set in terms of energy efficiency, carbon dioxide emissions and energy security. other specific measures are also needed in order to achieve these targets. as regards the decisions we are taking on the in writing. the dangers posed by terrorism to air traffic must not be underestimated or minimized. however, restrictive measures at the expense of passengers must also bring about a real increase in safety. the commission and council decisions which have been in force since november do not show this. the daily situation at europe's airports is characterised by unclear regulations, often differing from one airport to another; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the safety of passengers is being played up, but cannot be guaranteed in an emergency. the commission and the council are therefore invited to revise the regulation in question. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. it is also useful to involve airport practitioners in the preparation of these guidelines.

in terms of values, freedom, law and democracy. it was a long trip. we know that our european roots are in greek philosophy, roman law, the judeo-christian heritage, the enlightenment, in other words our common european culture. but it also includes the tragic european civil wars and the inhuman ideologies of totalitarianism in the 20th century and then, after 1945, the courage of the founding fathers to take the path of forgiveness and reconciliation, to build a new, better, peaceful, common europe. we should remember that today and rediscover our common ground. the great frenchman jacques delors, in the tradition of robert schuman, spoke of the 'soul of europe'. the great polish european, wladyslaw bartoszewski, once said: 'europe means above all individual freedom, political and economic human rights'. they're both right. i would like to speak about european values. they are based on the dignity of the human person. in the dignity of the person we respect the other, we commit ourselves and thus build an order of responsibility and solidarity. in our practical political action we should always serve the dignity of the human person, and i would encourage us all to defend human dignity and human rights throughout the world. this is not an abstract demand. we are not the world's teachers, but our image of humanity and our values become more convincing to others if we live them in a credible way. this has very concrete implications for our policy: we want to partner with a russia that is capable of acting and democratic. we therefore expect the russian authorities to make a clear effort to bring the murderers of ana politkovskaya, who has done so much for the freedom of the press in her country, to justice. preparations for the declaration on the future of europe, following my proposal last may. this declaration, to be signed in berlin, represents a real common point of reference – a confirmation of what the european union is for and a mission statement for what we want to achieve in the 21st century. last month, in this house, i made proposals i would like to see in the berlin declaration. i did not do it for the sake of making proposals. they correspond to results that european citizens want us to achieve. and i believe that it is by focusing on the goals of our common project that we will be able to reach a strong and enlarged consensus, including a consensus for an institutional settlement. i am convinced that if europeans see the european union addressing globalisation, promoting economic growth and jobs, showing social solidarity, tackling climate change, increasing democratic legitimacy, bringing security to its citizens, defending our values and interests worldwide, then they will trust the european union to reform itself to meet tomorrow’s challenges and to deliver practical results. we are all here to serve european citizens. if we are to enjoy public consent, we need to target our activities on citizens’ priorities and we need to work in a way that justifies their confidence, particularly respecting the principles of subsidiarity and transparency. we set out exactly this approach in our citizens’ agenda communication of last may. in order to achieve results, we need to preserve and develop institutional partnership; a partnership founded on the separation of competences, but also on the idea of institutional interdependence. while respecting the autonomy of each institution, we need to stress the commonality of our european principles. despite some natural political and ideological differences, those who are committed to these principles should build a truly european partnership. i believe that cooperation between parliament, the council and the commission is working well. it has proved itself against some stern tests. over the past year we have seen difficult dossiers resolved on services, chemicals, reach and the financial perspectives, to name but a few. this was a result of the three institutions working together with this spirit of partnership. i am committed to working closely with you, mr president, as well as with chancellor merkel and her successors at the helm of the council. i am convinced this is the best way to deliver the results our citizens demand. the resolution of the debate on the future of europe is not a sideshow: a more efficient and democratic european union goes to the heart of our ability to deliver policies and results. we all know this is what the constitutional treaty would have achieved, and there are limits to what we can achieve without it. as i often say, we cannot build tomorrow’s europe with yesterday’s tools. the nice treaty is not enough. (applause) i know that the european parliament shares the commitment of the european commission to give full support to the work of the german presidency to find the right way forward. the energy and commitment of chancellor merkel gives us real hope that we can find a consensus and make a compelling case for reform and progress to european citizens. but the presidency of the council can only achieve results if it is supported by all the member states. today, where all the european institutions are here reunited, i wish to repeat my call on member states to find a solution as regards the constitutional treaty. i know, after the ‘no’ votes in two member states, that it is difficult, if not impossible, to ratify exactly the same text. but let us not forget that all the governments signed the treaty. this has at least a double implication. first, member states recognised that the union needed to solve common problems and common challenges. and we have not solved them yet. second, the act of signing a treaty also implies a responsibility towards the other member states, towards european institutions and towards european citizens. it is the duty of all european governments to be constructive and active in the search to find a common solution. and i would like to stress the word ‘common’. at a historical moment like this, when we celebrate the peaceful unity of europe, we do not have the right to divide it again. regarding their positions about europe, sometimes some politicians remind me of james mill, the father of john stuart mill. john stuart mill once said that his father loved mankind in general, but hated each person in particular. (laughter)we also see many politicians in europe that profess their love for europe in general, but then resist european solutions to energy, climate change, immigration and, of course, the institutional settlement. let us be frank: we do not need declarations of intent; what we need is commitment. (applause)and we face decisive tests in the near future, starting with the energy and climate change package in the european council in march. i very much welcome the statement chancellor merkel made just now. let us be honest with ourselves. coherence is a requisite for credibility. we are not credible when we say that we want to speak with one voice to the outside world on energy and we keep speaking among ourselves with 27 voices and 27 markets. we are not credible when we set the fight against climate change as one of the most important priorities for europe and afterwards we are not able to agree on specific goals for our policies. so, we need to be coherent and credible. mr president, madam chancellor, honourable members, i have high hopes for the period between now and the end of this parliamentary term. i believe we have established the right priorities, and the right foundation of partnership to make them work. i look forward to working closely with president poettering and with this parliament, and with colleagues in the european council, to deliver real reform in europe and real change for europe’s citizens to the end of this decade. i believe we can build a europe that will be able to shape the future of our world around the values of freedom and justice that are so important for us. the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. as in previous years, this spring summit of heads of state or government will focus on economic issues, particularly the lisbon strategy. we are naturally pleased that this year's spring summit is taking place against a backdrop of positive economic fundamentals and encouraging developments in labour markets. we conclude cautiously that the lisbon strategy is bearing its first fruits, but we are nevertheless convinced that it would be completely inappropriate to put our hands in the air now. on the contrary, we want to take advantage of the positive overall trend and the optimism that is building up for further structural reforms. we want to make further joint efforts to safeguard and build on the successes of recent times in a sustainable way, because it is important to make europe in the best possible shape for global competition. after intensive preparatory work, which has also been characterized by very close and extremely fruitful cooperation with the commission, we have now entered the hot phase of preparation for the european council meeting on 8 and 9 march. the general affairs and external relations council yesterday discussed the annotated agenda for the european council prepared by the presidency. i am pleased to inform you that the member states are fully supporting the thematic line proposed by the presidency. in the coming weeks, the permanent representatives committee will coordinate the various contributions of the various sectoral council configurations and develop the draft conclusions of the european council in the light of these key points. i would like to remind you of the dates on which the various committees adopt their opinions: the energy council will meet the day after tomorrow to consider one of the most important issues for the european council, namely the energy action plan; the education and youth council will take place on 16 february, followed by the competitiveness council on 19 february and the environment council on 20 february. the council responsible for employment and social affairs and the ecofin council, which takes decisions on these matters, will meet on 22 and 27 february respectively. although the european parliament is not directly involved in this preparatory work, i can assure you that the presidency will take account of the opinions adopted by parliament on the topics of the summit. let me now go into some detail about the presidency's plans for this spring's summit. i can also refer to what the president-in-office of the council said here this morning. we will ensure that the european council fulfils its original role of focusing on key issues, setting the course, taking forward-looking decisions and providing policy guidance to the relevant bodies at european and national level. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one. in line with these general considerations, we have endeavoured to focus the european council's deliberations on issues where there is a generally recognised need for action and where further efforts are needed. in particular, it aims to support structural reforms initiated in the member states and to promote them through integrated country-specific recommendations. in the field of the internal market, we want to strengthen the common will to close gaps and identify weaknesses, to strengthen the union's competitiveness vis-à-vis third countries, but also to provide impetus for a revival of the doha round. strengthening innovation, research and education is as much at our heart as promoting employment and developing the european social model. the main themes are flexicurity and demographic change. better legislation - the chancellor also said this this morning - is an important concern for all of us. this has considerable potential to increase the competitiveness of the european economy. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council by the end of the year. we have set out to send out ambitious signals at the european council. in concrete terms, the main focus is on simplifying existing legislation and considering further improvements to the impact assessment tool. as legislators, the council and parliament have a particular responsibility to ensure that the commission's proposals for simplifying legislation are simultaneously thoroughly examined and dealt with swiftly. our main concern is to promote the reduction of bureaucratic costs, especially by setting clear quantitative targets. finally, as decided last year, the european council will adopt the comprehensive eu energy action plan, which commits to the three fundamental objectives of the union in this area, namely security of supply, competitiveness and to reiterate environmental sustainability. the strategic energy report presented by the commission in january shows that only an energy policy that takes account of all three pillars of this triangle will meet the challenges facing the union. we therefore actively advocate a package of measures which, when combined, will have the desired effect. this package includes measures to strengthen competition in the internal energy market, to give greater prominence to renewable energy sources and to develop better energy technologies and energy efficiency. the strengthening of the external component of energy policy is of the utmost importance in this respect. i would like to emphasize that europe must speak with one voice more strongly on energy issues. climate protection is inseparably linked to the energy issue. in the face of the century-old challenge of climate change, we are determined to take ambitious and forward-looking decisions, including quantified targets, in this area as well. the commission's proposals, which are fully consistent with those on energy, provide a good basis for this. the european council must work to send a strong signal on the further development of the international climate regime after 2012. only if the developed countries, led by the european union, come forward with ambitious commitments and measures will it be possible to expect the emerging countries to be willing to make adequate commitments of their own to limit their rapidly growing emissions.
i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this, but that it should be involved in the work of the council. we should take this as an example for the future in the reform of our parliamentary work. the council can also limit itself and still say something good.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, march offers a real opportunity for the european union. firstly, it gives us a chance to show citizens a european union taking ambitious, clear decisions on subjects that they care deeply about. secondly, we will be called upon to agree a declaration that will not only celebrate our achievements over these 50 years, but set out what we can do in the future. so, the two are closely linked. a successful spring council would provide the perfect springboard for an ambitious berlin declaration. europe has to take action. it has to be political, effective and play a key role when it comes to addressing the major challenges of today’s globalised world. growth and jobs, climate change, energy: these are subjects on the minds of europeans every day. we have a real opportunity to show what the european union can offer, of course, in full compliance with our renewed commitment to better regulation. i should like to focus on climate change, energy and the growth and jobs agenda. two weeks ago the un panel on climate change set out clearly, calmly and irrefutably the facts on climate change. the goal of limiting temperature gains to 2°c is still achievable – just! the next decade or so will determine whether we manage to bring the situation under control. our international partners, investors and citizens are all looking to the european union for clear, determined action. the scale of the problem is huge. a bold response is the only one that makes sense and that means practical policy proposals and binding targets. that is why we proposed that developed countries accept a 30% emission reduction target by 2020 compared to 1990 levels. at the same time, nobody questions the need to bring developing countries into the global efforts to cut emissions, and they can realistically be put on track to limit the growth in their emissions, to start with, and to start cutting by 2020. i expect the spring european council to send a convincing and strong signal on the need for determined action on climate change. the resolution on climate change, which this house will adopt tomorrow and which is both encouraging and stunning, contains an important and urgent message, which the commission will pass on to the heads of state and government when climate issues are being discussed at the spring council. however, we must also show both inside and outside the eu that we are prepared to act ourselves today. that is why the spring council should agree a firm, independent eu commitment to achieving at least a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2020. this will be a real demonstration of our commitment. energy is key to cutting emissions. however, it is more than that: secure supply, fairer prices and more choice are all issues that are central to citizens’ daily concerns for themselves, their families and future generations and, of course, to european industry. there is also an instinctive sense that these issues can only be tackled effectively at european level. therefore, this is also a stern test for the european union itself. last month, the commission set out its vision of how to put european energy policy on track and i very much welcome the supportive stance of this parliament. whenever we face a long-term challenge, it is essential that europeans can look to their democratically-elected representatives to explain why reform is essential, to put short-term change in the context of long-term purpose, to convince us that every one of us can play a part, for example through doing what we can on energy efficiency. the comprehensive resolution that you adopted on 14 december last year reflects the essential role that parliament plays in this context. so the ambition and conviction of the european council are critical. we cannot put off decisions any longer. europe needs to send the clearest of messages that it is committed to transforming the shape of european energy over the next few decades. investors are ready to step in on a massive scale, but they need a clearer signal. that means decisive action in the internal market. it means real steps to ensure solidarity between member states. it means making research in this area our top priority, for example as the first target for the european institute of technology. it means a precise, ambitious and, in particular, binding target of bringing renewable energy into the mainstream by 2020. with a clear green light from the european council, the commission is ready to bring forward a wide range of precise legislative measures this year. climate change and energy are integral parts of the broader issue on which the spring council will focus, the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. real steps are being taken to invest more in innovation, to make life easier for new and growing businesses, to help citizens prepare for change. the economic situation, as you know, is improving and europe has shown that it is facing up to the challenge of globalisation, but these first steps now need to accelerate. the consensus for change needs to be translated into action in all parts of europe and in all sectors. modernising our economies and societies is essential if our values and quality of life are to flourish in this rapidly changing world. the spring council needs to give a clear message that we will press ahead with reform at all levels as set out in the commission’s annual progress report on the lisbon strategy, including the country-specific recommendations. the commission strongly welcomes parliament’s support on this point. your resolution gives a timely reminder of some of the key benchmarks by which the credibility of action will be assessed. for example, reducing start-up time for new businesses to no more than one week, or cheaper protection of intellectual property rights. time is running out if we are to avoid the worst effects of climate change, tackle the global imbalance between energy supply and demand, and secure real modernisation. it is time to put our best wisdom at the service of these objectives. george bernard shaw said that we grow wise not by remembering the past, but by being responsible for the future. at a time when we are celebrating 50 years of the european union, this is a wise thing to remember. bold, ambitious and long-term decisions from the spring council in march will put the european union on the road to finding real answers to these most urgent questions.

challenges of the times in which we live and of the foreseeable future. this explains the peculiarity of the experience of the european parliament: the european parliament is a political body, a political body which does not follow narrow and divergent national logics, and which can certainly be divided on important issues, in votes which are certainly significant, but which converge to a very large extent in the vision of the fundamental objectives to be pursued in order to strengthen the construction of a united europe. when - as has happened so many times over the decades - the choice was between going further, making european unity wider and stronger, or marking the way and even going back, the european parliament always played a driving role, it spoke out clearly, with very large majorities, to advance the common construction and to broaden its horizon and ambitions. indeed, since the great new event of the election of the european parliament by universal suffrage in 1979, the path of parliamentarisation and constitutionalisation of the union had become a necessary prospect in order to strengthen the democratic foundations of the integration process and to guarantee the rights and opportunities for participation of citizens. the european parliament did so by adopting the draft treaty establishing the european union on 14 february 1984 - exactly 23 years ago. that draft, drawn up and discussed at the instigation of altiero spinelli, unfortunately did not become a treaty and, despite the long and not fruitless subsequent path, often inspired by the proposals of the same spinelli project, many questions remained open and new ones arose. thus, when, at the time of the signing of the disappointing treaty of nice, governments agreed on the need to tackle the major issues of europe's future and to launch a genuine constituent process, parliament gave its full support by working together to find satisfactory solutions to the questions raised in the laeken declaration of december 2001. the european parliament can be proud of the role it played more than ever in that phase, especially in the brussels convention, in its working groups, in its plenary sessions and in its presidium. members of the european parliament, 2001, 2002, 2003: there was no pause in those years, there was serious reflection, genuine and deep reflection. the final decisions of the intergovernmental conference were therefore based on a very rich analysis, a text which was thought through and discussed at length. the result was a compromise, but not a low-level one: a meeting place for different points of view was found; each party - including the european parliament - sacrificed some of its own demands and proposals in order to reach an agreement that would still advance the cause of european unity and integration. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. that this extraordinary and protracted political and cultural effort is destined to end in nothing? that the signatures of 27 heads of state or government at the bottom of that text no longer have any value? of course, we all know how traumatic it was to vote against ratification of the constitutional treaty in the referendums held in two of the six founding countries of the european community. and we also know what questions we are faced with as a result of the spread, also in other countries, of doubts and scepticism about the way forward in europe, about the present state and prospects of the european union. in reality, the consequences of a poor effort to involve citizens in the great choices of european integration and unification are paying off, to spread awareness among public opinion in all countries of the extraordinary achievements and progress made in 50 years, and of the new, ever more pressing needs for strengthening the european union, its cohesion and its capacity for action. this cannot, however, lead to an underestimation of the reasons for the constitutional treaty, signed in rome in october 2004, or of the solutions contained therein. these have already been concrete, albeit partial, responses that need to be better known and appreciated to citizens' demands, including for greater transparency and democracy in the union. while the constitutional treaty as a whole has been a successful meeting point, it should be remembered that a good compromise involves both the acceptance of certain points of view and the renunciation of others. let's not forget that when we talk about getting our hands on the 2004 text: no one can think of shifting the balance of the compromise reached to his own advantage. opening a new negotiation can mean opening a pandora's box, risking a fresh start, and starting a confrontation with unpredictable results and timing. eighteen of the 27 member states have ratified the treaty, representing 275 million european citizens: they deserve respect for having kept the commitment they signed in rome. it is clear, of course, that the majorities expressed in the opposite direction in the french and dutch referendums must also be respected and that all possible clarifications must therefore be sought as to the concerns which gave rise to those opposing pronouncements. but it is time for europe to break the deadlock. and it cannot seriously be argued that the union does not need, after the great enlargement, a redefinition of the whole framework of its values and objectives and a reform of its institutional structures. working on a draft constitution for europe was not a formality, a whim or a luxury: the european union has responded to a profound need of europe at this historic moment. nor can the europe of projects or results be proposed today as an alternative vision and strategy. it is true that the union has not stood still in the last two years. it has given the greatest proof of what it could represent on the international scene when it has managed to speak with one voice on the war in lebanon, promoting a new and challenging mission for peace in that region and throughout the middle east. alongside this renewed political initiative, the budget for this period includes the definition of some important directives, with the substantial contribution of the european parliament through the powers of the codecision procedure, and the agreement to a limited strengthening of the meagre financial perspective for 2007-13. but, ladies and gentlemen, in the way of achieving results, the current institutional framework does not allow us to go very far. it is certainly important to develop and outline the lines of new common policies: the commission has recently done the same for environmental and energy problems, which have now exploded in all their acuteness with climate change and the tensions over the supply of oil and gas. however, we know from long experience that commission documents, communications and even legislative proposals can lead to little or no progress: the european parliament has been a major player in the process of european integration. we also know that the creation of the single currency was not followed by the economic governance that would have been necessary to ensure the effective achievement of the objectives formulated in the grand plan of the lisbon strategy. so what is the key to making projects viable and to really growing a europe of results? the strength of institutions and political commitment is decisive. it is crucial for the union to have institutions that are stronger than the resistance of those member states that remain more closed in defence of anachronistic prerogatives and self-serving national presumptions. the principle of subsidiarity to the award of public contracts. it can rather be argued that it has innovated too little to adapt its operating rules and decision-making procedures to the challenge of social sphere and they are affected by changes in the climate. often these are countries which have not yet or only insufficiently participated in sustainable development. we find that previous approaches to help people in these countries to have a better perspective for their lives have not been successful or have not been sufficiently successful. budgetary assistance - this is the subject of this own-initiative report - is today one of the recognised instruments of european union development cooperation. over 20% of edf resources with a rising trend are already being spent in this way. if the framework is right, budgetary assistance can be an effective instrument of development cooperation. this instrument allows donors and beneficiaries to take a partnership approach to development cooperation, but it must be genuinely desired by both parties, since the donor's funds are left to the beneficiary for its own use without preconditions. the condition is that the beneficiary agrees to support development strategies and programmes, in particular comprehensive poverty reduction strategies. donors and beneficiaries agree to review the success of this support on the basis of a variety of performance indicators. the european commission has found an approach which has received much attention and also much support, by dividing the promised benefits into fixed and variable tranches and making the payment of the variable tranches dependent on the target fulfilment of the beneficiary. i see in principle a great value and advantage of this instrument in the opening of a general policy dialogue between donors and recipients. the actors who ultimately negotiate the budgetary support with the beneficiary are given access to and influence over the beneficiary's policies and budget. this will enable all major policy areas and measures to be developed and reviewed jointly with partners willing to cooperate. we must now ask ourselves in the european parliament how this advantage is reflected in our work, for example when we discuss commission strategy papers. will it also change our knowledge or influence on development cooperation? can we better account for the use of our development aid and report better results of our aid, now and in the future? have we developed sufficient expertise in the use of this instrument? the evaluation of the oecd/dac evaluation network on the example of seven countries, which has been available since may last year, warns against cautious assessment because it is too early to really assess this new instrument of budgetary assistance. we must also be clear about when budgetary aid should not be used or withdrawn. on the donor side, no one should be tempted to think that budgetary aid is a good thing because it could serve to accelerate the outflow of funds and thus boast the reputation of being an effective donor at international level, while upholding the principle of ownership in favour of the recipient side. it must never be about the flow of funds or the correct use of funds. the effectiveness of budget support must also always be assessed in the light of whether it actually achieves the desired objectives better than other means. the budget support instrument cannot be used if the recipient side does not manage public expenditure in a sufficiently transparent, accountable and efficient manner, if there is no defined overall economic policy or sectoral policy, defined by the country itself and agreed by the main donors, and if public procurement is not open and transparent. article 61 (2) of the cotonou agreement, which i have just quoted word for word, is clear in this respect. only if these conditions are met will direct budgetary support be granted for support or sectoral reforms. it is also interesting that budget support must be linked to a reform process. there is no budgetary support for a 'further so'. i believe that part of the reform process is to develop a tradition of accountability in these countries and therefore involve the parliaments and the supreme audit authorities in the evaluation. this is an important point for us parliamentarians in particular in our cooperation with our colleagues in these countries. i hope that with this report and with this evaluation we will reach a stage where we can intensify the dialogue, particularly in those countries where we think the commission is a little careless, in order to finally arrive at a clear position as to whether budgetary aid is really the best instrument for those concerned.

been taken into account. finally, i would like to thank the finnish and german presidencies of the council and the commission for their expertise in the project and for their smooth cooperation. we need this revision of the directive. in the past, more than once, individual companies have failed to acquire crossborder holdings or to make whole acquisitions. the reason for this was that there was no clear legal framework requiring supervisory authorities to apply uniform audit criteria and therefore a uniform procedure throughout europe. this is about to change. the draft directive presented by the commission last autumn aims to provide greater legal certainty, clear predictability and clarity in the decision-making process. this is a matter on which all the parties concerned agree and which we have therefore supported. all three institutions - the commission, the council and the parliament - believe that we must move in this direction and that we need maximum harmonisation to create a real level playing field for all market players in all member states of the european union. however, there were of course - how could it be otherwise - differences of opinion on one or other point, especially as regards the period of examination or also as regards the alternatives to action when a negative decision is taken, i.e. when a wish to acquire a holding or even to take over an entire company is rejected. but in the end, the negotiations were able to resolve these problems and we were able to reach a consensus. in future, therefore, crossborder consolidation will be facilitated increasingly in the area of credit institutions, insurance companies and also investment firms. this is mainly due to the following four reasons: first, supervisors will in future have a maximum of 60 days to decide on an increase in participation. the examination period may be interrupted only once for the purpose of requesting additional information, namely for 20 days in the case of a potential acquirer from a member state of the european union and for 30 days in the case of a third country acquirer. such a distinction between eu and non-eu companies takes into account the fact that the supervisory and market structures in third countries are often not identical to those in the european union and that, therefore, the european authorities are not always fully informed about the situation in these countries. therefore, it is necessary to allow supervisors more time to request and evaluate specific information. at the same time, these third country companies also require more time to prepare, translate and submit such information. both are ensured by differentiation of the interruption period without infringement of wto rules. secondly, the five test criteria are clear and conclusive. in doing so, member states shall have the possibility to define, on the basis of these criteria, the specific list of information to be provided by the prospective acquirer. information is required than in the case of complex, possibly cross-sectoral, acquisitions. two years after the entry into force of this directive, the commission is to check whether the various information requirements in the member states are relatively similar or whether there is a divergence here, and then perhaps the commission will have to intervene and make sure that we do not have divergences. thirdly, the supervisory authorities are encouraged the commissioner has pointed out to cooperate closely. at the same time, it is clearly stated that the final decision is taken by the supervisory authority of the target company. in the event of a negative vote, the authority with final jurisdiction must also state the reasons for the refusal. publication of the reasons is not mandatory but may be required of the undertaking whose acquisition intention is rejected. it is also possible for individual member states to publish the reasons in accordance with national law. deputy writer. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. i can follow directly what mrs berès has said. the two oral questions are essentially about the same thing. the takeover directive is what it is because there is no one share, one vote in europe. you have to say it clearly. it is also because it was not possible at the this house or in the council. the report now presented by the commission on the implementation of the takeover directive is, in my view, being misinterpreted in the public debate. it describes nothing but the fact that member states have, on the whole, properly implemented the directive, including making use of the options offered by the directive. that was the very purpose of this legislation. the commission will present its first report on the application of the transposition directive in 2011/2012 as laid down in the transposition directive. we are then at a point where we can draw conclusions from this, whether what we have done here, setting a benchmark and leaving it to market forces, has been successful or not, or whether it is then necessary to think about further legislation or not. but not until 2011 or 2012, not now, when the first concrete report on the application of the directive is available. we - parliament and the council - have, by the way, already made our position clear in a number of the subjects discussed today - including the transposition directive - as legislators, with a large majority in each case. we have said that the so-called breakthrough rule, which is the decisive benchmark, should cover all pre-bid and post-bid defenses. there have, of course, been some exceptions. we have left out the aspects which do not constitute barriers to adoption, on the basis of simple calculation examples and simple mathematical figures. the first is the so-called preference shares, which have been exempted from the breakthrough rule from the outset. why would you do that? first, because preferred stock is compensated by paying the holders of those shares a higher amount of money than others. secondly, because they are limited by company law to a maximum of 50% of the capital, so they can never commit more capital than the actual ordinary shares with voting rights. we also excluded the french double voting rights from the breakthrough rule for similar reasons. firstly, because it is not a question of voting rights for a particular class, guaranteed in perpetuity, so to speak, but of rewarding longterm investment and, after a certain period, automatically converting those voting rights into ordinary voting rights. secondly, because in the light of the breakthrough rule, when 75% is reached - that is normally the quorum for a breakthrough to be achieved - it is irrelevant whether it is double voting rights or simple voting rights. i always have a majority in the general meeting. that is why we have excluded these voting rights. but we have included in the breakthrough rule multiple voting rights and voting rights limitations because these are real barriers to takeover. we have the particular situation here, too, that we have a disconnect between ownership on the one hand and domination, or voting majority, on the other. we considered it justified to make this subject to the breakthrough rule where companies or member states make use of this option. i would like to make it clear once again - mrs berès has also mentioned this - that we have been very clear in the szejna report that we want to see the market forces unfold first, that we want to see how this directive works and that when the commission has presented the first report in 2011/2012 we want to decide whether further steps are necessary. i have now heard that the commission is toying with the idea of launching a recommendation on this subject. i want to be quite frank about this: i'm not very enthusiastic about this for two reasons. the first point is that we in parliament are generally increasingly sceptical about the application of such a soft law. the commission is also running the risk that parliament will take up such a recommendation in the form of an own-initiative report and then write something quite different into that own-initiative report than what the commission has envisaged in its recommendation. if that happens, the recommendation is worthless, because a recommendation only has effect if it can be assumed that the legislator is prepared to support such a regulation later in a further procedure. but if he says no, the recommendation is worthless. the second reason is that i am not entirely clear as to what is to be regulated in such a recommendation. we have adopted in article 10 of the merger directive extensive transparency rules requiring all companies to disclose fully all existing obstacles to takeovers. these are strict transparency rules. i wonder what else the recommendation is going to regulate. there is another reason for this request, and that was also mentioned in the text of the legal affairs committee's request. we are naturally interested in the commission's assessment of the development which has occurred as a result of the advocate general's closing arguments in the volkswagen case. this was the first time that the advocate general had to deal with a case which was not a classic case of golden shares, but one which involved restrictions on voting rights and other rules. but he considers it to be in breach of contract, much like a golden share. we are not going to be able to do that. doesn't that automatically remove all obstacles? it would be interesting to have an assessment from the commission.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission is not the principle of 'one share, one vote' is extremely attractive in the context of so-called shareholder democracy. deviations from this idea could - as the commissioner responsible, mr mcgreevy, feared - undermine transparency and restrict shareholder rights. however, a deviation does not necessarily have to be harmful, as it can lead to more competition and innovation and also accommodate the different interests and behaviours of different types of shareholders. the commission now plans to publish a recommendation on the proportionality principle between ownership and control in the autumn, based on the results of a comprehensive study. mr lehne has already pointed out the problematic nature of this recommendation, and i think mrs berès has rightly suggested that a study commissioned by iss, the european corporate government institute and sherman & sterling may not be as objective as this case actually requires. i therefore call on the commission to submit concrete proposals only after a comprehensive and objective examination of the situation in europe and after a critical evaluation of all the experience gained with the takeover directive. it is important to consider the advantages and disadvantages of all mechanisms which deviate from the principle of 'one share, one vote', whether it be the pyramid structures in italy, the preference shares in germany, the double voting rights in france or the a and b shares in the nordic countries. we must carefully distinguish and balance between the desire to make shareholder control proportional to ownership on the one hand and the desire of companies for contractual freedom, stable shareholder structures and sufficient freedom of action on the other. in any case, it must be ensured that any deviation from the principle of 'one share, one vote' is transparent. the shareholder has the right to know whether or not he owns or acquires shares which restrict his participation in the direction of the company and his control over management.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thanks to the work of your rapporteur, mr el khadraoui, and the members of the committee on transport, the european parliament has
