ago between american and european negotiators in brussels. in less than ten days i will submit this draft agreement to the transport ministers of the european union for political decision. you are speaking at a crucial moment and you can thus make the voice of the european citizens heard, not only in the council but in the american institutions themselves. these negotiations have been long and complex. four years of negotiations since the court's rulings in the so-called open skies cases. eleven negotiating sessions that have caused waves and air holes. but this long negotiation can help us to strengthen the transatlantic relationship and bring positive elements to the lisbon strategy. what is within our reach is the possibility for a european airline to fly from any point in europe to any destination in the united states, freely, and regardless of the nationality of the european airline. today, if you want to fly between brussels and washington, you can only borrow an american airline or a belgian airline. since the sabena went bankrupt, with no belgian carrier on this route, you can only fly to washington with an american company. that is why the court of justice has declared these bilateral agreements illegal. these agreements discriminate against our european companies on the basis of nationality. with this agreement, we are changing the game. the united states recognizes the european nature of our companies. too often we forget that not everyone flies to the united states. sixteen countries have open skies agreements, but eleven do not. you cannot fly directly from the baltic countries to the united states and the number of routes to the united states from spain, ireland and greece, in particular, is severely limited. we will thus open up new possibilities for these countries. but from the outset, the balance of the agreement between europe and the united states has been a problem. in november 2005, the council welcomed the progress made, progress in the approximation of european and us rules on state aid, competition, security, progress in terms of market access, but the council also called for more access to the us market. i want to explain why, at the end of the last round of negotiations, this agreement is more favourable to europe. i shall not go into the details of the freedoms of air transport, the fifth freedom, the seventh freedom, as they result from the 1944 chicago convention. they're important, but they're technical. any technician will see that in terms of these so-called freedoms, the european union has got more than it has given. i shall concentrate on the problems of ownership, investment and capital of airlines. first, the investment in the united states. the us law, which congress will not be reviewing any time soon due to intense political controversy, states that a foreigner cannot own more than 25% of the voting shares of an american company and cannot control it. under both of these constraints, we have secured for european investors the right to hold more than 50% of the total capital, without, however, this being presumed to constitute control of the company. and we've gotten the u.s. authorities to process investments fairly and quickly, expeditiously. we have also secured the right for european investors to enter into franchise agreements. lufthansa will be able to affix its name, its brand, its colours, sell its know-how to an american company for domestic transport in the united states. this is not a theoretical arrangement. the virgin group, which freely sells its books or cds in new york, is currently trying to sell its brand to create virgin america in san francisco. the operation has encountered serious obstacles. the commitments made by the united states clarify what can be done precisely for this type of investment. compared to the american reform, which failed in 2006 after strong opposition and which some of you have followed closely, the rights we have negotiated cannot be called into question. these new rights are etched in the marble of the agreement and will not be subject to unilateral changes in the united states. that's it for the investment in the united states. secondly, the investment in europe by the americans. since the united states cannot change its 25% rule, we have reserved the option of limiting american investment in european companies to the same amount. it's a rebalancing move. thirdly, investment by europeans in third countries. under the current rules, we cannot invest in and control a third country company without risking its rights to trade into the united states. example: virgin invested in nigeria. the united states disapproved of virgin nigeria's operations to the united states because the company no longer has the proper nationality. with our agreement, the united states will no longer be able to object to community investment in european countries outside the european union, for example switzerland, or in eighteen african countries. there will be no retaliation from the americans on this point. they will accept that these third country companies may be the object of significant investment by european companies. fourthly, the investment of third countries in european companies. the united states will not be able to interfere with community airlines flying to the united states if european countries such as iceland invest in their capital. this will help to attract european investment to our airlines and to standardise the air transport industry. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, this agreement is more balanced and more balanced for the benefit of europe. we must not miss this first step, because it is a matter of taking a first step before taking a second step towards the ultimate goal of an open space for aviation. certainly, some critics of the agreement fear that there will never be a second phase because the united states will have won in every respect in the first phase, which is not true. you are right to ask for a mechanism to ensure that we can move to the second stage: well, i have got it! the negotiations will start in january 2008 at the latest. if we do not reach a second stage agreement by mid-2010, we may suspend elements of the agreement. beyond retaliation, i am personally convinced that the dynamic we will unleash will overcome the last remaining resistance to ownership and control. we did not do the internal market all at once. we did it in three stages, but in less than ten years. so, ladies and gentlemen, these eleven negotiating sessions have really made progress. what is at stake behind this agreement? that's in five years, between six and twelve billion euros of economic benefit. it is also conceivable that in the next five years, 80 000 jobs will be created on both sides of the atlantic, and that 26 million passengers will have the opportunity to travel between europe and the united states, in addition to the 50 million passengers who already use transatlantic flights. so in five years, the number of passengers will probably go from 50 million to 75 million. these estimates are the result of serious studies. i therefore conclude by saying, ladies and gentlemen, that this agreement is obviously important and can be of great interest to europe. i would like to add that this morning's session will also help me to understand your expectations better, to answer any questions you may have, and i would say again that i am confident that we can take this first step and have the assurance that the second step is now also in sight. that, ladies and gentlemen, is the information i wanted to give you.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the epp-ed group warmly congratulates you, your negotiating team and daniel calleja crespo on the successful conclusion of this first part of the important us air transport agreement. but let us also thank the us negotiating team and john byerly, because it was not easy for him to bring these negotiations to a successful conclusion. we 're sure of it . the agreement will finally create a large transatlantic air transport market for the benefit of airlines and passengers. european airlines can now fly to the american market from all parts of the european union without national restrictions. at the same time, we are also living up to the judgment of the european court of justice in 2002. the restrictions on london heathrow airport, which are contrary to community law, will also have to be lifted. the open skies over the atlantic will also surely result in cheap deals for air passengers. the agreement is balanced because the commission has succeeded in opening up market access for european airlines in the usa for the first time. it could have been more in the opening, but still. we have new rules on ownership and control, licensing and trademark policy. i think that these advantages make it justifiable to say that this is now a balanced agreement. i think it is even more important that we have set up a joint committee with the participation of the business community, because this can prevent the americans or the europeans from taking unilateral security measures in the future to the detriment of airlines and passengers. the epp-ed group calls on the german presidency to ensure that this compromise is quickly approved by the council. that would be symbolic. i would like to thank our friend el khadraoui for the excellent resolution which i believe we will adopt tomorrow by a large majority in the spirit of what we have discussed.

the president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery poses perhaps the greatest potential risk to international security. that is why the european union, in its 2003 comprehensive strategy against weapons of mass destruction, underlined that a multilateral approach, including both disarmament and non-proliferation, is the best way to maintain security and international order in this field. in this context, the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons is and remains the key cornerstone of the global nuclear non-proliferation regime. the european union supports the npt provisions and endorses and supports measures to further strengthen them. the european union has already undertaken extensive internal preparatory work with a view to the first meeting of the preparatory committee for the 2010 review conference of this treaty. we are determined to continue to play an active and constructive role in the discussions to be held in the context of the preparatory conference in 2007. our aim for the european union is to start the review cycle in a constructive climate. the european union therefore expressly supports the plans of the designated chairman of the first preparatory committee, ambassador amano of japan. the european union considers that this review debate must take account of all three pillars of the npt, namely nuclear non-proliferation, disarmament and the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, in a balanced way. only such a balance will allow the forthcoming cycle of the review of the npt to proceed successfully. but this is the precondition for joint decisions by the review conference to strengthen the treaty. the common position of the european union adopted at the 2005 review conference remains the basis of these balanced eu positions. the early entry into force of the nuclear nonproliferation treaty has always been an important concern of the european union. this concern has been heightened by the north korean nuclear test. the european union is already contributing to supporting the nuclear test-stop regime by adopting joint actions which are also intended to further strengthen the verification system of the treaty. the european union also calls for the early opening of negotiations on a treaty prohibiting the production of fissile material for explosive purposes. such negotiations should be conducted without preconditions. the conclusion of such a treaty would be an essential step towards nuclear arms control and disarmament. it would thus make a decisive contribution to the implementation of the positions adopted jointly by the community at the 1995 and 2000 review conferences. the full and committed implementation of all the obligations of this treaty remains an essential prerequisite for consolidating and strengthening the provisions of the npt. in this context, particular attention should be paid to regional aspects. as you know, the european union is actively involved in the efforts to resolve the crisis over the iranian nuclear programme. we are convinced that a solution can only be reached through diplomatic means. for this reason, the european union played a key role in shaping the very broad offer to iran in june 2006, and - i stress this - it was supported by the united states, russia and china. the european union will continue to work for a peaceful solution to the crisis. the european union is aware of the risks which may arise from the further spread of enrichment and reprocessing technology and therefore supports the development of multilateral guarantees for the supply of nuclear fuel. initiatives in this field can help to convince countries interested in developing nuclear energy that there is no need to develop their own nuclear fuel cycle, so that they voluntarily abandon it. the european union will intensify its efforts to maintain and further strengthen the provisions of the non-proliferation treaty in order to meet the challenges identified here. this includes the discussion, largely initiated by the european union, on strengthening the treaty in view of the consequences of withdrawal. it is regrettable that the 2005 review conference on the treaty was unable to agree on a substantive final document to address the most pressing challenges of the treaty. this experience must be an additional reason for the european union to put all its efforts into a successful review process in 2010.
member of the commission. mr president, president-in-office of the council, honourable members, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and among them nuclear weapons, is potentially the iaea inspectors as part of this accord and i share his assessment that this is a crucial confidence-building process. i hope that the shutdown of the yongbyon plant goes ahead by mid-april. the 1970 treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons (npt) established the non-proliferation regime as we know it – with its fundamental balance between nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation and the peaceful use of nuclear energy. from it then followed several aspects which are of great importance to the european union, namely the principle of regulated nuclear trade, nuclear safeguards and the international atomic energy agency, which monitors compliance. strengthening the effectiveness of the npt will make the world safer. states parties should be encouraged to work towards this aim with a view to the upcoming review conference. while the headlines have focused on the regime’s difficulties, we should not underestimate its successes. south africa, argentina, brazil, south korea and libya, for example, have all decided to forego nuclear weapons programmes. my recent visit to india also gave me an opportunity to stress to the indian leadership our hope that india will come much closer to the npt regime and join the comprehensive test ban treaty. we are looking forward to civil nuclear cooperation with india, once the necessary preconditions are met. these developments should also increase pakistan’s willingness to cooperate with the international community in the non-proliferation context. nuclear non-proliferation is an area in which the commission makes an important contribution. since 1957, the euratom treaty has provided the commission with wide-ranging responsibilities. the commission’s safeguard activities are closely coordinated with the iaea, freeing up its resources to be deployed to more troublesome regions of the world. we are also playing our part in ensuring that the eu’s nuclear export controls are as robust as possible, supporting the dual-use regulation 1334 from the year 2000. we also assist third states in enhancing their export controls and combating illicit trafficking in nuclear and radiological materials. the commission is also a major provider of assistance for international non-proliferation efforts. one important example is the g8 global partnership against weapons of mass destruction, where one billion euros have been pledged for assistance in the former soviet union, 400 million of which have already been spent. for more than 25 years the commission’s joint research centre has been working closely with the iaea, providing it with scientific and technological support. as i said, in the future we will do more. under the new instrument for stability we will have resources to continue and strengthen work to enhance our security against nuclear proliferation threats. in closing, let me take the opportunity to thank this parliament once again for the support it has given the commission in setting up a new generation of non-proliferation assistance programmes through a series of pilot projects. chapters. the european council in madrid in december last year stressed the importance of the european union's role in the world, and called for the establishment of a european union with a stronger political will and a stronger political will. the second chapter is devoted to the main features of european unification and cooperation: the equal rights and obligations of the member states, and transparency and subsidiarity as fundamental elements of the community method. the third chapter is to be of crucial importance in relation to our core values on which european unification is based. in particular, it should be emphasised that the human person, whose dignity is inviolable, is at the centre of all political action. i also stressed this at the summit dinner with the heads of state and government, where we discussed this last thursday evening. the human being is the starting point and the goal of politics. the principle of solidarity should also be an important feature. it is an indispensable element of the european unification process and, in the present view, a present and current challenge in the energy sector. finally, a fourth chapter will identify the challenges of the future, such as energy policy, climate change, european foreign and security policy, internal security and civil rights, and the preservation of a social responsibility approach through greater economic success. in view of the berlin declaration and the ensuing debate on the future of the constitutional treaty, we as the european parliament must leave no doubt: the european parliament is the constitutional treaty. we want the substance of the constitutional treaty, including the chapter on values, to become a legal and political reality. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. since 1999, the european parliament has been deliberating on legislative proposals in the field of migration without a decision-making basis in the form of figures. the scope of immigration policy has been considerably extended. we therefore need more and better information to plan, implement, evaluate and monitor policies effectively. the commission, under the leadership of mr franco frattini, has responded to the european parliament's call and has presented a draft regulation on the statistical recording of migration movements. this is necessary because, on the current voluntary basis, member states do not supply statistical material or only partially do. in addition, data are collected differently and are thus not comparable. this regulation obliges our member states to supply the figures which are absolutely necessary. in addition, we achieve a harmonization so that the figures are comparable. the council's approach was relatively difficult, while in the european parliament all parties were convinced of the need for the regulation. the broad consensus of all the political groups also enabled parliament's position to be adopted in the comitology area. the excellent cooperation with all the shadow rapporteurs, to whom i would like to express my sincere thanks, has been instrumental in bringing this important dossier to a satisfactory conclusion. i want to thank you again for that.

(applause) last weekend, the europe of the past and the europe of the future met in berlin. as the declaration states, we celebrated 50 years of achievement in europe: peace, freedom and solidarity, and prosperity beyond the dreams of even the most optimistic founding father of europe. by one of those fortunate historical coincidences, we celebrated our unity in berlin, the city that was the symbol of a divided europe and is now a symbol of this new, enlarged, united europe, with 27 member states and almost 500 million citizens. the celebrations in berlin were a very inspiring moment for europe. i speak for many who were there when i say that we felt the european spirit among us. the berlin declaration proved worthy of the occasion, recommitting european institutions and member states to european values and european goals for the 21st century. i was delighted that the declaration, a proposal made by the commission in may 2006, became such a fitting centrepiece for the celebrations. i wish to congratulate chancellor merkel and the german presidency on the crucial role they played in this great european success. chancellor merkel, i believe that your personal commitment to it, your personal history and your understanding of the importance of freedom for your country and for europe was decisive in creating that spirit among all the leaders in berlin. two points. let me start by emphasising the success of the twin-track strategy. taken together, the two european councils in march represented the twin-track strategy in action. the spring european council demonstrated the commitment to delivering results in the area of energy and the fight against climate change. the berlin declaration showed the commitment to agreeing on an institutional settlement before the 2009 european elections. this shows that it is wrong to see conflict between a pragmatic approach and a political vision. on the contrary, this commitment to a twin-track strategy is the right one. on the one hand it will deliver results and recreate the political momentum to settle the institutional problem. on the other hand, in order to deliver still better results, we really need more efficient, more democratic and more coherent institutions. a europe of results is a political vision based on constructive pragmatism, designed to address the concerns of our citizens and to provide european solutions for european problems. we also need a treaty settlement because of the great global challenges that europe faces in the coming years. only together, in a more effective way, can the european union tackle the challenges of the globalised world. it is obvious that even the biggest member states cannot tackle climate change, energy security or mass migration alone. they cannot respond alone to the increased competitiveness of this global economy. we need to do it together in a true spirit of solidarity. i believe this is the message from berlin and that this message has now been translated into an equal commitment to find a solution to the institutional question before the 2009 elections. (applause)there is another reason why the commission strongly supports a rapid but ambitious institutional settlement. there is no doubt that the failure of the ratification process of the constitutional treaty leaves a permanent shadow of doubt hanging over the european union. even when there are significant results, such as those achieved at the spring european council, there is always this doubt, this negativism, this pessimism, this scepticism. we are always confronted with a question that deserves to be answered: ‘how can you convince us’, the most sceptical ask, ‘that you are serious about addressing those global issues when you are not even able to settle matters relating to your own rules and to the institutions in which you are working?’ what credibility do the european union institutions and european leaders have when they fail to come to a consensus on those issues? i therefore believe that we need progress in this regard. failure to agree on an institutional settlement will cause divisions which could threaten our common values. european history should remind us that we can never take the great achievements of peace, democracy, freedom and solidarity for granted. nobody should take those achievements for granted. we need permanently to nurture our progress in terms of politics and values. if we are to preserve and protect those common values – those we have named in our declaration, the inviolable dignity of the individual, freedom, justice and solidarity: all those values that make us not just a market but a political community and a union – we need to reform the institutions of our community of law. the preservation of our common values is a permanent work in progress, which i call the ‘unfinished european adventure’. to have a better europe, we need better institutions to deliver better results. i think the political will is there and we must now produce results in that area too. during the informal summit after our celebration, i asked member states to keep up the momentum during the coming months. i asked for the active cooperation of national governments. all member states signed the treaty, which was impossible to ratify as a result of two negative popular votes. however, the commitment undertaken obliges all member states to work in a constructive manner for a joint solution. as president of the european commission, it is my responsibility to call on national governments to make a special effort in the coming months and to support the german presidency in its very important efforts to reach a solution. (applause)let me repeat the message that i sent to the european heads of state and government and in berlin. it is important for the future of the european union to understand that when we speak about europe, it is not just about the european institutions: the european commission or the european parliament in brussels or strasbourg. i said during that ceremony, at which some of you were present, that the european union is not a foreign power invading our countries, it is our common project. europe is not ‘them’, it is ‘us’. i said to the heads of state and government that it is tempting but dishonest for national politicians to take all the credit and give brussels all the blame. let us resist that temptation. the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in your contribution you have just addressed a number of important questions also in relation to financial services. i can assure you that the council attaches the utmost importance to this aspect. i would like to reiterate that the european financial system is also seen as an important contribution to the lisbon strategy and plays a crucial role in consolidating the framework for financial stability in the european union. the aim is to improve the efficiency of financial supervision without imposing excessive supervisory burdens on the financial sector. this too should not restrict competition. let me draw attention to three main points in the council conclusions mentioned above. firstly, the council has stressed the importance of fair and non-discriminatory national supervisory practices in order to create a level playing field in the european union. at the same time, however, it has also stressed the importance of a proper balance between the obligations of the home country and those of the host country. the importance of adequate and independent financial supervision for ensuring financial stability was also reiterated. secondly, the council has asked the three level 3 committees to take into account in their efforts to achieve convergence of rules and practices the obstacles identified in their work and reports, as well as the report of the financial services committee on supervisory convergence. the aim is to develop common formats for reporting by financial institutions to supervisors in order to avoid duplication of costs. thirdly, the council supported the commission's intention to ensure that competition and aid rules are also respected within the limits of its powers. the council considered it a priority to promote the work of the three level 3 committees. to do this, they need appropriate monitoring tools. the council conclusions of may 2006 also contain a comprehensive short and medium-term action programme in this area, based on a report by the financial services committee. a milestone is the thorough revision of the supervisory rules for banks, insurance companies and investment firms. these will put supervisory cooperation on a new footing, which will be beneficial to financial stability and the competitiveness of our financial sector. the afd report identified three challenges that suggested that further action was needed. i believe that these challenges are particularly relevant for the period immediately ahead. first, there is a need to further strengthen convergence and cooperation in the area of supervision. secondly, the efficiency of the supervisory system must be increased and thirdly, international supervision must be improved in view of the increase in cross-border financial groups. in view of these challenges, the action programme approved by the council last may combines several instruments. these aim to promote the emergence of a european supervisory culture and a procedure for mediation and delegation, as well as arrangements for electronic data exchange and common reporting formats. i note that the muscat report also emphasized the latter aspect at the european parliament level. i welcome the agreement of the two sides here. the financial services committee has been asked to monitor in particular the progress made by the three level 3 committees in implementing the different instruments. the afd has also been entrusted with the task of monitoring the convergence of supervisory powers at an appropriate level. i know that the commission is also paying close attention to these aspects and i am confident that the european parliament will also promote this process in its dialogue with the level 3 committees. further findings are to be expected from the work of the interinstitutional monitoring group. i would like to turn now to the long-term perspective and the question of the approach to supervisory issues. in addition to the existing challenges already mentioned, afd must also take into account the issues arising from market developments when setting long-term strategic priorities. in this context, the afd has recently set up a new subgroup which will present a report on long-term supervisory issues by autumn 2007. this new strand of work will be based on the following bottom-up approach: further fundamental changes in supervisory tasks should only be made on the basis of identified problems. i would also like to emphasise that the general issue of supervisory convergence must be seen in the context of the consolidation of markets and financial institutions. i am therefore particularly pleased that the european parliament and the council were able to agree in march on a text primarily on the financial participation directive. this is a clear sign of our shared commitment to improving the eu framework for the day-to-day work of our supervisory authorities. in conclusion, i would like to stress the following: in these areas we must take account of all the challenges facing the eu institutions. these include strengthening financial stability through supervisory arrangements and procedures and promoting european competitiveness. both are intended to facilitate the consolidation of our financial economy. it must be carried out in a process which is also conducive to the protection of consumer interests. the council is cooperating with the commission on all these aspects and we also welcome the strong interest of the european parliament, which is also evident in this debate. i would like to thank you very much for your commitment to further progress.
member of the commission. mr president, honourable members, the european financial sector has changed dramatically over the last few years. capital markets have expanded and are increasingly integrated. new investment techniques have emerged. the consolidation of the banking sector has accelerated. pan-european conglomerates now play a major role on all national markets. these changes are positive for the efficiency of our financial industry and should be welcomed. but they also present new challenges to policymakers. we must ensure that our arrangements for financial supervision are adapted to the needs of a more integrated eu financial sector. this is vital for financial stability and for the competitiveness of our industry. greater cooperation and convergence between european supervisors is of utmost importance in this context. it has been one of my priorities since i joined the commission and will remain so until the end of my mandate. let me briefly recall what the commission has already done to foster a more effective and efficient supervisory system in europe. under the lamfalussy process it has created european committees of supervisors in the areas of securities, banking and insurance. these committees have already led to greater supervisory cooperation and more convergence in supervisory practices. i expect them to continue and accelerate work in this regard. it is crucial for achieving coordination in crisis situations. the commission has pushed for more streamlined supervision of large financial institutions, in particular through the establishment of the consolidating supervisor concept in the capital requirements directives. the consolidating supervisor is responsible for ensuring proper information exchange between supervisors, central banks and finance ministries in the event of a crisis. his role is key and i therefore intend to propose further and more ambitious steps towards consolidating supervision in the area of insurance in the framework of the solvency ii project. in investment services, we have the principle of more central control, with some limited exceptions for branches. in order to deal more specifically with financial stability issues, my departments have set work in motion on five interconnected areas on which clarity is required if we want to improve our ability to respond to financial crisis. these are liquidity arrangements, crisis management, lender-of-last-resort issues, deposit guarantee schemes and the winding-up of financial institutions. there will be a commission conference on these matters on 26 june, in which mrs berès, as chairwoman of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, will also take part. the commission’s efforts have to be seen in conjunction with the work undertaken in the ecofin council. a crisis-simulation exercise took place in 2006. as a follow-up to that exercise, the council will reflect in 2007 on how better to address cross-border crisis situations and clarify burden-sharing arrangements. in addition, the financial services committee has initiated work on issues related to improvement of supervisory efficiency. the interinstitutional monitoring committee on the lamfalussy process will also complete its final report in 2007. i hope it will contain useful recommendations as to how the committees of supervisors can improve their work and deepen their cooperation. this would place them in an even better position to address possible financial stability issues in the future. towards the end of this year, the commission will also produce its own assessment of the way in which the lamfalussy process works. clearly, the functioning of the committees of supervisors will be a crucial aspect of this overall assessment. i look forward to hearing parliament’s views. i am convinced that through close cooperation between parliament, the council and the commission we can move this debate forward. conclusions will need to be drawn from the various ongoing activities. i am open to suggestions on how to go about this. i think, however, that it would be too early to create a committee of wise persons at this stage. i would rather await the completion of the different initiatives later this year before envisaging the next move. let me conclude. eu financial markets are strong. we do not have a broken supervisory system in need of repair. major progress has been made over the last few years in terms of modernising eu supervisory arrangements, but further improvements are also necessary. they are the consequence of integration. on this we are all agreed. we should continue our efforts to make the lamfalussy structure the regulatory vehicle for delivering the effective, efficient and converged supervision required by a single market in financial services. work has been set in motion in order to determine how the lamfalussy structure and our financial stability arrangements can be further improved to meet the demands that arise from closer european integration. i look forward to discussing with parliament in due course what precise initiatives may be required to respond to the problems that have been identified, so as to equip our european financial sector with the best possible supervisory system. this is critical, because top-class supervisory and regulatory structures are crucial for long-term eu capital market competitors in the global economy.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not prepared to accept this. it is good that mrs berès's question on the committee on economic and monetary affairs is being discussed and answered here today. this is a seamless follow-up to the muscat report, but also to yesterday's discussion in committee, including with you, commissioner! the crisis simulation to check the financial stability of the eu, which was presented at the ecofin meeting in helsinki last september, has indeed revealed deficits. this scenario constantly evolving financial instruments such as hedge funds and derivatives illustrates the need for further discussions that take consumer safety into account. we therefore need a system of functioning, interlinked supervisory rules and practices in the european union. consumer protection, but also the effectiveness of the financial sector and the stability of financial markets are the main objectives of financial supervision, while at the same time helping the economy to fulfil its potential and creativity. therefore, good supervision must be based on the risks involved and be based on principles rather than on detailed individual considerations. it must not be an additional burden on businesses, the rules must be developed in close contact with the financial sector and cross-border financial markets must be treated in the same way as pan-european and global markets. supervision should be limited to what is really necessary and meaningful. existing measures should be applied more carefully and in a market-friendly manner. unnecessary strain must be avoided. at the moment, i am firmly opposed to a european central bank operating in addition to and in parallel with national supervisory authorities, which would eliminate the principle of subsidiarity of the eu and lack any democratic legitimacy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. let us wait and see how the supervisory bodies of the newly formed 27 come together and do their work. we do not need a single, centralised supervisory structure, but a common supervisory culture based on common values and objectives.

resources is very important. your committee on budgets has adopted an original political approach. the report submitted to parliament is a first stage report. firstly, the subject is major: behind the political crisis, the union is experiencing an equally serious budgetary crisis. the agreement on the financial perspectives was achieved only at the cost of stagnation in the community budget, which guarantees the financing of the cap and aid to the new member states, but does not allow, for example, the financing of the transport network or that of galileo and allows almost nothing for the common foreign and security policy. we come to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the treaty of rome. we are delighted with the success of the union, a union ever closer launched by the treaty. we have the courage to recognize that in budgetary matters, for fifty years, the union has been less and less 'narrow': budgetary solidarity has not increased, it has even globally diminished. ten years ago, the european budget represented 1.17% of gdp, whereas today, it reaches barely 0.99% with the 2007 budget. the first treaties laid down the principle of financing community expenditure from community resources, that is to say from fiscal resources directly allocated to the union: either from national resources, as in the case of customs duties, or even from a genuine european tax, as in the case of the tax on the turnover of steel and coal-mining enterprises under the ecsc. some colleagues who are very concerned about national sovereignty seem to have completely forgotten that the treaties to which they have acceded, sometimes after a referendum, contained a european tax. but this tax no longer exists, it has not been renewed, and customs duties account for more than 10% of the union's resources. the main source of these resources is now the contributions from the national budgets, and this is the reason for the crisis in community finances. the only way to remedy this is to return to the letter and spirit of the treaty of rome, by supporting national budgets and financing community expenditure with new fiscal resources directly allocated to the coverage of this expenditure. conscious of the problem, the european leaders met in 2008-2009 to open up the whole dossier of the european budget, both in terms of resources and expenditure. this commitment is expressly set out in the agreement on the financial perspectives. the second is the original political approach. in view of the sensitive nature of the subject, the budget committee proposed to associate the finance committees of the national parliament, and this was the case from the very beginning of our work. in two years we have had four joint meetings and the rapporteur has visited the national capitals of half the member states. the objective is not to reach an agreement between all the parliaments. it would not be possible either legally or politically. there is no procedure for national parliaments to decide, but we can prepare the ground for the commission and the council, dispel misunderstandings, act as a point of convergence of views and common political orientations, and agree on the paths to be excluded and those to be studied. the report today is therefore a progress report, which aims to make the point of the subjects on which there is a fairly broad consensus with the interlocutors whom the national parliaments have delegated to us. this consensus is threefold: consensus on the diagnosis of the weaknesses of the present system, consensus on the political orientations of a reform, consensus on the content of a first phase which could begin fairly quickly and which would consist, first of all, in simplifying the present system. thus, instead of obeying rules which had become infinitely complex over the years, the contributions of the national budget were simply calculated on the basis of gdp. however, there is no consensus at present on the urgency or content of a second phase. or, for us, she is essential. it consists in choosing, among the existing fiscal resources, those which could progressively replace national contributions without aggravating the total burden on the taxpayer. at this stage, the progress report merely draws up a list of taxes which could be eligible for this allocation, without any recommendation being made. this will be the subject of a second report which i shall present at the end of the year, after a final interparliamentary conference on the subject has been announced by the portuguese presidency for 4 and 5 november next. mutual recognition between the arab countries and israel if the 1967 borders were to be completely withdrawn. this initiative, which has been discussed in various forums for several years, has not just been accepted completely by israel and is again on the table today, put there by the arab countries with greater energy and determination. as you know, we europeans were able to introduce the that is to say, a meeting with the palestinians and a meeting with israel. it would be the first time israel has met with the quartet. to this day israel has never met the quartet. the palestinians have, but israel has not yet. this is the programme of work we have for these months, very important months in which i know that the president of parliament is also going to travel to the region; coordinating the efforts we are going to make seems to me therefore absolutely essential. as during the question and answer part there will certainly be many in relation to the middle east, i would like to stop here in the peace process and say a few words about iran. i also had the opportunity to meet the iranian foreign minister, mr motaki, yesterday morning in riyadh. i made it clear and emphatically clear to him that the european union cannot accept the detention of the 15 british seamen by the iranian authorities. there is no reason for this, there is no illegality in this case, and the european union must stand in solidarity with the friends of the united kingdom for the release of these seamen. a few words on the nuclear programme: as you know, on the evening of saturday 24 march, while we were in berlin, the united nations security council unanimously adopted resolution 1747. resolution 1747 is the third resolution adopted unanimously by the security council on the subject of iran, in order to comply with its obligations, which are obligations arising from the vienna opinions or reports, which dr el baradei, as director of the international energy agency, has put to the vote of the governing council. i would like to say that it is very important that the vote at this last session was unanimously taken by the entire international community represented in the security council. the constitution of the security council today, here and now, is a constitution which, in principle, could have been more complex than the previous one in the context of understanding the iranian question. the united nations security council is currently made up of countries such as qatar, indonesia, a major islamic country, and south africa, which symbolically represents the non-aligned countries, as well as many other countries, five european countries in this case. i think we have an obligation to explain our position very clearly, so that there is no divergence between our understanding of the difficulty that the problem of non-proliferation presents to the world - not just to one type of country, but to the world in general - so that they understand it well and we can have a good debate with them, with the non-aligned countries or with countries like the ones i have just mentioned. it was a success that in such a short period of time this resolution could be adopted by consensus. it is a clear message, an obvious message to the iranian authorities that the nuclear programme they are pursuing must be a programme compatible with the resolutions of the security council. at the same time as the resolution was being published, a statement was made from berlin, which i made on behalf of the european members and also the permanent members of the security council, in which it was stated that we still believed that the best way to solve this problem with iran was through a political solution, and that we were prepared to start or continue negotiations; and that there was no other solution than a political solution. and so, 48 hours later, i had the opportunity to speak with dr. larajani, the interlocutor of the iranian side, not to solve the problem, not to start a negotiation or a pre-negotiation, but yes, at least, to convey that clear message from us, a message that was welcomed by dr. larajani. we hope that in the coming weeks we will have the opportunity to see how the iranian leadership has the wisdom not only to solve the problem they have with the united kingdom today but also to resume negotiations which can lead us to a final solution of this problem. there is no other way, ladies and gentlemen, than negotiation, and we must resume it as soon as possible. i think that the commission should be able to take a decision on this matter. as i have said, the issue of non-proliferation is beginning to be an issue that can divide the international community. nothing could be more serious than that there is a difference of opinion, a different conception depending on whether we are countries of the north or countries of the south, more developed or less developed countries, on an issue as vital as non-proliferation. therefore, we should make every effort to explain this well and to share our concerns with them. nonproliferation is not something that affects one or the other, it affects the world as a whole. it seems to me, ladies and gentlemen, that one of the fundamental obligations we have as europeans is to introduce the debate on non-proliferation in three different ways: firstly, non-proliferation itself. secondly, the disarmament issue: i think we have abandoned the disarmament issue for too long, putting the emphasis mainly on the issue of non-proliferation, without also putting it on what the non-proliferation treaty tells us; it also says that the powers which have nuclear capabilities must start thinking about how to disarm, so that nuclear weapons begin to disappear from our planet. we must therefore insist - and i think this is a fundamental value which europeans must understand very clearly - that the issue of disarmament is fundamental. thirdly, we must also bring the issue of technology transfer into this debate, which is what makes some countries feel that there is a double standard in the use of nuclear energy. i believe that making a package on these three issues, starting a serious negotiation with other countries beyond the borders of the european union, led by the european union, can be a great contribution of the european union to the construction of a world in peace and a world in which weapons begin not to be the way to solve problems and where the means for solving problems are the word, dialogue and the normal language, which is the language that the european union defends. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would also like to give you a brief account of the latest developments in the balkans, particularly in relation in writing. with today's agreement at first reading on medical devices, the big move to ban highly dangerous substances in medical devices has been missed. it is a sign of poverty that the blockade imposed by eu member states allows the continued use of carcinogens, mutagens and substances harmful to reproduction (cmrs), even when safe alternatives have been available for a long time. these clear limits on the use of risky soft pvc in ventilation tubes, stomach tubes and infusion devices are overdue. these contain high levels of the reproductive toxic emollient dehp, which is particularly dangerous for babies, children and dialysis patients. premature infants ingest up to 200 times the dose of dehp from tubes alone. the labelling of dangerous plasticizers is a promising development, allowing medical staff to use products without soft pvc. consumers can now actively demand this. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. in any case, this is only a temporary solution, because this week the eu commission finally recommended, on the basis of a risk assessment that has been available since 2001, to ban the use of dehp in medical devices for certain risk groups. this ban is long overdue, but better late than never. the eu commission is invited to submit a legislative proposal by the end of the year at the latest.

not only for the committee on fisheries but also for my group - and i would first of all like to thank all the rapporteurs for their work. the vote in committee will show that we are in agreement on all the dossiers, as will the vote in plenary tomorrow. we have heard that the council is not exactly happy about some of the decisions or votes of parliament, but that there is still some discussion to be had. the sterckx report shows how closely the individual dossiers are interwoven. it is of course good that the member states are now finally identifying emergency ports and emergency shelters. it is also good that in all the countries an independent body decides what actually happens after a crash, that there are no discussion forums, but that one decides. but it is, of course, inconceivable that in a shipwreck, the lifeboat comes and asks the captain, "are you insured?" the captain replies, "no, i'm sorry, but my shipowner didn't insure me properly", and the rescue crew says, "okay, let's leave it at that" and leave. of course, we need help here. the question of insurance must be asked to the port state control. this is also provided for in the vlasto report, on which we were able to reach agreement. where we have not been entirely agreed - dirk sterckx has already raised this - is the question of which fishing vessels should be equipped with which systems. this is about more security. i still believe that it makes little sense to equip vessels under 24 metres with ais systems and that the same results can be achieved by other means from land. the accident statistics are not very telling. we would then have to include all private vessels, not just small fishing vessels. but there may be other technical solutions in the future. a few remarks on port state control, which i also make on behalf of my colleague robert navarro, who cannot be here today. i think it is very sensible that we should abandon the rigid principle of controlling 25% of the ships. it was probably necessary at the time as a first step. but the control of 25% in each member state is less useful than what is now emerging, namely the concentration on high-risk vessels. that means you control the black sheep, so from the black sheep to the dark gray, gray to the light gray sheep. but controlling white sheep doesn't make much sense. this procedure certainly makes sense. the commission's proposals have not yet been adopted, although we have repeatedly called for it in the sterckx report and in the report by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection. everything that has to do with the so-called human factor - the social dimension, the good working conditions on board a ship - has an impact on ship safety. a ship certainly must not only be technically sound, but it must also be socially orderly. if not, then overall safety is compromised. we have said it many times here: 80% of accidents are due to human error. that is why we need more proposals from the commission on this human factor, including in the direction of safety checks. then the whole thing is complete.

the commission's vice-president president mauro, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to congratulate mrs lichtenberger on her very constructive report. the agreement on the common european aviation area is not the least of the challenges. the agreement was signed last june by 37 parties, which is probably an unprecedented number for an airline agreement. it is leading us to create a unique global network that will bring people, countries and cultures closer together. air transport in this respect plays a vital role in the integration and further development of europe as a whole. the agreement on the common european aviation area goes beyond the simple opening up of markets. it creates a unique space. it brings the whole of the balkan and south-eastern european countries into the european family. the air links facilitated by this agreement will not only be more numerous but also of better quality. these links will promote people-to-people exchanges, whether for trade or private travel, for example in the context of tourism, which is booming in most of the countries concerned. the commission has also taken note of the fact that the air transport sector is a key sector in the development of the eu. like the energy treaty for south-east europe, the agreement on the common european aviation area is a necessary step towards an ever closer union of europeans, which remains the union's deepest calling. it represents a key step towards establishing a single aviation area between the european union and its neighbours by 2010, together with the recent agreement with morocco and the negotiations which have just started with ukraine. the purpose of this agreement is clear and promising, but it is also necessary to emphasize the value of the method chosen. this method is based on two pillars. the first pillar is regulatory convergence, i.e. the harmonisation of european standards and rules in the field of air transport in such crucial areas as safety, security, competition, social policy, consumer rights and environmental protection. the harmonization of national and community legislation demonstrates the desire of the balkans to share the values and principles of the european union, and the level of regulatory convergence is unprecedented: all partners in this agreement have committed themselves to align their national legislation with community legislation. the second pillar is the creation of new opportunities through the opening up of markets. we are in the process of creating a single aviation market of 35 countries for over 500 million people, and this market is expanding rapidly. since 2001, air traffic between the european union and south-east europe has grown by almost 120%. this trend will accelerate with the full integration of a region which is forecasting growth in aircraft movements of 6% per year until 2011. the number of seats on flights between the european union and the balkans has increased from 12 million to 14 million since 2005. the benefits of this agreement are felt by all. for this venture to be successful, the commission must also rely on a third pillar: technical assistance. we intend to monitor the application of the legislation while providing the partners with the support they may need. and i will keep you informed, ladies and gentlemen, of the progress made and the evolution of the situation. i would like to thank your rapporteur, mrs lichtenberger, again for supporting this european initiative to create a common european aviation area. once again, mr president, the alliance between parliament and the commission is making it possible to achieve very important results in the general interest of europe.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank and congratulate the rapporteur, mr seeber, for his excellent work on the flood directive, and the whole environment committee for its positive contribution. i am particularly pleased with the rapid progress made both at first and second reading. the european parliament has played a very constructive role in reaching agreement on a very good text and i would like to extend those efforts. the aim of the proposal is to reduce the risks posed by floods to human health, economic activities and the environment. the text, in its present form, does indeed reflect these objectives and enables the european union to achieve them. the main features are as follows: the directive introduces a three-stage procedure, as mr seeber has already mentioned, which starts with the identification of areas where there is a potentially significant risk of flooding. the next step is to map expected floods under intermediate and extreme scenarios. the third stage concerns the preparation of flood risk management plans. these will be coordinated along entire river basins, basins shared by more than one country, and coastal areas. in addition, provision has been made in the context of flood risk management to deal with a possible increase in the frequency and intensity of floods due to climate change and - i agree with mr seeber - i am particularly pleased that parliament has insisted on a strong reference to climate change. as climate change is already happening, it is clear that in addition to addressing and reducing it, adaptation will inevitably be needed. the european union will need to prepare for even worse flash floods associated with more intense and unpredictable rainfall. coastal flash floods due to storms, combined with sea level rise, are likely to increase flood risks in coastal areas. the european union must be prepared to face the risks that these natural phenomena may cause. the commission has also taken steps to ensure that the water sector is not left behind. integrated river basin management must include both water quality management and flood risk management. i am very pleased that the european parliament has supported the commission in this matter and that the scope for possible synergies between the two procedures has been widened. the main points raised at first reading were retained. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is applied throughout the european union, with particular emphasis on river basins shared by more than one member state. with this new and important piece of legislation the european union will be ready to reduce and minimise the potentially devastating effects of floods.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission welcomes the report by mr swoboda on croatia. the report is balanced and addresses the main challenges that croatia will face on the path to eu membership, particularly in the political field. i am sure that the adoption by the european parliament of a resolution on this report will make a significant contribution to the process of enlargement to croatia. the accession negotiations with croatia have started well. the analytical review process was successfully concluded in october 2006. it gave an overall overview of the current degree of alignment with the acquis, as well as issues requiring further efforts. the pace at which croatia progresses towards membership will depend largely on its ability to meet all the necessary criteria. this is not an easy task. croatia must align its legislation with the many regulations of the european union and ensure that they are implemented and complied with. it must also continue its efforts in the context of political and economic criteria. six of the 33 negotiating chapters have been opened so far. for two of them, negotiations were provisionally closed. the objectives have been set for nine chapters and will have to be met before the opening of negotiations in areas such as competition policy, public procurement and the free movement of capital. the european union and croatia are preparing their negotiating position in many other chapters. we hope to be able to open negotiations on other chapters during the german presidency. overall, croatia has a solid basis for further progress. however, there is still work to be done, particularly with regard to the political and economic criteria, where difficulties remain. we believe in particular that it is urgent for croatia to continue its efforts and achieve concrete results in the reform of the judiciary, public administration and the fight against corruption. croatia has started to implement its strategy of judicial reform and the first results are appearing. that's a good point. but the croatian judicial system has serious shortcomings and needs to be improved, as mr swoboda rightly points out in his report. the legal backlog is significant. the procedures are far too slow and care should be taken to ensure the proper execution of judicial decisions and to strengthen the independence and professionalism of judges. the government must also present its plan for the rationalization of the judicial organization. the conduct of war crimes trials also needs to be improved. corruption remains a worrying problem. some measures have been taken in the anti-corruption programme, but their implementation is only just beginning. the programme needs to be implemented in its entirety, and strong political will is needed to step up efforts. the many weaknesses that remain in public administration do not help to facilitate the fight against corruption. croatia needs to accelerate the reform process in this area as a matter of urgency. croatia is moving in the right direction in terms of minority rights. but it still faces several particular challenges in the future, as regards the return of refugees. some issues remain unresolved, including the allocation of housing to refugees who had occupancy and rental rights before leaving croatia. the report rightly highlights croatia's positive influence in the region, particularly as chair of the south east european cooperation process. it stressed, however, the need to continue to encourage croatia in its efforts to achieve good neighbourly relations, in particular by intensifying work to resolve outstanding bilateral issues, particularly those relating to the delimitation of borders. as regards the economic criteria, satisfactory progress has been made overall. croatia can be considered to have a functioning market economy. however, it is in its interest to continue to move towards an open and competitive economy, so that it can meet the competitive pressures of the european union in good time. it has to pursue economic reforms and take some difficult decisions, notably on industrial restructuring, particularly in the steel and shipbuilding sectors. the progress of the negotiations depends on croatia. only the future will tell when it is ready for membership. the commission's position is not to set a target date for accession until accession negotiations are in the final stages. croatia still has a long way to go and the progress of the negotiations will depend on its ability to meet the requirements of accession. the commission will continue to do its utmost to help croatia achieve this objective.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. it is a great pleasure to welcome the president of the republic of india, mr abdul kalam, to the european parliament behind when it comes to reaping the benefits of advanced technology, because technology, if used properly, creates growth and can help improve the daily lives of the poor. we can certainly share your approach and are therefore pleased that india is participating in eu-funded research programmes and working with the european union on galileo, for example. apart from the key role you have played in promoting science and technology, we were also impressed by your election as president of the republic of india in 2002, which you achieved with an overwhelming majority across party lines. for you,
