(applause) i would like to thank
president of the republic of india. friends, my greetings to all of you. i would particularly like to greet mr hans-gert pöttering, mr harald rømer, mr klaus welle and mr ciril stokelj. good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. i am delighted to be with the honourable members of the european parliament on the occasion of the golden jubilee year of the european union. i was wondering what thoughts i could share with you. as you are aware, as a democratic nation india has experience in providing leadership to over one billion people with multi-language, multicultural and multi-religious systems. i wish to share this experience with you, friends. european civilisation has a unique place in human history. its people were valiantly engaged in the adventure of exploring the planet earth, resulting in the discovery of many ideas and systems. europe has seen the birth of pioneers in science, leading to the development of technologies. europe was the theatre of conflicts among the nations lasting hundreds of years, including the two world wars. now, with this backdrop and these dynamics, you have established the european union with a vision of peace and prosperity for the entire region. the european union has become an example for connectivity among nations, probably with no possibility of war, leading to lasting regional peace. before i started out on my journey to europe, i was thinking: why are europe and india unique and natural partners? do we share a common history and heritage and, possibly in the future, a common destiny? this was the question. i was astonished by what i found: the depth and vitality of our inter-connectedness, through language, culture, ancient beliefs, ideologies and the movement of people, have stood the test of time. this has matured into a very strong bond through sustained trade and intellectually satisfying collaboration in many areas of science and technology. for example, on 23 april 2007, the italian scientific satellite agile was launched by the indian polar satellite launch vehicle rocket system into a very precise orbit. scientists from india and europe are very excited. let us congratulate them. india is a country that has learnt over the years to evolve and maintain a unique unity amid diversity. similarly, the european union’s greatest contribution has been to demonstrate to the world that it is possible to build a strong union of nations without compromising national identities. it has become an inspirational model and an example to emulate for every region in the world. the european union and india support a social form of economic development and we encourage a model of growth with equity. both are conscious of the need for growth to respect the environment and to make it sustainable for future generations. with india’s and the european union’s centuries of valuable experience, we can develop a doctrine of global cooperation based on the foundation of regional collaboration and core competencies of our nations. the european union and india radiate a message to the world that regional cooperation and interregional collaboration will lead to a win-win situation for all, so that we can have a politically and socio-economically emergent civilisation. our contribution will be successful if, before the 21st century is over, we are able to make all regions transform into happy unions leading to the emergence of a world of unions. in this context, i am reminded of the dream of an indian poet who said 3000 years ago in the tamil classic: ,which means, ‘i am a world citizen. every citizen is my own kith and kin’. he said that 3000 years ago. against this backdrop, i have brought from india a message to launch three important indo-european tasks that could contribute to global peace and prosperity. i propose these missions on the basis of india’s experience and the european union’s dynamics. the first task is the evolution of an enlightened society, in which citizens have a system of values, leading to a prosperous and peaceful world. the second idea is creating energy independence. normally people talk about energy security. i am talking about energy independence: a three-dimensional approach to energy choice that aims to achieve a clean world. the third aim is a world knowledge platform to bring together the core skills of the european union and india in certain areas in order to provide solutions to critical issues like water, healthcare and capacity-building. when nations join together to build a cohesive society, it is necessary to ensure that the benefits of development encompass all sections of society. worldwide poverty, illiteracy, unemployment and deprivation are driving forward the forces of anger and violence. these forces are linked to some earlier real or perceived historical enmities, tyrannies, injustice, inequalities, ethnic issues and religious fundamentalism that are flowing into an outburst of extremism worldwide. both india and the european union have witnessed and are witnessing the unsavoury acts of certain misguided sections of society. together we must address the root causes of such phenomena in order to find lasting ways to promote peace. how do we do that? we need a carrier of eternal goodness and wholesomeness in human conduct, which is called ‘righteousness’. as we say in india: ‘where there is righteousness in the heartthere is beauty in the character. when there is beauty in the character,there is harmony in the home. when there is harmony in the home,there is order in the nation. when there is order in the nation,there is peace in the world.’ (applause) honourable members, this is true for the whole world. when we need peace in the world, we need order in the nation. we need harmony in the home. whether in europe, india or in any part of the world the origin is righteousness in the heart. how do we instil righteousness in the heart of every citizen of the world? this is my area of specialisation and i would like to talk to you about it. first, i wish to discuss the evolution of an enlightened society. with this spirit of righteousness in the heart, i would like to present to this important gathering a methodology for developing a happy, prosperous and peaceful society in our world, which i call ‘evolution of enlightened society’. i have shared these thoughts with many intellectuals in national and international circles. we need to create an enlightened society with three components: 1) education with a value system; 2) religion transforming into spirituality; and 3) economic development for societal transformation. beginning with the first component, we have seen that the seeds of peace in the world have their origin in the righteousness in the heart of every individual. such righteous citizens lead to the emergence of an enlightened society. education with a value system has to be designed so that the righteousness in the heart is developed in young minds. that should be the mission of education. the prime learning environment is five to seventeen years of age. that reminds me of what an ancient greek teacher said a few thousand years ago: ‘give me a child for seven years; afterwards, let god or the devil take the child. they cannot change my child’. this shows the power of great teachers and what they can inculcate in young minds. parents and teachers must instil moral leadership in children. it requires the ability to have insight into the uniqueness and universality of human consciousness. true education is the acquisition of enlightened feelings and enlightened powers to understand daily events and to understand the permanent truth linking man to his environment, human and planetary. i remember the lectures given when i was a student a long time ago – nearly 57 years ago – at the jesuit institution of st joseph’s college in tiruchirappalli in southern india by the college’s highest authority, the reverend father rector kalathil. every monday, the reverend father would take an hour-long class. he used to talk about good human beings present and past and about what makes a good human being. in this class, he used to give lectures on people such as buddha, confucius, st augustine, caliph omar, mahatma gandhi, einstein, and abraham lincoln and to tell moral stories related to our civilisational heritage. in the moral science class, father kalathil used to highlight the best aspect of how these great people had evolved as good human beings through parental care, teaching and the companionship of great books. even though these lessons were given to me in 1950 during my college days, they inspire me even today. it is essential that in schools and colleges in every nation, important teachers at the institution give hour-long weekly lectures on civilisational heritage and the derived value system. this may be called a moral science class and will teach young minds to love their country and other human beings and to elevate them to higher planes. i have suggested this methodology to education experts in my country. the european union may like to consider developing a system that would enable a student to learn these fundamental lessons for the benefit of all. let me turn to the issue of transforming religion into spiritual force. many in the world believe it is a difficult task, but i disagree. i would like to share an experience that convinced me that it is possible for religion to be transformed into a spiritual force. how do we do that? as you all know, religion has two components: theology and spirituality. even though theology is unique to every religion, the spiritual component spreads the value to be absorbed by human beings in order to promote a good life and the welfare of society in the pursuit of material life. i witnessed the coming together of religion and science in a major task. in the early 1960s, the founder of the indian space research programme, professor vikram sarabhai, and his team had located the most technically suitable place for space research after considering many alternatives. the town of thumba in kerala in southern india was selected for space research as it was near the magnetic equator. this made it ideally suited to ionospheric and electrojet research in the upper atmosphere. i was fortunate to work with professor vikram sarabhai for about eight years. the major challenge for vikram sarabhai was to locate the site in a specific area. as was usual, professor sarabhai approached the kerala government administrators first. after seeing the land and the sea coast, he was told that thousands of fishermen lived there and that the place had an ancient church, the st mary magdalene church, a bishop’s house and a school. it would be very difficult, therefore, to allocate this land and the administration was willing to provide land in an alternative area. similarly, the political authorities also believed that it would be a difficult situation owing to the existence of important institutions and concern for people who were to be relocated. however, the professor was very determined. it was suggested that he should approach the only person who could advise and help. that was the bishop, father peter bernard pereira. professor sarabhai, approached the bishop one saturday evening. i still remember their meeting, which proved to be historic. many of us witnessed the event. father pereira exclaimed, ‘oh vikram, you are asking for my children’s home, the fishermen’s home, my home, the bishop’s house, and god’s home, the church. how is it possible?’. both had a special quality: they could smile even in difficult situations. father pereira asked professor sarabhai to come to church on sunday morning at 9 a.m. and he turned up on sunday with his team. prayers were taking place with a reading from the bible by father pereira. after the prayer was over, the bishop invited professor sarabhai to come to the dais. the reverend father introduced him to the congregation. ‘dear children’, said the bishop, ‘here is a scientist, professor vikram sarabhai. what does science do? all of us, including this church, experience the light from electricity. i am able to talk to you through the microphone because of technology. doctors treat patience thanks to medical science. science through technology enhances the comfort and quality of human life. what do i do as a preacher? i pray for you people, for your wellbeing and for your peace. in short, vikram and i are doing the same: both science and spirituality seek the almighty’s blessings for human prosperity in body and mind. professor sarabhai says that he will build within a year alternative facilities near the coast. now, dear children, can we give our homes, my home and god’s home for a great scientific mission?’ he asked the question. there total silence, as there is now. then the entire congregation got up and said ‘amen’, which made the whole church reverberate. that was the church where we had our design centre and where we started rocket assembly, and the bishop’s house was where the scientists worked. later, the thumba equatorial rocket launching station led to the establishment of the vikram sarabhai space centre and the space activities led to the emergence of multiple space centres throughout the country. this church has become an important centre of learning, where thousands of people learn about the dynamic history of india’s space programme and the great minds of a scientist and a spiritual leader. of course, the people of thumba received well-equipped facilities, a place of worship and an educational centre elsewhere as promised. when i think of this event, i can see how enlightened spiritual and scientific leaders can come together to give reverence to human life. of course, the birth of terls and the vssc gave the country the ability to launch vehicles, spacecraft and space applications that have accelerated social and economic development in india to unprecedented levels. professor vikram sarabhai and father peter bernard pereira are no longer with us, but those who are responsible for creation and making flowers blossom will themselves be a different kind of flower, as described in the bhagwat gita. it says, ‘see the flower, how generously it distributes perfume, honey. it gives to all, gives freely of its love. when its work is done, it falls away quietly. try to be like the flower, unassuming despite all its qualities’. what a beautiful message to humanity on the purpose of life, reflecting the spiritual component. can we bridge the spiritual component of the religions to bring peace to nations and to the world? i was asked to talk about cultural dialogue and would like to recall an incident that commonly occurs in many parts of my country. i witnessed this event as a young boy of 10. in our house, periodically, i used to see three unique people meet: pakshi lakshmana shastrigal, who was the head priest of the famous rameshwaram temple, a vedic scholar, reverend father bodal, who built the first church on rameshwaram island, and my father who was an imam in the mosque. all three used to sit and discuss the island’s problems and find solutions. in addition, they built several religious connectivities with compassion. these connectivities quietly spread to others on the island like the fragrance from the flowers. this sight always comes to my mind whenever i discuss with people the dialogue of religions. india has had this advantage of integration of minds for thousands of years. throughout the world, the need to have a frank dialogue among cultures, religions and civilisations has been felt now more than ever. these two instances give me confidence that religions can be bridged through spiritual components. whenever i meet the young and experienced in my country, i narrate these two experiences. many in my country and the world over may have such experiences. we have to spread such ‘glad tidings’ to every part of the world. now let us discuss the third important component of enlightened society, which is to achieve economic development for societal transformation. let me take india as an example; it may be true to many parts of the world, including the european union. the indian economy is in an ascent phase. there is considerable growth in the manufacturing and service sectors. we have a mission of spreading this economic growth throughout the country, including the rural sector. nearly 220 million people out of a billion people must have their quality of life raised in both rural and urban areas. even though gdp growth indicates our economic growth, people’s participation is essential to achieving the required targets. it is essential to ensure that citizens are empowered with good quality of life encompassing nutritious food, good habitat, clean environment, affordable healthcare, quality education and productive employment, integrated with our value system drawn from civilisational heritage leading to the comprehensive development of the nation that will bring smiles to one billion people. these are indicators for the growth of the national prosperity index. to achieve that growth rate, we have identified five areas where india has a core competence for integrated action: 1) agriculture and food processing; 2) education and healthcare; 3) information and communication technology; 4) infrastructure development, including pura (providing urban amenities in rural areas); and 5) self-reliance in critical technologies. we propose to realise the vision of transforming india into a developed nation before 2020 by energising and igniting the minds of the 540 million youth of the nation below 25 years of age. so far we have discussed the three-dimensional approach of providing value-based education, religion transforming india’s spiritual force and economic development for societal transformation leading to the evolution of an enlightened society. this integrated three-dimensional methodology for the evolution of enlightened society will pave the way for peaceful, prosperous, happy nations and, thereby, for a world free from extremisms and further seeds of extremism. on my website www.presidentofindia.nic.in, i have stated how an empowered world body is essential to evolve the nations of enlightened citizens. i will be very happy to exchange thoughts, ideas and action related to this mission with the honourable members after they have seen my website. let me now discuss the second mission, ‘leading to energy independence’. when we analyse the critical problems facing the planet today, two important issues come to our minds. firstly, the continuous depletion of fossil-material-derived oil, gas and coal reserves, as predicted by the world energy forum, of which you are all aware. the second is the continuous degradation of the environment, primarily due to extensive use of fossil materials to generate energy. the solution to these problems can be found through energy independence, which i have presented to my country. it may be applicable to many nations. what form of energy independence do i propose in india? india has 17% of the world’s population, but only about 0.8% of the world’s known oil and natural gas resources. based on the progress visualised for the nation during the next two decades, its power-generating capacity has to increase to 400 000 mw by the year 2030 from the present capacity of 130 000 mw. this takes into consideration the energy economies planned and the design and production of energy-efficient equipment and systems. i have proposed various systems. solar cell efficiency, common to the european union and india, has to increase from the present level of 20% to 55% through intensified research on carbon-nanotube-based solar cells. regarding thorium reactors, thorium is a non-fissile material. it has to be converted into a fissile material using fast breeder technology. in the biofuels area, the challenge is biofuel plantation for higher yield, esterification technologies for higher output and changes to automobile power plants. these three research areas need intensive cooperation between the european union and india. i would suggest setting up an india-eu renewable energy development programme for advanced r&d in all forms of renewable energy, leading to the availability of commercial-class large-scale power plants within the next decade. (applause) i should like to conclude with the ‘world knowledge platform’. with india’s experience of two successful international cooperative ventures from concept to realisation and marketing, i would suggest developing the ‘world knowledge platform’ to bring together the core competences of the nations of the eu and india in science and technology, leading to the development of unique systems for global applications. the ‘world knowledge platform’ will enable joint design, development, cost-effective production and marketing of the knowledge products, systems and services in various domains based on the core competence of partner nations in the international market. the ‘world knowledge platform’ is a meeting place for science, technology, industry, management and marketing. you may ask about the missions of the ‘world knowledge platform’. the convergence of biotechnology, nanotechnology and it is expected to touch every area of concern to humanity. the ‘world knowledge platform’ will take up missions in some of the areas discussed further, which are of the utmost importance to all of us and to making our world a safe, sustainable, peaceful and prosperous place to live. the first is water: desalination of sea water using solar energy, channelisation, networking of rivers and cost-effective safe drinking water. the second is healthcare: diagnosis, drug delivery system, development and production of vaccines for hiv, tb, malaria and cardiac diseases. the third is agriculture and food processing: increased production of food grain in an environment of reduced land, reduced water and reduced manpower; preservation of food; food processing; cost effective storage and distribution. the fourth is knowledge products: hardware, software and networking and storage products, including handheld micro and nano electronic devices. the fifth is transportation systems: fossil-fuel-free transportation systems using renewable energies, safety systems, hardware and embedded software integration. the sixth is habitat: an energy-efficient, water-efficient, pollution-free habitat. the seventh is disaster prediction and management: earthquake forecasting, assessing in advance the quantum of rain for particular cloud conditions. finally, capacity-building: quality human resource development for all the above areas, including the development of personnel with world-class skills. the european union represents a wealth of scientific potential with a rich culture for research. india has emerged as a leading country, with its demonstrated scientific and technological potential in many societal missions, and is now on the ascent. the combined strength of the nations can be utilised for the advantage of both india and the eu by joining together as partners in creating the ‘world knowledge platform’. in conclusion, as we have seen, there is a visible common thread to our dreams and problems. when i am with you, i have a feeling that there are beautiful solutions from beautiful minds. beautiful minds generate creativity. this is the common heritage of both india and the european union. i have presented three missions: ‘the evolution of an enlightened society’, ‘leading to energy independence’ and ‘creating the ‘world knowledge platform’. these indo-eu missions will reinforce further our strategic partnership and become the foundation for making changes to the life of 1.5 billion people, ultimately leading to the confluence of civilisations. to meet the challenges of these missions, we can draw inspiration from the member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to start by recalling that in its statements on homophobia of 17 january 2006 and on the rise of racially and disposal to combat homophobia. it is necessary to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, which is explicitly prohibited by article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights, and article 13 of the treaty allows appropriate measures to be taken at european level to combat discrimination on grounds of sex. in 2000, the council adopted a directive on the general framework for combating discrimination in employment and occupation based on a number of grounds, including sexual orientation, on the basis of article 13. the commission shall monitor the proper implementation of the directive in all member states, including poland. it will not hesitate to initiate the necessary proceedings against the member states concerned if the directives are not properly applied. the commission recalls that in 2005 it launched a study on the national legislation in force concerning the prohibition of all forms of discrimination, including discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, outside the field of employment and occupation. the study shows that all the member states concerned go further, and often much further, than community legislation in some areas. however, there are significant differences between member states as regards the scope of protection. the commission also announced that in its annual policy strategy for 2008, it would propose new initiatives aimed at preventing discrimination outside the labour market, including discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. in this context, the commission launched an impact assessment in february 2007 to determine whether additional eu action beyond employment and occupations is warranted. at the same time, the commission shall organise a wide consultation of the general public and stakeholders such as non-governmental organisations and social partners. the results of the impact assessment are expected at the end of 2007. the commission is aware that legal protection alone is not sufficient to ensure the effective protection of the persons concerned. it is equally important to fight prejudice and stereotypes. the european year of equal opportunities for all, 2007, has the following objectives: to inform citizens of their rights, to promote diversity as an asset, to promote equal opportunities for all in economic, social, cultural or political life. the european commission welcomes the national strategies developed by the member states in the context of the implementation of the european year. all countries, including poland, have taken into account all grounds for discrimination in their strategies. the commission has taken note of a statement by a member of the polish government announcing his intention to table a bill prohibiting the promotion of homosexuality in schools and all other youth or leisure facilities. according to the information available to the commission, this draft law has not yet been prepared and the declarations made to the polish government are not binding. this law, if enacted, could be in conflict with the fundamental rights enshrined in the european convention on human rights and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. it could be contrary to the principle of non-discrimination applied in the field of employment and occupation, and thus contrary to directive 2078/ec. the commission will closely monitor further developments and will not hesitate to intervene if there is an infringement of community law.

the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the commission has already done so. i am glad that we are talking about the economic and monetary area of the european union at this late hour. this own-initiative report is the first time that parliament has commented on the revision of the stability and growth pact, which was adopted by the heads of state or government in march 2005. the revision covered both the preventive and the corrective aspects of the pact. the aim of this pact was and is to avoid an excessive deficit and to achieve a balanced budget and sound public finances in the medium and long term. this report is a one-year review. the period of experience is therefore very short, in fact too short, and it falls in a year, 2006, which was marked by a very favourable economic situation. this favourable development has had a positive effect on the fiscal policies of the member states. it is clear that an assessment based solely on this short period cannot be definitive. the real stress test for the revised pact is in the years ahead. the report is an assessment of the present situation. the rapporteur, mr kurt joachim lauk, who unfortunately cannot be here today, has deliberately avoided naming the individual member states by their individual achievements. the report was not intended to give grades, which would not have been helpful in the rapporteur's view. it seems appropriate to make an overall assessment of what has been achieved so far. the economic and monetary committee has dealt with this report in detail and the exchange of views has been very constructive and fruitful. on behalf of mr lauk, i should like to thank in particular the socialist shadow rapporteur, mr rosati, and the liberal shadow rapporteur, mrs in veld, for their good and constructive cooperation. the report was adopted by an overwhelming majority in the committee. i would like to make a few brief comments on the main points. the statistical surveys underline that the gap between deficit and growth is too wide and that there is a correlation between high deficit and low growth. the 2006 figures show that 21 out of 25 member states with a low deficit or a slight surplus are at the same time experiencing high growth. this fact supports the view that deficit reduction promotes activity and economic performance and thus reduces unemployment. in this context, the report has highlighted three key points. firstly, the economic committee's report makes a strong plea for taking advantage of the economic good times to bring about the structural recovery of public budgets. the member states must use the economic recovery, in particular as a result of improved tax revenues, to reduce their debt. we must always remember that stimulating growth leads to higher demand and higher employment. the critical issue is that the favourable cyclical environment is not being used sufficiently in english. mr president, the commission is pleased that this item has been put on the agenda because it is now more than two years since we last discussed switzerland. it was in 2004, on the occasion of the conclusion of the 10 new bilateral agreements. let me start, therefore, with a general remark. the bilateral and multilateral relations that link the eu and switzerland are very good. switzerland is a highly valued partner for the eu in many areas. our bilateral relations are based on a solid foundation of around 20 important and over 100 smaller sector-specific agreements. these agreements range from free trade in goods and the free movement of persons to swiss participation in our research and schengen cooperation. any existing differences should not have an inordinate impact on our relations. in february, the commission adopted a state aid decision on swiss cantonal tax favours for certain types of companies, in particular holding companies. this decision has received much media attention in switzerland and has been dramatised, by some, into a major conflict. legally, the commission has no doubts that the cantonal tax schemes qualify as subsidies, because these tax regimes offer unfair tax advantages to companies established in switzerland for profits generated in the european union. income generated in switzerland is taxed higher than profits made in the eu. this unequal treatment is at the heart of the state aid problem. the rules in question are liable to distort competition and may affect trade between switzerland and the eu. all the criteria of article 23 of the 1972 agreement, the provision which declares such state aid incompatible with the proper functioning of the agreement, are therefore fulfilled. politically, too, it seems hard to accept that a neighbouring country that enjoys privileged access to our internal market and takes part in a large number of our programmes and other activities should grant such tax favours. the benefiting companies are often set up with the sole aim of avoiding the taxation of profits in our member states. i would point out that tax schemes of this kind or similar are not allowed within the eu, pursuant to the state aid rules set out in the ec treaty. in the past, the commission has adopted decisions against them. we are not against tax competition, which also takes place among the member states, but it must be fair. the commission wants to find a mutually acceptable solution. therefore, we also asked the council in february for a mandate to start negotiations with switzerland on this topic. the commission is also working on a new mandate for the european parliament to be given to the council. i am also counting very much on parliament's support in this matter. we proceed from the belief that we will find a solution for this problem, just as we have always found solutions for problems in our relations with switzerland in the past. on a different matter of importance, i would like to express the commission's expectation that switzerland will, hopefully, soon be ready to negotiate the inclusion of bulgaria and romania in the agreement on the free movement of persons. if switzerland were to exclude the citizens of two member states from this very important agreement, it would be unacceptable for legal, institutional and political reasons. bulgaria and romania should also receive a financial contribution from switzerland for the reduction of economic and social disparities, on the same terms as the other 10 new member states. in view of the swiss position on eu accession and the european economic area, there is currently no alternative to further strengthening of bilateral relations. with that in mind, the commission is prepared to look into the swiss proposal for the negotiation of a general framework agreement, provided that it brings added value to our relations, for example with regard to the updating of existing agreements in line with the evolving community acquis.

president of the italian council of ministers. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are at a crucial moment for the future of europe and for the construction of europe: it is with this awareness, and not without emotion, that i address you today. i thank president hans gert poettering for this opportunity. between now and the 2009 elections, europe's future is at stake. in a month's time, the european council will decide on the start of an intergovernmental conference at the end of which we will be able to say that we have lived up to the commitments we all made together in berlin on 25 march. it is about deciding what europe needs, what we all need, in order to meet the challenges that the world is putting before us. it sounds like an abstract question, but it's very concrete. we should have understood by now that the ability of us europeans to interpret the global world and seize its opportunities depends on how we manage our common institutions. let me say at the outset, quite frankly, that i do not share the view of those who continue to oppose the need to produce results to the need to strengthen the european institutions. it is precisely to achieve more results that i hope for and have always fought for stronger and more effective common institutions! we're not starting from scratch this time. we don't have to reinvent anything new. in october 2004, all european countries signed a treaty and 18 countries have ratified it. in the last two years, the reasons of those who hesitate have been heard above all. it is now time to hear from those who ratified the 2004 treaty. who have committed themselves, even in front of their own citizens, to continue on that path. a journey that began a few years earlier in laeken, and which had been twisted from a fundamental and unimpeachable assumption: the european council in brussels in december 2006 stressed that europe could not achieve ambitious results without equally ambitious reforms. well, i'm convinced that assumption still holds. and so we must start again from october 2004, putting aside the mourning and the pauses for reflection of the last two years and thinking seriously and responsibly about our future and that of our children. it is not just about agreeing on the new rules we need. there are other equally priority needs without which europe cannot function: a true balance sheet and real policies on the great challenges of our time: but let us start today with the most urgent issue, that of overcoming the constitutional impasse and reforming the institutions. to do this, we must adhere to a principle which is at the heart of our being in the european union. a principle so fundamental that it defines the very ethics of our being together. it is the view that in the development of the european project, an effort must always be made to understand the reasons of others, to take responsibility for them in some way. we have always made this effort and we will continue to do so. but we expect others to be equally understanding. we expect these others to share our aspirations. which in this case, as you all know, are those of those who want a closer union. it is with this principle in mind that we will make every effort to help the german and portuguese presidencies to preserve the maximum of our union ambitions, while taking the utmost account of the reasons of others. in view of this, i should now like to say what i think we cannot afford to do at the european council in june and at the intergovernmental conference that will follow. first of all, let us remember that this time the respect of time is directly linked to a question of democracy. in 2009, european voters will have to know what kind of europe they are voting for. what role will the european parliament play? what are your duties? if there is a permanent presidency of the council, a european foreign minister. how the commission will be formed and so on... the mandate of the intergovernmental conference must therefore be precise and selective. by pointing out the few significant trading blocks and, above all, how to dissolve them. only then will we be able to deliver on our promise to define the new rules by 2009. with an open mandate, the conference would hardly close by the end of 2007, and the time for national transitions to the new agreement would not allow the process to be completed by the first months of 2009. the impasse would be automatic. let me make a point here. this is a thought that comes to me spontaneously after re-reading the 2004 constitutional treaty just these days - i would like to invite everyone to review it now that time has passed and that greater detachment is possible. well, the 2004 text is a good one. it's really nice. with a big european breath. the first part of the report, in particular, clearly and comprehensibly conveys the meaning and vision of the great common undertaking we have undertaken. let us therefore think twice before we put it on the shelf and go the way of the total or partial comb grafts in the existing treaties. we would lose a wealth of simplicity and readability at the expense of citizens' understanding of and, therefore, their commitment to the european project! but above all, we would lose a text that reflects a coherent conception of europe, a text that combines the ideal aspirations of many of us with the practical and commonly felt need to give our union more solid rules and adequate means to meet the new challenges. the way the negotiations have been going so far leads me to believe that unfortunately we will have to go back to the 2004 text. and yet i would like to stand here today before you all with my conviction that in doing so we would be depriving ourselves of something very important! and that for us who believe in the european project, this would be a huge sacrifice, a very high price to pay for those who have ratified and democratically invested in ratification. let's keep that in mind. we cannot therefore accept a reversal of the existing institutional package. the strengthening of the common foreign and security policy through a foreign minister, a stable presidency of the council, the extension of qualified majority voting, the overcoming of the three-pillar structure and the legal personality of the union are all aspects which are essential to us and must be safeguarded. i should like to warn against certain appeals to 'realism' which are typical of the eve of an important european council and which are invariably geared to downward compromises. i would like to point out that if it is true that the great global challenges can only be tackled at european level, then the only real realism is that of those who want a europe that can meet these challenges, not those who do not want it! on the internal level, i am thinking of defending the european social model and creating a genuine area of freedom, security and justice. how can we fail to see that this is an indispensable complement to a european citizenship which is not only economic? on the external front, i am thinking of wars, the fight against international terrorism, the global challenges of energy and climate change (hydrogen). how can we deny that the only way to make our choices and our values stand out on the international scene is to be able to express a foreign policy worthy of the name, communicating it to the world with one voice? as regards the structure of the european union, do not think that this is a purely theoretical question. the complexity of the union is one of the main reasons for the distance between it and its citizens. how can we not see the advantages of going beyond the pillar structure, especially in terms of clarity and understanding by the citizens? the 2004 constitutional treaty provides convincing answers on these points. we are not going to be able to do that, because we are not going to be able to do it. do we really want to risk adding to the complexity of the system by failing to affect it in depth and merely tinkering with a few surface touches? we are not going to let the european parliament, the council and the commission, be the ones to decide on the future of europe. so, ladies and gentlemen, representatives of the european people, let us not indulge in negative rhetoric about europe. we can't keep hiding it from our fellow citizens. let us show you this europe instead. with pride. let's show everyone what it has given us in terms of peace and well-being, let's explain how fundamental it is to our existence. we say once and for all to our fellow citizens that in a world which is now a system of continents it makes no sense for a state and its citizens to live outside a political and economic aggregate which is strong at home and authoritative abroad. italy will therefore work in these negotiations to reach a high compromise. i believe we can do this, we must do this together. of course, if an agreement at 27 were to prove impossible, then the question would arise as to how to proceed. and the only way to solve this dilemma is to recall the fundamental principle i spoke about at the beginning of my speech: it is the very ethos of the union that no one should be too much and for too long a burden on the aspirations of others. italy, which has always believed deeply in europe, therefore feels that it has an additional duty today. the idea is to imagine, or to begin to imagine, how to enable those countries which so wish to make real progress in the construction of european unity. i think that we should not necessarily all go at the same speed. i hope so, and i will see to it. but i realize that's not always possible. on the other hand, some of europe's most significant political choices, such as the euro and the creation of the schengen area, have already been made by only a few member states. not against anyone; without excluding others; i'm not saying that i'm not going to, but i'm going to keep the door open. and it was a choice respected by those who at the time did not feel ready to go in a certain direction right away. i hope that this same constructive approach will prevail in the future. and may he prevail over any temptation to veto. italy has always felt, as you know, that being europeanist was the best way to be farsighted. but today, foresight does not mean merely drawing up ambitious scenarios for the future of european integration. it also means that we must take up the problem of allowing the peoples who wish to achieve their ambitions for union at the time and in the manner most suited to them. if no one ever takes the trouble to even imagine such an eventuality, we risk undermining the european project, frustrating the ideals of those who have so far believed in it. even countries like mine, which have invested unreservedly in the construction of europe for 50 years, may eventually exhaust their vital capacity. i would therefore like to conclude with a double message. italy will give the greatest possible support to the german and then the portuguese presidency so that the european council of 21 and 22 june and the intergovernmental conference that will follow will be a success in which all the member states can recognize themselves. at the same time, italy knows that a compromise is not an end in itself. and if we were not convinced by such a compromise, we would not sign it. a vanguard of countries might then prove to be the best way to continue the path towards an ever closer union, provided that the door is always left open to those who want to join at a later stage. finally, i would like to make a strong appeal to the members of parliament, the direct representatives of the people. i am speaking in particular to the members of the european parliament who represent the people of europe. you have an irreplaceable role to play in making the public aware of what is at stake. only if your work is combined with that of the governments can we create the conditions for a successful constitutional negotiation. we must be aware that we cannot fail, or else decline. the decline of an advanced idea of europe; of a europe that knows how to be an actor in the world thanks to the values that constitute its foundation. we risk becoming once again the little western appendage of the asian continent, to which not only geography but also future history would condemn us. thank you, sir.

amsterdam and nice, are calling for an amending treaty. that is a successful continuation of the monnet method: small steps forward, with concrete meaning. it highlights the improvements, the democratic guarantees, the increase in efficiency. that way we can have a positive debate and come out from under the shadow of the rejected constitution. in short: the name, the form and the content of the constitution are all things that need to be reconsidered. i come to my second point. the netherlands is very keen to improve the democratic functioning of the union. a key lesson from the referendum is that the dutch want to be sure that they are involved in the decision-making. they want their voice to be heard in europe. the institutional proposals of the constitutional treaty are a step forward. i am merely mentioning the rule that the european parliament always takes part in the decision-making process when the council adopts a majority decision. but improvements are possible. the subsidiarity test of european legislative proposals should give national parliaments a greater role. if a majority of national parliaments express a negative opinion, there must be consequences. the european parliament should not be deprived of the opportunity to involve national parliaments more closely. this review takes place at the very first stage of decision-making. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council. the european parliament will retain its full role in the codecision procedure. the commission's right of initiative is not affected. as you said to me the other day, mr president, the european parliament and the national parliaments are complementary. as democratic partners. i come now to my third point: the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is not only more democratic, but also more effective. and then we'll talk about the important issues of our time that people are concerned about: climate change, energy policy, the fight against terrorism and migration require a forward-looking common approach. the constitutional treaty contains important improvements, with more majority decision-making. but we can't help but notice that people are afraid of vetoes. fear of a stealth expansion of powers. that's why we need to be clear here. no action without support. we must therefore dare to take the step of majority voting where necessary. and i'm prepared to defend those choices. but only if the transfer of sovereignty is a conscious choice, surrounded by the right safeguards. the union's competences must be clearly defined. only then can we reduce the hesitation about transferring sovereignty. the netherlands will make proposals in this area. a related point has also been the subject of intense debate in your parliament. i am talking about the relationship between the internal market on the one hand and the freedom of movement of member states in the design of their public services on the other. there too, clarity can be brought about without prejudice to the internal market. i am in favour of a strong single market. citizens of all member states benefit from this. but in matters such as pensions, social security and education, member states want to be able to tailor the design to national circumstances. europe must provide space for this. for example, by establishing a number of criteria for services of general interest. and finally, my fourth point. i think it is right to include the criteria for enlargement in the new treaty. we have collectively had the wisdom to enlarge the union and i fully support that decision. it says something about the future of europe and the change after the divided europe of the post-world war ii period. but no one can ignore the doubts that citizens have about enlargement. in the netherlands, there is a perception that the union does not take its own rules seriously or not seriously enough. we have the criteria, but in the eyes of the dutch they are not strictly observed. this is affecting public support for europe. the criteria should therefore be incorporated into the new treaty. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, europe has come a long way in 50 years. expectations are high. together, we can lead by example in tackling climate change, in fighting poverty and insecurity in the world. together we can unlock europe's economic potential in an increasingly integrated global economy. we must work together to ensure a reliable supply of energy and raw materials. we must work together to combat the inhuman waste of illegal migration and to do so we need a strong and effective european union. a union that enjoys the confidence of its citizens. i will defend in the netherlands a treaty which contains the four elements i have just outlined. because i believe the time is right. because i have great confidence in the presidency of angela merkel, and then josé socrates. and because i believe that together, we can take the next step. but above all because it is necessary to face the challenges of our time together. i recently came across the words of robert schuman, one of our visionary founding fathers, again. and i was struck again by its wisdom and correctness. in his statement of 9 may 1950 he said - and i quote - 'the unification of europe cannot be achieved all at once, nor can it be brought about by an all-embracing creation. the european union must be built on concrete achievements, based on genuine solidarity.' i think that schuman's words have not lost their relevance and can still be a guide for our common task of building europe. thank you very much. there were reports from the committee responsible, the committee on the environment, public health and food safety; there were opinions from the committee on agriculture and rural development and the committee on internal market and consumer protection. this process has been very intensive and constructive under the codecision procedure. a series of informal trialogues took place which led to the council’s general approach, which not only accommodates most of the member states’ concerns, but also reflects the european parliament’s powers of codecision by taking the vast majority of its proposals on board. one proposal in particular that has been taken on board is the abolition of the initial proposal for the categorisation of spirit drinks; secondly, the introduction of a strong quality policy for spirit drinks; thirdly, the withdrawal of the proposal to allow flavours to be added to eau de vie; and fourthly, the strengthening of the powers of the european parliament by introducing the regulatory committee with scrutiny procedures in most of the cases for which provision is made for comitology. those are just a few of the essential amendments which were introduced on the initiative of the european parliament. during this whole procedure, my colleague, commissioner fischer boel, has played a constructive and pragmatic role with a view to finding a result that we hope the european parliament will be able to endorse. in line with the international obligations deriving from the tbt agreement and following the council’s request of 23 april 2007, the commission sent the file to the wto, setting a two-month period for comments. this notification was formally made on 1 june 2007. as regards vodka, the commission still has some reservations at this stage, which are primarily of a legal nature. the commission has always taken a clear stance that it must ensure that a definition of vodka is compatible with eu law and fits the wto context. the definition of the raw-material bases for this popular product – which is enjoying considerable market buoyancy worldwide – has been subject to considerable debate in the last month. the general approach of the council distinguishes the labelling of vodka between one group based on potatoes and cereals, and those products which are derived from other raw materials which shall bear the indication ‘produced from’ and list the products that go into it. the commission’s legal service has expressed concern about the compatibility of this solution both with eu law and with wto obligations. any restriction of the present legislation needs to be duly justified and proportionate; regulations and many accession acts which could not achieve all this. there is no categorization of wonderful. we don't have a quality classification of spirits. that would be very bad. but we have a quality ban on flavoring the fires. so you're not allowed to flavor fires. i have said, somewhat exaggeratingly, that i do not want the spirits to be covered by the chemicals regulation because there are so many chemicals in them, but by the spirits regulation. but of course it is a question of protecting the producers who produce and manufacture in a professional manner, and we must not allow the production of spirits to become, to put it exaggeratedly, a toxic mixture. the question of sugaring is also a subject which parliament has pushed through. i say to the commission right now: when we five teaspoons of sugar in it doesn't taste good anymore! we'll be careful here. the methanol content has been reduced to 10 g per hectolitre compared with the old regulation of 50 g per hectolitre. this is a health issue. the blue acid content of stone fires has been reduced by 3 g to now 7 g per hectolitre of pure alcohol. these are accomplishments that cannot be praised enough. the traditional procedures were also reflected in the new proposal. we have therefore taken care to ensure that in particular what is traditionally produced may continue to be produced. this is a very important matter. now, about the vodka, a very controversial subject. i could live with the commission's proposal that the labelling of vodka should always indicate what it is made of. but then there were the objections of the traditional countries, like poland and finland. i have taken these objections to tradition into account. i said, well, then we will exclude potatoes and cereals from the labelling and only indicate the other agricultural raw materials used to make vodka. it is a correct solution, because if i look at the amendments now before us and take the commissioner's comments into account, i know that all the other amendments will not be accepted, either by the council or by the commission or by the wto. in order to take account of the tradition in poland and finland, it is right to remove these two products from the labelling. we must not be tempted to introduce amendments to the legislation to prohibit the manufacture of products for which there are no reasons of health, internal market or consumer protection. that would be going too far. we have always held that in the legislation before us. that is why i ask you to vote for the compromise tomorrow. there is no other compromise. if the present proposal is not adopted, all the other elements of the compromise will also be obsolete. the commission will then try again to impose its ideas, which have been hotly contested, and the council will again be at loggerheads. we won't have a regulation for years! i would like to point this out so that later on no one will say: 'if he had told me, i would have voted differently.' i look forward to the discussion.

it is very important that the european union should take a common line and speak with one voice. if russia makes an agreement with one of our member states or does not honour an agreement, then russia is acting unlawfully towards the whole of the european union. we must not, therefore, turn a blind eye to this. secondly, russia must create a better investment climate for european companies, not by changing the law, but by better applying and, above all, enforcing the law. russian legislation on intellectual property must be harmonized with international conventions. the energy charter is an important point in our relations with russia. russia has signed it, but does not feel bound by it. that is unfortunate. without abandoning the energy charter, the eu should try to incorporate the important elements of the charter in the new partnership and cooperation agreement. i hope that agreement will be negotiated soon. the european union is also interested in russia's wto membership. russia would be subject to a whole bunch of international obligations. this will help ensure that russia is fully involved as an economic and trade partner and cannot pick the raisin alone. but we don't have to accept this at any cost. in short, despite some dark sides, we can look to the future with optimism and confidence.

member of the commission. mr president, mr martin, the commission bases the european union's climate policy and its scientific and economic analysis of climate change on rigorous, available and up-to-date information. the commission is aware that, according to the results of recent research, with a stabilisation of greenhouse gases at the level of 550 parts per million in co2 equivalents, the chances of reaching the target of a maximum warming of two degrees are slim. accordingly, in the communication entitled 'limiting global warming to 2°c', adopted this year, the commission states that in order to have a 50% chance of not exceeding that 2°c limit, it will be necessary to keep greenhouse gas concentrations substantially below that level of 550 parts per million, in co2 equivalents, for the next few decades, and that emissions will then have to be reduced to stabilise at around 450 parts per million. this means that between now and 2050, global greenhouse gas emissions will have to be reduced by at least 50% compared to 1990 levels. the commission's analysis has shown that this target is technically feasible and economically viable if the main emitters act quickly. this technical feasibility has recently been confirmed by the report of working group 3 of the intergovernmental panel on climate change. the scientific studies carried out by mr mainhausen and cited in the question also support this ambitious objective. to limit climate change to two degrees celsius, to increase by two degrees celsius, the developed countries must take the initiative and collectively reduce their greenhouse gas emissions by 30% by the year 2020 compared to 1990 levels, which is the target we set in the proposals we adopted in january this year in the commission and which were subsequently endorsed by the european council. at the same time, developing countries' emissions should peak between 2020 and 2025. we are facing a global challenge in which the european union, which is responsible for 14% of the total greenhouse gas emissions on the planet, is ready to take international leadership. the european union hopes that the united nations climate change conference in bali this year will give a boost to negotiations on future international cooperation on climate after 2012, which should lead to an agreement on the effort required to achieve member of the commission. mr president, mr posselt, the european union applies strict rules to shipments of waste between member states and to shipments to third countries. the community regulation on shipments of waste aims to prevent the illegal transport of waste, including cases where waste is transported illegally from one member state to another in what is called, as you put it in your question, 'waste tourism'. transport of waste is only allowed if the subsequent recovery or disposal operations meet the environmental protection requirements laid down in european and member state regulations. european legislation sets the strictest requirements for the transport of hazardous waste and waste destined for disposal. it is illegal under these rules to transport such waste to another member state without first notifying the competent authority of the country of dispatch in writing. in addition, authorizations from all the competent authorities of the countries of dispatch, destination and transit must be obtained before the shipment can proceed. the commission's main priorities include ensuring that member states apply european legislation on waste shipments correctly and preventing and reducing illegal shipments. the commission has adopted a number of measures to achieve these objectives. this year awareness-raising events and meetings were organised with the member states in order to improve the implementation and enforcement of waste shipment rules in the states. the adoption by the commission of a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law will also be an important step. we cannot accept the illegal transport of waste from germany to the czech republic, nor the illegal dumping of waste at its final destination. we are not unaware that similar situations may exist in other member states, in addition to what you mention in your question. the commission will monitor the situation closely to ensure that european environmental legislation is properly applied. both the commission and the member states share the responsibility for ensuring that these rules are effectively applied. member states must provide for on-the-spot inspections and controls of shipments of waste and provide for effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties to punish infringements.

applied which has been applied in many other cases to many other countries in the past. in the coming weeks, and once the council's positive decision on the enlargement of the euro area to include cyprus and malta has been confirmed, the commission will issue reports on the state of preparation for the changeover to the euro by both countries. i am also aware of the concern of some members on this point. that report on the degree of readiness for the changeover to banknotes and coins is not a convergence report, it is not a convergence criterion and the commission regularly publishes reports and communications on this subject, as we shall do in the coming weeks. in these circumstances, ladies and gentlemen, we can predict that on 1 january 2008 the euro area will be enlarged to 15 member states with the accession of cyprus and malta. it is a very positive development for these two countries, for the euro area and for the european union as a whole. the euro is undoubtedly one of the greatest achievements of european integration and the more citizens enjoy its benefits, the greater the recognition of the union's ability to offer all its citizens greater guarantees of prosperity and social well-being. ladies and gentlemen, this debate on the application of cyprus and malta to join the euro area is the fourth time that the european institutions have spoken on the composition of the area. the first of these was held in 1998 and aimed to determine which countries would initially be part of the euro area on 1 january 1999. at that time it was decided to join the area of eleven member states. two years later, in 2000, the greek application was examined and it was agreed that greece could join the euro area as from 1 january 2001. last year, all the european institutions discussed and agreed that slovenia would be part of the euro area as from 1 january 2007, and finally this request from cyprus and malta, which i hope will be finally approved by the european council and the ecofin council on 10 july. so it is not at all true that the euro area is, as has been said, a closed club. it's a club that's totally open to all members who want to belong to it and who are prepared and meet the conditions to get to that point. after these four procedures for the creation or enlargement of the euro area, there will be 15 member states from next year, two more with an opt-out clause (the united kingdom and denmark) and 10 member states which are not yet part of the area and which i hope will join in the next few years. without making any forecasts as to when they will be able to meet all the conditions for joining the euro area, i think it is safe to say that, for the next few years, year after year, the european institutions will have to decide on new revenue in the area in accordance with the treaty which proclaims the euro as the official currency of the member states of the union. the treaty also lays down, in articles 121 and 122, the criteria for determining whether a member state fulfils the conditions for adopting the single currency and lays down the procedure to be followed by the european institutions. and since the honourable members have prepared a draft resolution on these procedures for consulting parliament on the enlargement of the area, i should like to refer to that aspect in the second part of my speech. the treaty provides for five players to be involved in the procedure: the commission, the european central bank, parliament, the european council and the ecofin council. but the treaty contains no specific provision as to the time limits within which each institution must give its opinion. the four times we have spoken, the timing is similar: first, the application for membership of the euro area by the member state or member states, which is usually submitted at the beginning of the year preceding the year in which the euro area is wished to be joined; second, the assessment by the commission and the european central bank of whether or not the criteria have been met, which is carried out in the spring; third, the final decision by the council, which takes into account the opinion of parliament and the debate in the european council, which is usually taken in the middle of the year preceding the introduction, and finally, the adoption of the euro by the member state or member states on 1 january of the following year. there are a number of conditions for these steps, and i want to mention them because they affect all our institutions. firstly, why is the euro introduced on 1 january? given the enormous legal, economic, fiscal, accounting and practical implications of currency change, it is absolutely inadvisable to contemplate a date other than 1 january for the adoption of the euro, and i believe there is general agreement on this from all sides. secondly, there is a time limit which should be given to the member state to carry out the preparations for the changeover to the euro in an orderly and effective manner and, having the experience we already have in previous enlargements, it can be said that, in the interests of the citizens of the country concerned, who would be the first to suffer the consequences of an unprepared adoption of the euro, it is desirable to complete the decision-making process by the european institutions several months before 1 january, when the banknotes and coins are introduced and the irrevocable exchange rate in the country that is part of the euro comes into force. these are the practical conditions, and of course neither of these is in the commission's hands. what is left for the commission, in coordination with the european central bank, is to adopt the convergence report on whether or not the criteria are met. and the date on which the commission is to adopt the convergence report is determined, first, by the moment when the member state submits the request - the commission cannot decide on behalf of the member state when the request is to be submitted - and, second, by the moment when the commission can have reliable and rigorous data at its disposal in order to be able to make an adequate, rigorous and correct assessment of whether or not those convergence criteria are met. the date of the commission's convergence report therefore depends on when the member state submits the request and on when the commission can have the appropriate, accurate and valuable data to make the assessment. in 1998 and 2000, the commission adopted the convergence reports, in general terms, at the beginning of may. in 2006 and 2007, the approval was made in mid-may because, as from 2005, the deadline for member states to submit data on their budgetary positions was postponed by one month, from 1 march to 1 april. this has been done in order to obtain reliable and accurate data on the budgetary execution of the candidate country for the euro area in the previous year. experience has shown that the notifications on 1 march did not contain all the precise data needed to give us a fair idea of how the previous year's budget had been closed. in these circumstances, and given that cyprus and malta met the exchange rate stability criterion on 2 may this year, the commission has had two weeks, as it did last year in the case of slovenia, to complete the preparation and adoption of the convergence reports. what i want to say to you with this perhaps too detailed presentation is that all the institutions have a sense of the time limits within which we have to take decisions in this procedure. the time available to parliament is determined, on the one hand, by the approval of the convergence report by the commission and the european central bank, but also, on the other hand, by the dates that the council decides for its decisionmaking procedure, both in the european council and in the meeting of the ecofin council, and that is obviously not in the hands of the commission. in any event, the president of the commission, mr barroso, has written a letter to president pöttering showing the commission's readiness to explore how to enable each institution to exercise in the best possible way the powers which the treaty confers on us in this procedure and the commission wants to reiterate to you today, i want to reiterate to you personally today, in response to this parliament's draft resolution, our willingness to find the form, the procedure, an agreement between the three institutions to improve the way we work, given the objective limitations with which we have to do so in order to take decisions in this matter. in any case, ladies and gentlemen, the committee on economic and monetary affairs knows perfectly well, and you all should know that the commission and i myself are of course at your disposal for all information available before these deadlines expire - on the economic situation of the applicant countries, on the degree of compliance with the convergence criteria - even before the member states submit their applications.

member of the commission. mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to reiterate in this last intervention in the debate my personal and commission congratulations to cyprus and malta for the effort they have made to get here and for the effort they are making to successfully introduce the euro, both for their economy and for their citizens. i think this shows once again that the euro area is not a closed club and that joining the euro is not only an obligation for the member states, but a great opportunity both for those who want to share the single currency with 318 million other europeans and for the countries that already belong to the economic and monetary union. i think it is therefore a good decision to support, as does the langen report, the accession of cyprus and malta to the euro area. two comments on the fulfilment of the criteria: mr langen's speech questioned the way in which cyprus and malta fulfil the criteria or the way in which the commission's convergence report has assessed the fulfilment of the criteria. i should say that the repeal of the excessive deficit procedure in which malta was involved, which took place at the last ecofin council on the commission's proposal, is a necessary condition for malta to meet the maastricht criterion on this point and what the commission's convergence report said on 16 may, namely that if the ecofin council approved the repeal of the excessive deficit, malta would meet it. we have done so in order not to delay the convergence report, because otherwise we would have had to wait until 5 june to publish the convergence report and you would have had even less time to debate it. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. the figures: the deficit and debt figures for cyprus and malta reported under the excessive deficit reporting procedures, which take place twice a year, on 1 april and 1 october, are as reliable - after being analysed by eurostat and published in its opinion on 23 april - as those for the other member states. there is no reservation on the part of eurostat with regard to the figures notified in relation to the deficit and debt. there is no basis for questioning the figures for cyprus and malta and not questioning the figures for france, italy, spain, portugal, germany, sweden, denmark or any other member state. no foundation. there are other difficulties with other figures: there are those with quarterly figures for financial accounts in the national accounts, with unemployment statistics at the moment of the german labour force survey or with french figures, but that is the everyday statistical work, and if parliament wants to give more resources to eurostat, welcome. if parliament wants to support the work of eurostat, you know that i, as the commissioner responsible for eurostat, always appreciate the support of parliament, the commission and eurostat, but i do not want there to be any doubt about the validity, the quality of the figures against which we are assessing whether cyprus and malta meet the convergence criteria. as for the procedure, mr langen, i wanted to address you directly on this point. there is no marginalisation, no will to marginalise, no reason why the commission should want to marginalise parliament or make parliament's work in this debate more difficult. on the contrary, i have expressed, and president barroso has also expressed in his letter, the full availability of the commission and the commissioner for economic and monetary affairs. i want you to listen to me, mr langen, because i am telling you that - i repeat what the president of the commission said in the letter to mr poettering and what i said on 7 june in the econ committee to the coordinators in his presence - we are fully prepared to share information with you, to anticipate the information available. but what they cannot ask the commission to do is to consider that a country definitely meets the deficit criterion when the council has not yet abolished the excessive deficit procedure. and next year, if slovakia makes a claim, we will also have that problem, because slovakia is now included in an excessive deficit procedure which can only be abrogated - if it can be abrogated - once the final figures for the 2007 budget have been validated by eurostat. we will therefore not be able to anticipate, nor will the ecofin council be able to anticipate, decisions on the abrogation of the excessive deficit procedure for slovakia before the dates on which the excessive deficit procedure for malta has been abrogated this year. we can anticipate the convergence report by saying that if the ecofin council approves the derogation, slovakia fulfils the criterion. it's a hypothesis. but we cannot say in february that slovakia meets the deficit criterion when the derogation can only be approved in may or june next year. just as we cannot make a rigorous assessment - and you are right to ask us to make a rigorous assessment - of whether countries meet the maastricht criteria, the convergence criteria, before we know in may 2008 the spring economic forecasts, which cannot be approved or published earlier by the commission and its services, because if we anticipate the spring forecasts they will be winter forecasts and will not be valid for knowing what the economic situation and the spring economic data are. i therefore want to make it clear to this parliament that next year's convergence report cannot be brought forward before may. from there we have to talk, we have to agree between the commission, parliament and council how we can work rigorously, coherently and cooperatively to reach sound decisions that allow us all to work rigorously and make decisions in good time so that the citizens of the next countries to join the 13 current members of the euro area do not suffer the consequences of a late decision and poor preparation for the introduction of euro coins and banknotes. this is the attitude and conviction of the commission, the agreement between the three institutions. it is desirable. it is pointless that in every enlargement of the euro area we are debating here, not about the countries that are joining and the beneficial consequences for their citizens, but about procedures. we must solve this problem, but we will only solve it by maintaining a cooperative attitude between the three institutions and by taking account of the objective limitations with which the three institutions have to make this decision.
