in writing. i voted against the report on the portability directive. the real objective of strengthening the crossborder mobility of workers between member states has clearly been missed. on average, only 10% of all workers in the eu receive an occupational pension. the high minimum standards just adopted mean that there is little interest in setting up or expanding occupational pension schemes because of the expected cost increases of at least 20%. i fear that what workers and employers have created at the national level for mutual benefit over decades is now being called into question. the minimum age for the acquisition of occupational pensions has been abolished. the five-year limitation period has been abolished. the minimum standards are also intended to apply retroactively, which is in clear contradiction with the principle of protection of legitimate expectations. i also voted for the abolition of the dynamisation, which the ecj is likely to interpret as a 'fair adjustment' and interpret as an obligation. if employees who have changed their company are treated in the same way as employees who are still employed, the german federal council calculates that additional costs of 30% will be incurred. eu commissioner špidla has announced that he will present a new proposal. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of workers against the risks of exposure to carcinogens and to the use of carcinogens in the manufacture of foodstuffs.
in writing. i voted against the portability directive because it has failed to achieve its main objective of strengthening the crossborder mobility of workers between member states. the system of transfer of occupational pension rights is only a recommendation to the member states. i have therefore repeatedly advised that the directive should be rejected altogether, as it has become superfluous.

the president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i would like to thank the rapporteur in particular. we have evaluated the recommendations and largely agree with the evaluation and, of course, with the conclusions of parliament on the meda programme. it was found that the support provided by the meda programme was appropriate and made an important contribution to the achievement of the meda objectives. it was also recognised that the aid was in line with the development plans and needs of the beneficiary countries. i would like to make this very specifically because i remember certain discussions. the council welcomes the efforts of the commission which have led to significant improvements in the speed and efficiency of planning under meda ii. the meda programme has now been completed and the transition to the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument has been completed as of 1 january 2007. the neighbourhood and partnership instrument has been created as a tailor-made instrument for the implementation of the european neighbourhood policy. the european parliament's call for cooperation between mediterranean partner countries to be strengthened is reflected in the southern regional programme, which has been endowed with €343.3 million until 2010. we share your view that the continuation of all the objectives of the barcelona process is of crucial importance for the whole region. the fact that we have managed to tackle and develop together, despite the tensions in the region, shows that the barcelona process, the euro-mediterranean dialogue, is still the appropriate framework for achieving change in the mediterranean. the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, through its interparliamentary dialogue, makes an important contribution to the deepening of north-south relations. whether civil society, government or parliament we have the objective of advancing the mediterranean partnership, despite our different structures and tasks, and we want to contribute to it together. i now turn to the part of the report dealing with financial aid to the palestinians. first of all, however, i should like to say that we are following with great concern the recent developments in the palestinian territories, and particularly in the gaza strip. the heavy fighting between fatah and the radical islamist hamas last week has claimed over 100 lives and injured a large number of people. the hamas militias have taken de facto control of the area, using brutal violence against the legitimate national security forces, civilians and humanitarian workers. president abbas has therefore been forced to dissolve the government of national unity, declare a state of emergency and set up an emergency government. the internal palestinian reconciliation achieved in mecca in february with the help of saudi arabia is thus obsolete, and hamas's participation in the government is over. the humanitarian situation in gaza, already difficult, has also deteriorated further. hospitals are completely overwhelmed and medically understaffed. the vast majority of the population in gaza is dependent on food aid. aid agencies have had to suspend some of their work because they fear for the safety of their staff - and rightly so, as the deaths of two unrwa staff members in the fighting have shown. the european union's foreign ministers called at the general council on monday for an immediate end to the violence and assured president abbas of their full support for his decisions. they decided to resume normal relations with the new government of fayyad without delay and declared their intention to create the conditions for the resumption of direct financial and practical assistance. the foreign ministers also reaffirmed their determination not to abandon the people of gaza in their humanitarian emergency. the further detailed consequences to be drawn from the changed situation are currently being discussed. the launch of the tim financing mechanism by the european union in june 2006 has been instrumental in addressing the most urgent needs of the suffering palestinian population. the structure of the tem is transparent and the mechanism has proved to be a flexible and effective instrument. the european commission and the member states have already provided over eur 300 million in aid directly to the palestinian people through tim last year and continue to do so, especially in the current situation. this is something that must be emphasized and stressed again and again, because the public is sometimes told something different. we therefore welcome the decision of the quartet to extend the mandate of the tem for a further three months until the end of september. the report rightly calls on israel to pay the palestinians the customs and tax revenue that has been withheld. the european union has also repeatedly called on israel to do so, most recently in the statement of the general council of 18 june. the israeli government has announced - we have had a dialogue with the israeli foreign minister, mrs livni - that it is now ready to pay. we also expect it to provide a much-needed boost to the palestinian economy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the european union is also already taking action on the necessary reforms of public finances, including financial control and auditing, which you mentioned. the commission is supporting the palestinian ministry of finance with technical assistance in further developing transparent structures for the palestinian budget. the european union's objective is and remains: two states israel and palestine living side by side in peace with each other and with their neighbours in the region. we want to help create better living conditions for the palestinians in the long term, rather than engage in crisis management. the last few weeks have made it abundantly clear why this is so urgently needed.

the president of the council. article 28 of the treaty on european union lays down the principles governing the financing of civilian and military crisis management operations. operations with military or defence implications may not be financed from community funds. athena is the mechanism created by the council in 2004 to manage the financing of the common costs of such operations. the common costs are less than 10% of the total additional costs of an operation. the remainder of the expenditure is financed directly by the member states on a 'costs are borne where they are incurred' basis. athena is managed under the supervision of a special committee composed of representatives of the member states, who are accountable to their national parliaments through their respective ministers. as for operation althea, both the european union and nato are paying their share of shared facilities, personnel, etc. nato does not receive any reimbursement from athena for services rendered.

member of the commission. mr president, on behalf of commissioner mccreevy, i would like to thank warmly the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, and in particular the rapporteur, mr fruteau, for his excellent work in preparing the report on the review of the remedies directive in the area of public procurement. before listening to members’ remarks, i should like to congratulate mr fruteau on his election to the french parliament. i wish him all the best in this new challenge, and i am sure he will continue to fight for european values from a different perspective. i also want to pay tribute to the committee chairman, the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs for the way in which they conducted the negotiations between our three institutions. public procurement is a cornerstone of the internal market and accounts for about 16% of eu gdp. it is therefore crucial that public procurement markets be open and transparent, guaranteeing fair competition between bidders from different member states. only this will lead to the best value for money for public authorities in terms of procurement. let me underline that the ultimate beneficiaries of this are the european citizens and taxpayers. european public procurement rules contribute to more open, transparent and competitive procurement markets. with the rules in place, we now need to make sure that they are respected. the commission has identified situations where rejected bidders in a public procurement procedure encounter difficulties in seeking legal redress. this is especially the case when the public contract has already been concluded. in such situations a rejected bidder very often cannot reverse the decision, even if he is in the right. the new directive aims to remedy this in two ways. first, by imposing a mandatory 10-day standstill period between the communication of the award decision and the conclusion of the public contract. second, by introducing a new mechanism which enables a national court to declare public contracts ‘ineffective’. ineffectiveness implies that the contract is null and void. ineffectiveness is the proposed sanction for contracts which have been illegally awarded to a single supplier without prior transparency and competitive tendering. ineffectiveness is also the proposed sanction where the 10-day standstill period has not been respected and the tenderer’s chances of obtaining the contract have been adversely affected. the commission believes that by strengthening national review procedures in this manner, business will have stronger incentives to bid for contracts anywhere in the eu. adoption of the proposed directive should, therefore, have a major impact, stimulating a further opening-up of the public procurement markets. i draw your attention to the fact that the compromise contains an obligation that member states report to the commission on the specific decisions of national review bodies which are based on the directive. this obligation has been included in the text at the request of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. the commission wishes to underline the principle of loyal cooperation which member states have to observe in fulfilling this obligation. a statement along these lines will be added to the minutes of the council meeting at which the proposed directive is adopted. the report adopted last may by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, under the leadership of mr fruteau, has played a very important role in the negotiations. the compromise that is now on the table as amendment 86 seeks to meet the objectives of the committee and, in particular, its call for a strengthening of national review procedures in the area of public procurement. let me conclude that european companies today need open public procurement markets. effective procedures for seeking redress are essential to make sure that public contracts ultimately go to the company that has made the best offer. this will help to build confidence among businesses and citizens that public procurement procedures are fair and correctly implemented. this new directive constitutes another major step towards more competition in our european single market.

course, if the eu council had not achieved a result, europe would not have been destroyed, but the consequences would undoubtedly have been difficult to describe. the fact that this was avoided is therefore of the utmost importance. the unification of brussels makes it possible to preserve the substance of the constitutional treaty. i think we are all agreed in the end that the outcome of the european council is a success. it is a success for europe. it is also a success of the european parliament. you have always defended the substance of the constitutional treaty, and now the reform treaty can enter into force in time for the 2009 european elections, and this is of the utmost importance for all those who will be standing before the citizens. (applause from the centre) the reform treaty takes account of the citizens' concerns about a supposed european superstate, about the over-abandoning of the identity of the nation states. i do not share these concerns, but i had to respect them and i respected them. that is why we have decided to abolish the use of state symbols and names in the reform treaty. at the same time, the reform treaty is making important progress in the european union's action. we have even developed some areas beyond the eu treaty. climate protection and energy solidarity have been included, national parliaments are being involved even more in shaping national european policies, the competences between the eu and the member states are being defined even more clearly, and the conditions for enhanced cooperation, especially in the field of internal and judicial policy, have been facilitated. ladies and gentlemen, the reform treaty will bring to life three essential elements for the future of the european union. first, the eu's ability to act, both internally and externally. the union's single legal personality and the extension of the decision-making process in the council by qualified majority contribute to this. the new double majority system, which gives greater weight to the demographic factor, will only come into effect in 2014, at the same time as the first reduced commission and with a transitional period until 2017, but it is becoming a reality. this is not a sufficiently high estimate of the progress of europe. the new treaty will also bring greater continuity to the work of the council through a president of the european council and the team presidencies. the reform treaty also brings progress in policies, for example in the field of the european union's external action. a coherent foreign policy, speaking with one voice, is becoming more important every day for a europe that wants to assert itself in the world. we will have the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, he will head the foreign affairs council, he will have a european diplomatic service and he will be a member of the commission, namely as vice-president of the commission. this is a political quantum leap for europe. (applause from the centre) the european union is also making important progress in the area of justice and home affairs, which is of great interest to the people, for example in the joint fight against crossborder crime. the new qualified majority voting system will considerably speed up the procedures. we will also be able to make it clearer that transfers of competences are not one-way streets through which new competences are always being added to the european union, but that there can also be situations in which competences are transferred back to the national states when this is necessary. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. ladies and gentlemen, secondly, with the reform treaty we make it clear: closer ties with the people for europe! the european parliament has been asked to vote on the draft budget for the european union. progress in the social dimension will be made effective and there will be clearer regulations in the area of social security. in addition, the igc will adopt a protocol in which services of general economic interest are recognised and it is made clear that member states have a high degree of freedom of design in the non-commercial sector. i am very glad - and i think that is what unites us in the vast majority here - that we have succeeded in finding a solution for the charter of fundamental rights as well. the charter of fundamental rights strengthens the rights of citizens vis-à-vis the institutions, the charter of fundamental rights is given legal binding force, which i believe is a good thing for a europe that is conscious of its values. (applause from the centre) we know that britain has chosen its own path because of its own legal tradition. we have to respect that. but the alternative would have been to restrict the legal binding of all, which would not have been acceptable to the majority of member states. it is therefore good that this has been avoided, and i believe that this is also the majority view of parliament. (applause from the centre) ladies and gentlemen, finally, the third element which makes the progress of the new reform treaty visible: more rights for parliaments! the treaty reform will make the european parliament the co-legislator with equal rights, and the european parliament will in future elect the president of the european commission. at the same time, it was important for many member states to give greater recognition to the role of national parliaments. this will be done in a new article. we have also agreed to strengthen the parliaments' control of subsidiarity, but we have respected the right of proposal of the european commission and there will be no veto of individual national parliaments in the future. i think it's right. (applause from the centre) ladies and gentlemen, treaty reform was one of the objectives of the german presidency of the council of the eu. the other objective of the presidency of the european council was to reorient the content of the european union towards the things we can only achieve together in the european union. because i am deeply convinced that only by acting together and in a targeted way can we achieve tangible progress for our citizens. of course, we have seen it again in the decisions of the eu council, there will always be exceptions, there will always be cases where individual member states decide not to participate in certain policies, or not to participate at first, while others do so within the framework of the treaties. this is not the case with the so-called two-speed europe. let me be perfectly frank: i don't think that's the case. (applause from the centre) this must not be the aim of our policy, otherwise we will open new holes in europe and weaken the european parliament. it is worth every effort to seek again and again the common path of all the member states of the european union. an african proverb says: "if you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together". i believe that this african proverb contains the wisdom of the idea of european unity. only by acting together and in a targeted manner can we preserve the great and unique thing that has been the idea of european unity for over fifty years: peace, freedom and legal certainty for the citizens of europe. only by acting together and in a targeted manner can we strengthen citizens' rights in the european union, for example by incorporating the prüm treaty into the eu legal framework. this will allow for enhanced police cooperation in the crossborder fight against terrorism, crime and illegal migration in the eu. only by acting together and in a targeted way can we increase the competitiveness of the european location. that is what the roaming regulation, which we have signed here, for example, stands for. only by acting together and with purpose can we tackle one of the greatest challenges facing humanity, the threat of climate change. the decisions taken by the spring european council on an integrated energy and climate policy are groundbreaking. it was also the prerequisite for the g8 meeting to reach agreement on the need for a follow-up agreement under the kyoto protocol under the auspices of the united nations, and all the g8 participants have made themselves known to this. this would not have been possible without the spring european council and the support of the european parliament. this is a defence of european interests! president of the commission. let me express my appreciation for the achievements of chancellor angela merkel. a very difficult task has turned into a success for europe. in particular, i would like to acknowledge the political ambition that led the chancellor to insist on a reform treaty that would give the union the right instruments to face the challenges of the 21st century. chancellor merkel and the entire team of the german presidency deserve the highest appreciation for their tenacious struggle to achieve the objectives and for their ability to sustain the negotiations to a successful conclusion. this compliment is not just to the outcome of the june council, but to the total number of successes achieved by the german presidency during the whole semester! (applause from the centre) we can honestly say that europe is fully on track. i believe it's useful to remember where we were some time ago. let me step back from the events of last week and look back over the last two years. just over a year ago the commission adopted an approach which i called 'the twin-track approach'. the first track was for the european union to use the existing treaties more effectively to deliver results for europe's citizens. we have done this, for example, through our package of measures on energy and climate change; through our focus on innovation; through our drive against red tape; through legislation which delivers practical benefits for consumers, such as the legislation we proposed on roaming, which was signed before us here today. i want to thank this house our interests and our values in the 21st century. i believe that the discussion on the berlin declaration was an important moment to gather the necessary support which made it possible to achieve good because the twin-track approach was the right approach. we cannot give our citizens the impression that we are just talking about institutions: we have to concentrate on practical results for our citizens, and governments and citizens will have the confidence to tackle sometimes very difficult institutional issues if they have the confidence that the institutions can deliver when it comes to stress this point. let us not forget that before this council we started from a division between 18 member states which had rectified the constitutional treaty and 9 member states which had not ratified it, and 2 of them explicitly refused the constitutional treaty after a referendum. now all 27 member states are united around a common mandate for a reform treaty. the fact that we managed to reach an agreement is already an outstanding political result and we should be grateful for the willingness of all governments to compromise. now we should look forward to the ratification process as a great moment of solidarity and unity in europe and as a historic opportunity to consolidate the enlarged european union. at the same time, the advances from the nice treaty will guarantee a union with a greater capacity to act to deliver results. the reform treaty will probably not be an example of the finest poetry, but i have no doubt that it will be a very good example of excellent prose if it is focused precisely on the capacity of the european institutions to act. i said before the european council that we really needed to reinforce the european union's capacity to act. i believe the reform treaty will bring important advances to the union and will reinforce its ability to act. first of all, the union will be fully consolidated by overcoming the pillar structure and by acquiring a single personality. in this area of capacity to act, i would like to stress in particular three specific points. first, the most substantial advances are in the area of justice and home affairs. there are more than 40 new cases of qualified majority voting in the reform treaty. they include external border control, asylum, migration, criminal law and police cooperation. the treaty therefore intends to fully integrate these areas into the community's method of decision-making. it is in fact the 'communitarianisation' of the third pillar. this is a fundamental reform which will create a true space of freedom, security and justice in europe and it will be a priority for the rest of the mandate of this commission. the union needs the efficiency which more qualified majority voting brings. second, the reform treaty will offer new possibilities and reinforce legal bases to deal with the challenges of energy policy and climate change. in particular, the commission is very pleased with the solidarity clause on energy security and agreement to add combating climate change to the treaty. energy security and climate change are now core priorities for the union. it is right that this is reflected in the treaties. third, the reform treaty will enhance the union's cohesion as regards external affairs. in the 21st century world, it is only by combining the forces of our member states and our institutions that we can compete with other leading powers. our prosperity, our freedom and our security depend on the capacity to compete at a global level, the capacity to promote our interests and our values. europe will increasingly speak with one voice in diplomatic, security and defence issues in trade, in monetary aid, in development, and as such will be better equipped to defend our values and interests in world politics. we want the conditions and the instruments to shape globalisation and we cannot miss such a historic opportunity. but the reform treaty also addressed other issues, namely in terms of accountability and democratic legitimacy. with the reform treaty, the union wants to reinforce its accountability and democratic legitimacy. again let me emphasize three cases of clear improvement compared to the nice treaty. first, the european parliament wants to have greater participation in the legislative process of the union by an increase in codecision procedures. under the new treaty, the vast majority of european laws will be adopted jointly by the european parliament and the council, with full respect for the commission's right of initiative. secondly, national parliaments want to be more involved in the workings of the union. this is about subsidiarity and we are for subsidiarity. the new treaty will amend the protocol on subsidiarity and proportionality. this commission has always welcomed a greater role for national parliaments. however, the commission also made clear that involving national parliaments in scrutinising subsidiarity should not undermine the essentials of how the european union works. first, any new procedure on subsidiarity would have to respect the community method and the commission's right of initiative. secondly, the european parliament and the council should be on an equal footing. finally, the thresholds regarding majorities should rise to reflect the importance of the procedure. we managed to secure all our demands and as such to preserve the institutional balance of the union, while reinforcing the control of subsidiarity. thirdly, and in my view this is one of the most important points, the reform treaty will give legal force to the charter of fundamental rights. the fact that the charter is legally binding is a powerful symbol of the strong ties that exist between the union and european citizens. it is also a very good signal and symbol that we are committed to fundamental rights. we cannot promote fundamental rights all over the world and not say that we consider them binding at home. (applause) i would like to thank the charter is not, and was never intended to be, a charter of the rights of european institutions above the member states. the charter is for european citizens and the rights of the citizens against any power that could limit those rights. the charter will be a safeguard, both for european citizens and for national institutions, and will be a central part of the system of checks and balances in our union of law, because that is what makes us different from many other projects: we are a union based on law. i have always said that a step back from the existing acquis would be unacceptable. this is particularly important in respect of the single market. the results of the european council were entirely positive from the commission's point of view, specifically from the point of view of the commission's competence. the protocols on services of general interest and on the internal market and competition, both proposed by the commission, guarantee a fair and undistorted functioning of the single market, while respecting legitimate concerns expressed by some member states. before concluding, i should like to warn against the temptation of a perverse alliance between those who resist a political europe and those who oppose the single market. to those who support an open and global europe, i say that they will only get this if they support political integration. without political power, europe will never be able to shape globalisation and to defend its interests and values in the world. europe will never be able to defend its commitment to an open economy and to open societies. (applause) to those who accept a strong political europe, but are not as enthusiastic about economic integration, i say that they will only get that strong political europe if they support the single market and economic integration. the president of the council. mr president ! it is an interesting situation in the european parliament when all the heads are still there. i am grateful for the debate on this. i would like to make two brief points. firstly, the question of the internal market and competition, which has caused great concern here. there was a discussion in the council about whether competition is an objective of our efforts. i believe that competition is not an end in itself, but a means. that is why we have removed it from the heading on objectives, but have made it absolutely clear by the protocol which we are going to insert on the internal market and competition that this instrument will remain unchanged and in its full meaning, and the commission has also clearly taken this into account. so nothing changes. employment and prosperity are our goals, but our goal is not competition as such, but competition as a means. secondly, a lot has been said about the voting system. i want to repeat for the sake of clarity: all possible forms of weighting, including root systems, are conceivable if they are taken as the only form of coordination. if we started at zero, we could talk about anything. but there is a double majority, and this double majority brings the weighting between population and the principle of 'one country, one vote'. it is only in this duplication that the voting system is acceptable, and we have now also found a way which leads us back to real international world problems and at the same time has a high degree of justice. i would like to close by thanking you very much. i can report on behalf of our government that we had a cabinet meeting today in which we took stock of the situation and that all members of the government were proud to have led this presidency with enthusiasm and a lot of commitment, and that the social democrats as well as the christian democratic members of the government made their contribution to this. member of the commission. mr president, the commission has on many occasions declared – and, through its actions, proved – its commitment to ensuring that the legislative framework on genetically modified food and feed, which was approved by the european parliament and the council, is fully respected. we have the obligation – and i believe we are delivering on this obligation – to make sure that the legislation is properly and fully respected. under the legislation, gm food and feed can be legally put on the market only if it is safe and appropriately labelled. i would remind the house of how the legislation provides for the division of work between risk assessment and risk management. the commission has no discretion on the safety assessment of a gm product. the legislation clearly distinguishes between risk assessment, which is carried out by efsa, and risk management, which is carried out by the commission. this approach is defined not only by general food law but also by the regulation on gm food and feed. whenever new scientific questions emerge, the commission adheres to the separation of competences and asks efsa to evaluate the information and its impact on the risk assessment of a product. the commission’s role is to take relevant risk management decisions, provided that, and only when, such a risk is identified by efsa as the european union’s body responsible for risk assessment. in other words, we manage a risk once it has been identified and assessed by the body responsible. it was a very specific decision, when the legislation was adopted, to give the risk assessment to a separate independent body. however, if there is no risk identified by the authority, then there will be no sound scientific basis for the commission to take a risk management decision. on this specific issue, mon 863 had already been evaluated twice in 2004 before the authorisation was adopted. in both cases, efsa concluded that mon 863 maize would not have an adverse effect, and this opinion was reached with the involvement of the national authorities of the member states and was further reviewed and confirmed by the authority in 2006 following a specific request to the commission by the honourable member ms breyer. there were intensive repeated analyses, which were carried out as part of the authorisation procedure, and then there was the publication by professor séralini in march this year – that is the sequence of events. the work presented by professor séralini was not a new study but only a statistical review of the existing rat-feeding study, which supported the authorisation of this product in the european union. despite the fact that it was not a new study but only a statistical review, as soon as the commission became aware of professor séralini’s paper, it immediately asked efsa to analyse it to verify whether the newly proposed statistical interpretation was well founded and, more importantly, whether the statistical differences were relevant for food and feed safety. in order to take into account all new elements and thus to eliminate any possible sources of uncertainty, efsa conducted a new review asking member states to provide any relevant analysis or comments, set up a specific task force of internal and external statistical experts and held a meeting with the author of the statistical review. in the commission’s view, the procedures set up by efsa to evaluate the review of professor séralini’s report represent a sufficient guarantee of independence and expertise. efsa first responded to the commission request in march by discussing the issue at the plenary meeting of the gmo panel, before issuing a statistical report and a scientific statement by the panel on 20 june.in particular, the authority underlines that the statistical analysis made by the authors of the paper did not take into account certain important statistical considerations and that the assumptions underlying the statistical methodology employed by the authors led to misleading results. the conclusion of the authority is that the paper does not present a sound scientific justification to question the safety of mon 863 maize and, therefore, it sees no reason to revise its previous opinions that mon 863 maize would not have an adverse effect in the context of the proposed use. parliament will be informed in more detail of the background i have outlined in the replies to the written questions on this subject by ms breyer, which are currently being finalised following the recent efsa statement. against this background, two conclusions emerge. first, and most importantly, there is at this stage no scientific basis to question either the safety of mon 863 or its status as a legally commercialised product. second, the conclusions of the eu official body for risk assessment, made up of some of the best specialists in europe, have been drawn after consultation of the national competent authorities as well as external experts. by trusting the outcome of this work, which confirms the previous evaluations, the commission has, i believe, acted as a responsible risk manger, especially within the context of the legislation and the apportionment of responsibilities as i explained them during my introduction. the commission will continue to work along these lines on the basis of a precautious and science-based approach. the commission, i would emphasise, has full determination to make a case-by-case risk management decision taking into account any scientific questions emerging during the evaluation procedure or even after the authorisation. we will always be vigilant; we will always be ready to examine every new piece of scientific information that emerges. but, of course, our final decision will have to be based on the risk assessment, which will be done by the body in charge of this responsibility based on european legislation. we believe that our legislation and the commission’s approach offer the best way to provide our citizens with the high level of safety they expect and demand. i hope that i can count on the trust and support of the european parliament as we continue our rigorous and impartial approach.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. it is not the commission's intention to make a distinction between the two. it is not the council of ministers that wanted an independent efsa, an authority whose statements could be relied upon, an authority which was not in danger of receiving studies of compliance. the european parliament had then asked efsa to carry out the risk assessment of gmos and the council of ministers had supported this in the co-decision procedure. in april 2004, efsa assessed mon 863 maize as being as safe as conventional maize. a second efsa safety assessment carried out in october 2004 came to the same conclusion. this, of course, undermines the worldview of the green soul, and because it is not allowed to be what green does not want, it is commissioned to conduct its own study. the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of genetically modified maize. a scoundrel who thinks evil! the efsa experts then requested a repeat of the rat test. and again, there was no sign of any acute toxicological effects. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the so-called scientific results of the green study were therefore once again deliberate panic-mongering, deliberate uncertainty among the population, popular deception! it is the typical ideologically motivated policy of prevention with which they are so happy to campaign. they waste taxpayers' money by demanding repeated repetitions of the efsa risk assessments. but, for example, will they also question the nutritional profiles of the efsa on the health claims regulation? member of the commission. madam president, i think i should begin where vice-president vidal-quadras ended, by first of all thanking him for all his work and his dedication. i should also like to thank the committee on industry, research and energy for the active debate and those who made it possible for this report to be adopted within such a short time limit. this is really an achievement and one that is very much appreciated. the report, if adopted – and i hope it will be adopted tomorrow – will pave the way for a commission legislative proposal which we are aiming to have ready by september. it is really necessary to have the report and that we spend the remaining months of july and august preparing a good legislative proposal that will really reflect on all the points raised by the parliament. i would like to begin by saying why we need this proposal. i think it is very important never to lose sight of the reason why the commission really believes in this proposal. from a formal point of view, there is the argument that two reports by the commission and the final report on the sector inquiry on energy clearly indicated that there is a need for new legal measures at european level to achieve the basic goals of security of supply and competitiveness. however, these are not the only reasons. there has been a substantial change in the energy world which justifies this proposal. firstly, we have historically high energy prices. the price of oil today at usd 70 per barrel is definitely very high. we are hearing less from those who usually argue that oil prices will come down. if oil prices are high, it means that gas prices are also high and it has an influence on the price of coal – basically, all energy costs are higher. we can predict that high prices will prevail due to greater consumption and with increased global demand due to the growing population. the second challenge, that of climate change, is much more clearly pronounced. we know that the energy sector is a major contributor of greenhouse gases, so we need to strengthen the instruments to fight against climate change. last but not least, there is also the challenge of eu enlargement. with new member states joining the european union, we have a much greater need for stronger solidarity mechanisms to be in place in the energy sector in the european union. many of these countries depend on just one supplier and are extremely vulnerable if supplies are disrupted. the energy policy objectives – security of supply, sustainability and competitiveness – very much depend on the situation on the eu common market. on 1 july 2007, there was a major change in perception because now each consumer legally has a chance to choose his supplier. this should bring a real message for investment and should bring better quality. but the message was downplayed because, in many member states, steps have been taken only half-heartedly and not consistently enough. it has been said that world commodity prices are rising because of liberalisation, but the reason has never been liberalisation. the reason is that liberalisation has never happened, which means that, whatever steps are taken, we must provide guarantees that each citizen and each company in the european union has the opportunity and the right to choose a supplier. if the price or the service is not satisfactory, then it must be changed without fearing this process. i believe that it is absolutely necessary to take stronger measures that bring more competition and more europe, because europe’s strength is in its scale and scope. the main measures were well reflected by the rapporteur. i would just like to reflect on a couple of them. unbundling is definitely the key. we are very glad of the wording on the unbundling of electricity. with respect to gas, some additional arguments should be put forward because, basically, the gas situation is no different. as regards gas as well, if unbundling is not done properly, supplies will not reach consumers and, as a result, the market will starve from the lack of gas. transparency is important. with regard to regulation, we should look at two levels. firstly, we should look at the level of cross-border market energy flows and, secondly, see that national regulators should have powers, but also obligations that new investments are made. they are not responsible merely for overseeing the market. they should actually be responsible for those investments being made. cooperation between transmission system operators should be strengthened, as should interconnection policies. i would emphasise also that there have been a couple of other good, important points on energy efficiency, smart grids, biogas and balance with long-term contracts. i would defend one point that perhaps was avoided in the report, or said very cautiously. on regional cooperation, developments of the pentalateral market definitely demonstrate that are many opportunities also working on the regional market. at the same time, i agree with parliament that we should always be cautious not to split the internal market but actually to use this initiative to promote the whole market. in conclusion, i would again like to thank all involved. each of the points made in the report will be taken into due account in the commission proposal. we should not forget that energy is a particular commodity, like earth, water and air. at the same time, i could say that it is a scarcer commodity at this stage, until we have learnt how to get more energy from the sun, the wind or from biomass.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the rapporteur for this important report which follows on from the presentation of an initiative by the commission. it is clear that the protection of critical infrastructure is a priority for the european commission as well as for the member states, partly because the need to protect critical infrastructure from, for example, a terrorist attack also stems from the nature of the infrastructure itself and from the interconnection and interdependence between them. if a physical or technological infrastructure of a member state is attacked, the effect is inevitably transmitted to other member states. this is why a common european framework for prevention and protection is needed. we thought the best way forward was to involve the private sector first. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's research programmes are properly coordinated and that the results of the research are available to the european community. the idea is to have real security programmes for the different infrastructure sectors and a real network of liaison officers to guarantee this common european framework. our idea is to consider only those infrastructures which are truly transnational and certainly not those which are confined to the territory of a single member state, except where the implications of this critical infrastructure go beyond the national borders of that state. as you know, last december we adopted a communication to establish a european programme for the protection of european initiative to protect critical energy, transport and technological infrastructures, which require strong prevention and protection because the threat of terrorism is unfortunately directed member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to warmly thank the committee on transport and tourism and in particular the rapporteur, mr ferber, for the excellent work they have carried out in the preparation of your report on the postal directive. this is all the more impressive as the preparation involved five other committees and nearly 600 amendments. moreover, the dossier is highly sensitive politically and technically complex. our proposal is based on sound preparation. it is not the implementation of abstract theories dreamed up in an ivory tower or based on ideological zeal. market opening is not an end in itself, but good for the consumer, good for business and therefore for the whole economy. after months of discussion there is always a risk that we may lose sight of the original intention. therefore let me just remind you of what our proposal actually entails. first and foremost, the commission’s proposal aims to guarantee a high quality universal service for all users throughout the european union. postal users and consumers are entitled to top-class postal services. they must be accessible to all at affordable prices. secondly, based on detailed study and wide consultation, the commission confirms in its proposal that 2009 is the target date for the abolition of any remaining exclusive rights and monopolies. such exclusive rights and monopolies prevent competition and the positive effects it has had on innovation, quality and prices. thirdly, our proposal confirms the availability of a broad range of financing mechanisms member states may choose from in order to finance any net cost or unfair burden the universal service obligation may impose on the universal service providers. fourthly, the proposal allows for more flexibility in terms of pricing of postal services so that they can better reflect actual costs, while maintaining the possibility for uniform tariffs for consumer or single-piece tariff mail. the commission attaches great importance to the role postal services play for territorial and social cohesion. uniform tariffs for consumer mail are a reflection of this. the proposal also reinforces consumers’ rights in terms of redress, for example. fifthly, the proposal seeks to amend provisions concerning authorisation and licensing to reduce unjustified barriers to entry. the proposal also clarifies rules on access to postal infrastructure. finally, the proposal provides for greater clarity on the role and independence of national regulatory authorities. these elements build on the success achieved to date with the gradual opening of the market and will provide a framework that will allow the postal sector to develop its potential. it is truly the final step in a long process started the better part of two decades ago. it is common knowledge that a ‘communications revolution’ is taking place. this is a significant challenge for all of us in our daily lives. it poses a threat for those postal operators that fail to adapt. no reserved area can protect any postal operator from the competition from other means of communication. the only option is to reform and to adapt and to turn the challenge into an opportunity. this fast-changing context makes it all the more necessary to finalise the reform process which started more than 15 years ago. the european parliament has shaped this reform significantly at all stages. the commission is ready to assist so that the internal market on postal services can finally be accomplished. experience with market opening to date has been overwhelmingly positive. efficiency, quality and performance have substantially increased. a high-quality universal service at affordable prices is being provided throughout the european union. it is our joint responsibility that this continues to be the case. full market opening is the right way forward. in the past months some have tried to portray market opening and the success of other postal operators as threats. however, most have now realised that these are challenges that we must face and that it is much more important to focus on how to face them. on the whole, the constructive approach prevails. this makes me optimistic that common ground on this important file can be found at the end of the day. in conclusion, this directive constitutes an essential element of the lisbon agenda. the time is now ripe to give eu citizens the choice they are entitled to and expect. mail users and consumers will be the main beneficiaries of the directive. market opening in 2009 will introduce controlled and regulated competition that will foster innovation, new business models and new services. it is not the question of dividing up the cake differently, or of introducing reform at the expense of the people working in the sector, but it is the question of increasing the size of the market and letting everyone benefit from this.

some of the new member states are, for example: they charge a very high toll for the transport of goods by rail. the eight highest rail user charges are levied in the new member states. at the same time, this high toll subsidizes passenger transport, which receives little or no government subsidy, and allows goods to be transported duty-free on the road. this is a model to shift transport from rail to road - the exact opposite of what the commissioner responsible, the eu, always claims to want to do. so we want a fair competition. this fair competition is not yet complete. the railway companies, which have no long tradition of state ownership, are the ones who feel themselves handicapped in europe. these include complaints that network access or a favourable route cannot be granted because it has already been awarded to the group's own railway, that their wishes cannot be met because a loop has previously been extended or a bypass has been dismantled by the state-owned companies, that slow stops are imposed without reason so that the wishes of the new freight transport companies cannot be met, that track prices are drastically increased when state-owned railway companies are sold to another company, that cross-subsidisation is not prevented, that non-state-owned companies often pay higher energy prices than subsidiaries. you see, despite our success, there's still a lot to do! regulations which created the single aviation market in europe. the creation of this single aviation market has enabled air transport in europe to expand in an unprecedented way. the number of served is increasing, especially in remote areas. the emergence of new competitors has led to a significant reduction in fares on many routes. more and more europeans can travel by air. this contributes to economic growth and the creation of direct and indirect jobs. in view of this success, the commission intends to maintain the basic principles of this liberalized market. the proposal is simply to simplify the consolidation of existing legislation. it also proposes some adjustments to improve the efficiency of its application. firstly, the revision allows for a cleaning of the text to remove obsolete parts related to the transition phase towards the liberalised market. the text is clarified, ambiguities are removed, and three regulations are consolidated into one text. secondly, has to invest more in a modernization agenda. just over seven years ago, the then prime minister of portugal, antónio guterres, came to this house to present the lisbon strategy, which has been the roadmap for the modernisation of the european economy and society. it is therefore with particular pleasure that i can tell you that the 'lisbon strategy' will once again be at the centre of our concerns. the strategy set out in 2000 to strengthen competitiveness with social cohesion, by focusing on knowledge and innovation, remains on track and enjoys the support of the main european political forces. what we are going to do is to actively contribute to a new round of the lisbon agenda which will be adopted in the spring of 2008 during the slovenian presidency. but we will prepare for this new cycle by maintaining the balance between the three components of that agenda, the economic component, the social component and the environmental component. the review of the internal market will allow emphasis to be placed on the competitiveness of enterprises, the opening up of markets and the elimination of context costs, as well as the role that cultural industries can play in terms of job creation, economic growth and innovation. the next six months will also be particularly important for energy and environmental policy options, and in this respect europe can have only one objective: to maintain its leadership in the environmental field and, in particular, in the fight against climate change. we will immediately pursue the objectives of promoting the debate on a technological action plan for energy and the environment and will stress the role of biofuels, particularly in the context of the relationship resulting from the first summit between the european union and brazil. we want to give the social dimension of the 'lisbon strategy' the visibility and relevance it deserves. ten years after the launch of the 'european employment strategy', we believe it is essential to promote debate on the best ways of coordinating employment policies in order to foster the creation of sustainable jobs in a globally competitive environment. this line of action of the portuguese presidency will be closely linked to the qualification of human resources, the reconciliation of work and family life, and the fight against poverty and exclusion. the european social model, in its acknowledged diversity, requires joint reflection on the sustainability of pension systems and the identification of the necessary reforms in labour markets and in systems of protection against social risks. in this context, the debate on 'flexicurity' should be guided by the search for integrated and balanced solutions, a practical translation into general principles common at european level that takes into account the diversity of social realities in the different member states of the union. ladies and gentlemen, for the portuguese presidency, one of the structural values of the european project is based on the binomial freedom and security. in this context, strengthening police and judicial cooperation in the fight against terrorism and crime will be a priority for the presidency. terrorism remains one of the greatest threats to international peace and security. but democracies are not afraid of terrorism and know how to stand firm in the face of this threat. if there is a good example of this firmness, it was given last week by the british government, to whom i would like to express the solidarity of all the countries of the union. the fight against terrorism must therefore remain a common objective for all member states. because only european cooperation can prevent, protect and prosecute terrorism. the portuguese presidency will work towards the implementation of the ongoing initiatives under the eu counter-terrorism strategy, the implementation of the counter-terrorism action plan and the continuation of the implementation of the strategy against radicalisation and the recruitment of terrorists, which will be reviewed over the next six months. we therefore consider it urgent to replace mr de vries and to define the means and mandate which will enable him to carry out his task effectively. ladies and gentlemen, there is no freedom without security. this is the lesson of history. that is why the union's security policy is also essential to preserve the open and tolerant nature of european societies. i am therefore proud to say that it was portugal that proposed, and it was also a portuguese company that conceived, the technological solution (sis-one4all) so that the new member states could fully join the schengen area and so that the borders with these countries could disappear at the end of the portuguese presidency. we shall thus be satisfying one of the greatest aspirations of these citizens: the free movement of persons within the union. i would also like to say a word about immigration policy. we shall pay particular attention to this during our presidency. europe is now a place of welcome for millions of immigrants who live here, work here, educate their children here and whose contribution is indispensable to european economic growth. we must therefore build a european immigration policy based on the fight against illegal immigration, but also on a policy of inclusion and integration of legal immigrants and effective cooperation with the countries of origin, which is capable of regulating migration flows to mutual benefit. only a policy that acts on the origin and the destination, on the causes and the effects, will be able to cope with the scale of the phenomenon and be in harmony with our values and our responsibilities. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the current international situation in turn creates special responsibilities for the european union and i would now like to tell you about the european union's foreign policy agenda under the portuguese presidency. european citizens are unequivocal in their demand for active international leadership, based on the values of international law, mutual respect, dialogue and concertation. the expectations of the international community are also clear: the union must be committed and consistently involved in major international issues. the second half of 2007 saw the convergence of key decisions on sensitive issues on the global agenda - the future of kosovo, the nuclear issue in iran, the humanitarian crisis in darfur - with a series of particularly relevant bilateral summits: india, china, russia and ukraine. the relationship with the united states, within the framework defined by the washington summit under the german presidency, will be closely monitored, as the strategic importance of the transatlantic relationship requires and requires. we will in all cases assume the responsibilities of the presidency, in close coordination with the high representative for foreign affairs, javier solana, and the european commission. but i would like to highlight three initiatives to which we are particularly attached and which deserve special mention: the summit with brazil, which has already taken place, the second summit with africa and, finally, the euro-mediterranean meetings. in this first week of the presidency we have already held the summit with brazil, with a view to taking our relations to a higher level of mutual knowledge and close cooperation at all levels. this initiative is particularly dear to us portuguese, who share the language and much of our culture and history with brazil. we want to create the political conditions so that, like the other emerging economic powers, a formal relationship can be institutionalized for the future, mutually beneficial for europe and brazil, thus also contributing to the deepening of the more general relationship we want with all of latin america. closer relations with brazil will also bring concrete results in responding to global challenges. the summit last week with president lula da silva also allowed a window of opportunity to remain open which must now be exploited in the doha round negotiations, and we will do everything we can to support the european commission's action in this context. i am of the opinion that the doha round negotiations represent a relevant element in the regulation of globalisation and that their conclusion will be very positive and that they should continue to be a priority for the european institutions. the euromed ministerial meetings, in turn, are part of a rounded cooperation framework, the so-called barcelona process and the new neighbourhood policy, but they underline the value we attach to the relaunching of a thorough political debate with our partners on the southern shore of the mediterranean. we share common concerns and are faced with development and social cohesion challenges which underline the growing interdependence of the two shores of the mediterranean and we are convinced that we can contribute to overcoming some of the blockages in key areas such as the management of migration flows and the contribution that diasporas can make to the development of the countries of origin, with the support and commitment of european countries and the relevant international institutions. finally, we are proposing to hold the second european union-africa summit, after having been the basis for the previous one in cairo in 2000, which was held, as you will recall, under the portuguese presidency. without ignoring some of the difficulties that will have to be overcome, it is our conviction that nothing can justify the fact that for more than seven years there have been no such meetings at the highest level when the relationship between two continents is at stake, which are so close from a historical point of view and so interdependent in today's world. portugal is particularly well placed to assume this responsibility and is counting strongly on the contribution of the african union and all european and african countries to make this summit a moment of relaunching dialogue and cooperation on issues of greatest common interest. we therefore accept the need to define a new strategic partnership between the european union and africa, with a view to the objectives of sustainable development, peace-keeping, the fight against endemic diseases and a balanced partnership for the management of migration flows in a mutually beneficial way. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is our agenda, which i have just briefly described to you. i am aware that we are assuming the presidency at a delicate moment in the international situation and that we are ambitious in defining our own objectives. we know that presidencies alone do not solve all the problems that arise, but we also know that they can make a difference if they set clear objectives, are humble in the way they pursue them and are willing to promote the necessary consensus. many european philosophers characterize today's world as being a post-world. post-democratic, post-modern or post-industrial, and so on. a world after. but really what this concept means is just this: we live in a changing world, and it's changing fast, and what we see happening we don't fully understand yet. but in the midst of all the uncertainties and unknowns, one thing we know for sure: in a changing world the worst mistake is to stand still. this is the mistake europe cannot and must not make - the mistake of standing still. that, ladies and gentlemen, is our firm purpose: to ensure that europe does not stand still, to advance the european project in the service of a better world. in writing. why i am against the eu "reform treaty" and the mandate of the igc: ireland's prime minister ahern says: 'about 90 per cent of the core package remains unchanged from the european constitutional treaty'. that is analytically correct, but fraud on the population in france and the netherlands. the second chapter contains the provisions of title v of the existing teu (including the european external action service and permanent structured cooperation in the field of defence) as amended by the 2004 intergovernmental conference. (mandate of the igc) the aim is to incorporate all the provisions of the constitutional treaty on the military sector into the new eu treaty on reform. the following specific provisions are to be laid down in the contract: 1.the eu's arms supply obligation; the eu arms agency (now also in the treaty); 3.new options for military intervention such as 'disarmament measures', or 'disarmament missions' involving violence; 4.military assistance to third countries 'in the fight against terrorism on their territory'; 5.close cooperation between the eu and nato; 6.no parliamentary control over foreign and military policy; 7.the court of justice shall have no power of decision in foreign and military policy; the european union is also committed to the development of a common foreign and security policy. 9.eu battle groups for rapid eu military interventions worldwide (now also in the treaty); 10.military structured cooperation. individual eu member states can take the lead in military policy; 11.to enable an independent eu military budget in addition to national military budgets. the eu's armament and militarization are accelerating. the military was the backbone of the constitutional treaty. the foreseeable reform agreement is also a military agreement.

the ecb mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. i have the honour to present to you today the annual report of the european central bank for the year 2006. it is an important tool for reporting to the citizens of europe, to their elected representatives, to the parliament, on monetary policy and our activities in the areas of our competence. i will first give you a brief overview of the economic and monetary developments in 2006 and explain the monetary policy measures taken by the ecb. i would also like to make some comments on the financial market stability and the payment systems. i will start with the economic and monetary issues. in 2006, the ecb's monetary policy continued to anchor medium and longterm inflation expectations at levels consistent with price stability, reflecting the credibility of the ecb in conducting its monetary policy. as has been said by the rapporteur very eloquently, in 2006 the euro area economy expanded at the highest growth rate since 2000. notwithstanding the impact of high and volatile oil prices, real gdp rose by 2.9% compared with 1.5% in 2005. the economic recovery gradually broadened in the course of 2006, and the nature of economic expansion became increasingly self-sustaining, with domestic demand acting as the main driver. the latest data and survey releases have remained broadly positive, supporting the view that economic activity in the euro area in the second quarter of 2007 continued to expand at solid rates. looking ahead, the mediumterm outlook for economic activity remains favourable and the conditions are in place for the euro area economy to continue to grow at a sustained rate. regarding price developments, average annual hicp inflation in 2006 was 2.2%, unchanged compared with the previous year. this was above the ecb's aim to keep inflation over the medium term below, but close to, 2%. although this outcome mainly reflects the increases in oil and commodity prices and although inflation has been slightly below 2% in the first half of 2007, there is no room for complacency. the outlook for price stability over the medium term remains subject to upside risks. as capacity utilisation in the euro area economy is high and labour markets are gradually improving, constraints are emerging which could lead in particular to stronger than expected wage developments. in addition, pricing power in market segments with low competition may increase in such an environment. our assessment that upside risks to price stability prevailed has been confirmed throughout the period from the start of 2006 to mid-2007 by cross-checking with the monetary analysis. the marked dynamism of monetary and credit growth in 2006 and 2007 reflected a continued persistent upward trend in the underlying rate of monetary expansion, adding further to liquidity accumulation. to address the upside risks to price stability identified by the ecb's economic and monetary analyses, the governing council has, as you know, adjusted the monetary policy stance gradually in eight steps since the end of 2005. as i said last thursday in explaining the governing council's assessment, after the adjustments in the key interest rates, the ecb's monetary policy remains still on the accommodative side, with overall favourable financing conditions, vigorous money and credit growth, and ample liquidity in the euro area. firm and timely action continues to be warranted to ensure price stability over the medium term. the governing council will continue to monitor closely all developments in order to ensure that risks over the medium term do not materialise. with regard to fiscal policies, the ecb shares the view expressed in the draft resolution that fiscal consolidation is key and all the more necessary in good times in order to achieve long-term growth. for the governing council, as was very eloquently said by both the rapporteur and the president of the eurogroup, it is important that all governments comply with the provisions of the stability and growth pact on fiscal consolidation and that all the countries concerned honour the commitments made at the eurogroup meeting in berlin on 20 april 2007. as agreed in berlin, taking advantage of favourable cyclical conditions would enable most euro area countries to achieve their medium-term objectives in 2008 or 2009, and all of them should aim for 2010 at the latest. i have to say that we also very much welcome the emphasis which has been placed by the ecofin council on measures to improve the quality and efficiency of public finances. turning to structural policies, the motion for a resolution adopted by the econ committee refers several times to economic divergences in the euro area. let me stress first that, overall, inflation differences among euro area countries have fallen and are currently relatively limited by historical standards. the magnitude of current inflation and output differentials at the moment i am speaking is similar to those that are observed across regions or states within the united states of america, a vast continental economy which has an order of magnitude, a dimension, which is of the order of magnitude of ours. that being said, a single currency means a single monetary policy and a single exchange rate vis-à-vis other currencies. it is therefore all the more important to ensure that all the national shock adjustment mechanisms function perfectly. the efficient and smooth functioning of economic adjustments within the euro area requires the removal of institutional barriers to flexible wage and price-setting mechanisms as well as the completion of the single market and thus greater cross-border competition. indeed, well-designed structural reforms implemented by national governments are crucial to improve the functioning of product, labour and financial markets and to reinforce competitiveness. we also consider that free and undistorted competition fosters long-term economic growth and job creation and facilitates the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. let me say a word now on financial stability, which i know is a very important issue for parliament. we would acknowledge the positive role that hedge funds play by contributing to enhancing the efficiency and liquidity of financial markets. we should also be aware, however, that hedge funds can also represent a source of risk to the stability of the financial system. against this background, the report which was issued in may 2007 by the financial stability forum at the request of the g8 on highly leveraged institutions is welcomed. the report contains a number of recommendations addressed to supervisors, hedge fund counterparties and investors, and the hedge fund industry itself, which i fully share. as for the role to be played by the industry, more than ever we will support the proposal that the hedge fund sector would strive for best practices and that industry-led benchmarks would be a suitable tool to pursue this objective. in this vein, the recent initiative that has been undertaken by the industry to set up a working group to review best practices is a very welcome development and i look forward to the result of such work. my final remarks perhaps concern the integration of payment systems in europe. i have noted with satisfaction that the approach of the single euro payments area and the target 2 project is very positive and we will continue in the eurosystem to play our role in this regard. as far as t2s is concerned, we have put in place a governance model for the development phase which seeks to involve all stakeholders through the creation of an advisory group on t2s where market players are well represented. in april 2007 we launched an official public consultation on the principles and proposals underlying the t2s project. the first preliminary assessment of these comments shows that their feedback is generally positive. out of 67 proposals, we have obtained a total of 3200 comments from 56 institutions and we have noted that 60% of these 3200 comments indicated full agreement to the proposals, while only 6% indicated full disagreement. all the feedback received has been published and is being very carefully considered. thank you very much for your attention.
