you all deserve a vacation. you all look well rested and i hope you will now take great pleasure in our european work. first , i regret to inform you of some things . since we last met here, we have learned with great sadness of the deaths of two great europeans, gaston thorn and raymond barre, both of whom were distinguished members of the european commission and prime ministers of their respective countries. gaston thorn was a member of the european parliament for ten years, from 1959 to 1969. he was foreign minister of luxembourg from 1969 to 1974 and prime minister from 1974 to 1979. from 1981 to 1985 he was president of the european commission. under his presidency, the european community negotiated the conditions for the accession of spain and portugal, launched the common fisheries policy and settled disputes over the community's budgetary resources and future financing. raymond barre was vice-president of the european commission from 1967 to 1973 and prime minister of france from 1976 to 1981. as commissioner for economic and financial affairs, he put forward the first proposals for the creation of an economic and monetary union in europe in 1969 and 1970 as part of the barre plan. both men were active in promoting european unification until the end of their lives, and they made very important and practical contributions to this process, often in the difficult conditions of the time. last weekend, altiero spinelli would have celebrated his 100th birthday. as one of the architects of today's european institutions, altiero spinelli was a member of this parliament for ten years. i had the great honor of working with him for seven of those ten years until his death in 1986. during his ten years as a member of the european parliament, and in particular as chairman of the committee on institutional affairs, he played a key role in pioneering an ambitious agenda for institutional reform. his draft treaty on european union, which was adopted by a large majority in the european parliament in 1984, laid the foundations for many of the important changes introduced by the subsequent treaty reforms, including a substantial extension of the european parliament's legislative powers. during the summer break we have experienced a whole series of natural disasters, from the dramatic floods in the united kingdom to the heat wave in the eastern mediterranean to the recent tragic fires in greece. these events have caused great suffering for many people in europe. in greece, the fires killed more than 60 people. it goes without saying that we are dealing with this tragedy as the first important item on our agenda this afternoon, and i am sure that i speak on behalf of the whole of the european parliament when i express our deepest condolences to the victims of these and other tragic events. we also express our condolences to the families of the more than 500 people who died in the earthquake in peru on 15 august and to the deceased in silence. create a dynamic european economy based on the lisbon strategy. another challenge is to create a transeuropean transport network to bring us closer together and deepen the european internal market. the challenge of an information society reveals not only the importance of human capital but also that of social inclusion. the european union will be all the stronger the more its citizens are involved in this unique project in the modern history of peoples. the current challenge - and one that is being felt quite acutely in some regions - of climate change must be met by the development of renewable energy sources and a more efficient and socially responsible use of natural resources. all these challenges arise in a context of globalisation of the world economy which poses a serious challenge to our old europe which we must meet, at economic and social level, with policies that boost the productivity of the european economy and that strengthen social cohesion. this is what all europeans demand of our governance. we all have to redouble our efforts so that the budgets we draw up can respond effectively and efficiently to the areas which are high on the political agenda. for this reason, in addition to our efforts to reduce administrative burdens, the council and the european parliament share the concern that the commission should speed up the process of approving operational programmes and projects in order to avoid delays in implementation. this increased speed of approval should not, however, call into question the principles of sound budgetary management. we want more flexibility, yes, but without sacrificing the efficient and responsible use of european taxpayers' money. before going into more detail on the draft budget for 2008, i would like to recall the main principles which guided the council's decision. let me summarise these elements: adequate financing of the various priorities of the european union; a carefully controlled increase in payment appropriations; compliance with the current ceilings of the financial framework, creating, where necessary, sufficient margins below the limits of the various headings and subheadings; and finally, financial discipline and sound budgetary management. let me just mention one detail. in its examination of the preliminary draft budget the council made use of a set of budgetary tools which have proved to be very useful and which have been developed in the context of budgeting by objectives and activities. among these i would like to highlight the activity sheets, which, after a number of them have been examined in depth, the council considers that the overall quality of the process has improved significantly and expects this budgetary approach to be further developed in the future. the draft budget for 2008 amounts to eur 128 billion in commitment appropriations and eur 119 billion in payment appropriations. as regards payment commitments, i would remind you that the council considers it essential that they reach an appropriate overall level in the 2008 budget, taking due account of absorption capacities. as you know, we do not consider that overestimating the payment appropriations is a solution for the rest to be liquidated. one of the principles we used was to assess needs - real and well-defined needs - which resulted in a 3.4% increase in payments compared to the 2007 budget. as regards subheading 1a competitiveness for growth and jobs , the council intends to provide for adequate funding for the priorities related to the lisbon strategy, leaving a significant margin to cover also the priorities of the european union set out in the conclusions of the june european council, as well as other needs not yet foreseen. although the council intends to limit the increases in this sub-heading compared to the 2007 budget, i would like to stress that for scientific research the increase envisaged by the council will remain very significant, namely 7.75% more in commitments and 45% more in payments, taking into account the execution rate of previous years and absorption capacities. this increase demonstrates the great importance which the council attaches to the efficient implementation of the lisbon strategy, which is, as i have already said, an essential element of the economic development of the european union. as regards subheading 1b - cohesion for growth and jobs - the council intends to accept the commitment appropriations proposed by the commission in its preliminary draft budget. as regards payment appropriations, i would like to stress that the planned increase is still very significant, namely 6.2%, taking into account the absorption capacity and the experience of the past with regard to the completion of the old programmes and the implementation of the new ones. as regards heading 2 'conservation and management of natural resources', the appropriations provided for by the council are based on past performance and previous experience has shown that, although they are applied horizontally, these appropriations are always very close overall to the figures resulting from final implementation. i would like to add a few comments on the approval of operational programmes and projects in the field of rural development and the structural and cohesion funds for the period 2007-13. this matter was the subject of a joint declaration which we adopted at our conciliation meeting, and i can assure you that the council attaches the utmost political importance to the fact that all operational programmes and projects are implemented as quickly as possible and in an appropriate manner. as regards headings 3a and 3b citizenship, freedom, security and justice , the council intends to make only a slight adjustment in the appropriations for commitments and payments in accordance with the absorption capacities and the previous rate of implementation. as regards heading 4 'the european union as a global partner', the council intends to include some politically relevant priorities in its draft budget. i am referring to palestine, for which eur 80 million is added to the reserve, and kosovo, for which eur 180 million is also added to the reserve. we are still at the first stage of the budgetary procedure and i am sure that we will have further opportunities to agree on more precise figures in this area. at this stage the council intends, as far as it is concerned, to accept the common foreign and security policy budget proposed in the preliminary draft budget as a minimum precaution. however, it is quite likely that the amount proposed for the budget of the common foreign and security policy will prove insufficient in the light of developments in the international situation. i think we all understand what's at stake. i would like to conclude my speech by referring to heading 5 administration. the council's approach is based on both horizontal criteria, such as efficiency gains, and the specificities of each institution, especially in terms of allocating new seats for enlargement. for its own section of the budget, the council intends to provide for an increase of only 0.2%, which seems to me to be an unambiguous political signal. the budgets of the decentralised agencies were also examined in detail. a methodology based on horizontal criteria was followed, both in terms of grants and in terms of the number of new places to be accepted. i would also like to take this opportunity to speak briefly about the need to ensure sound financial management of the institutions of the european union. in this context, the council welcomes the joint declarations we adopted at the conciliation meeting, which deal with issues such as decentralised and executive agencies, assigned revenue and recruitment in the context of recent enlargements. we all know that this is only the first step in the budgetary process, but i am fully confident that together we will be able to explore all the possibilities in order to reach a final agreement and produce a satisfactory budget at the end of this year. we have as our main objective to have a budget for 2008 in time which is adequate to meet the political priorities of the union, but not overestimated because that would mean complacency with a likely lack of effectiveness and efficiency in its implementation. we must bear in mind not only the impact this budget will have on the well-being of each and every citizen of the union, but also that it is the taxpayers of each member state who are financing it. hence the need to find a proper balance point. i am sure that the three institutions here today will do everything in their power to achieve this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, thank you very the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. yes, the proposal for a directive on the inland transport of dangerous goods is an important dossier, because in fact some 110 billion tonne-kilometres of dangerous goods are transported in the eu every year: 58% by road, 25% by rail and 17% by inland waterways. the aim of this draft directive is to simplify and consolidate the existing rules on the transport of dangerous goods. in addition, the scope of eu rules, which currently covers road and rail transport, will be extended to inland waterway transport. this simplification leads to a reduction in red tape and an improvement in intermodality. the common rules on road, rail and inland waterway transport ensure a uniform level of safety in national and crossborder transport throughout the community. the single rules for the modes of transport will facilitate and promote multimodal transport operations. in particular, the extension of the scope to inland waterway transport is welcome. the same safety rules apply to all inland waterways in the community. this has a positive impact on working conditions on board, on transport safety and on the protection of the environment. the uniform standard reduces costs by avoiding multiple approvals and certificates. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the water supply in the community, and it is hoped that the commission will be able to take action to improve the quality of the water supply. the amendments adopted by the committee on transport mainly reflect the council's position. we are in agreement and we want to try to reach an agreement on first reading if possible. i would like to emphasize that an amendment which the rapporteur has already mentioned and which represents a compromise will be accepted by this house. it is important that meaningful provisions be incorporated into this dossier. we agree with the commission and the council. the amendment refers to the provision which gives member states the possibility of adopting special rules and perhaps also of imposing requirements on the transport operators if they can justify it to the commission. finally, i would like to thank the rapporteur for the excellent cooperation he has given us and to ask the house to close this dossier at first reading.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur for the excellent work and the very good report that he has produced, and also the other members of the committee who have supported him and worked with him in producing such an interesting, useful and positive report. i do not want to repeat much of what has been included in the communication or in the report, and i begin by saying that i am very happy that we see eye to eye as to how we can solve and deal with such a difficult and important problem. we know the statistics, which are worrying. almost 200 000 people a year in the european union die of diseases related to excessive alcohol consumption. we have 43-45 million people who drink at hazardous levels in the european union which amounts to 70.4% of all ill health and early deaths, and this is one of the largest causes of death among young people. so the statistics are worrying, but we have to emphasise from the outset that we are not dealing with alcohol as a product on its own: it is the excessive consumption and the abuse of alcohol that are creating these problems. sometimes it makes it more difficult to educate and teach people how to consume, in moderate and more responsible ways, a product which has been around for centuries; it is the excess or the abuse that is causing the problems. i am very happy that parliament agrees with the need for a european strategy and for european action in this respect. it is true that we have to complement the policy of the member states, as is stated in article 152, but that does not mean that we do nothing. on the contrary, we are there to support, complement and add to the actions taken by the member states. it is also true that we have different cultures and different traditions in the member states but, unfortunately, we now see the problems that until recently existed only in some member states spreading everywhere in the european union. unfortunately, bad habits travel fast and are very easily copied, especially by young people. the possibility exists to exchange best practice through cooperation and working together, before it is too late. we can take action before the problem gets out of hand, and this is one of the most important aspects of this strategy. we should focus on young people. binge drinking is now a main concern regarding young people, but drink-driving is also one of the highest causes of deaths among young people. at the same time, it is extremely important to focus on the priorities, and i am glad that the report agrees with the commission on the main priorities, as i said, especially regarding young people, but also pregnant women. unfortunately, it is still a problem in the european union that we still have children born with problems because of alcohol consumption during pregnancy. one would have expected, in this day and age, with the highest level of education in the european union, this would not happen, but unfortunately it does. i have noted with great interest the reference made in the report to the problem among elderly people. this will be seriously taken into consideration for the next actions because i can see that this can also be a serious social and health problem. the european union as a whole will work on two levels. firstly, there is the committee on national policy and action, where the member states are represented, and this will coordinate national alcohol policies and develop further policies, especially those identified in the communication. but, at the same time, we also have the european alcohol and health forum, where all the stakeholders are present and there we will develop concrete actions at the appropriate levels. however, it will not be a debating society or just a ‘talk show’. on the contrary, we are asking for firm commitments which will not only have to produce specific results but also will have to be made public and closely monitored, and the results of the monitoring will also be made public. we are optimistic that this will be able to deal with some complicated issues, for example responsible marketing, responsible advertising – as identified in the report – and, at the same time, other aspects, like responsible serving, because it is not just the producers but also the retailers who have a serious responsibility in this area, and we will focus on this as well. most of the issues raised in the report confirm the policy orientations set out in the strategy outlined in the commission’s communication. some points strive to further develop this strategy and, of course, i will pay close attention to these; other points go beyond the recommendations of the commission’s communication on some issues, such as labelling and taxation. we will reflect on these issues as well. concerning the warning labels on alcoholic drinks, which i know has been an issue of great debate both when the communication was being drafted and in parliament as well, we will study the experience obtained by member states which are already in the process of introducing them and we will explore the possibility, in cooperation with the member states, of developing official common approaches throughout the community regarding this issue. we have evidence that warning labels raise awareness – and that is why member states introduced them – but, at the same time, they have to be part of a broader strategy; on their own, they cannot achieve the goals we wish for. therefore, we need campaigns for raising awareness of education programmes. for example, we can put warning labels on bottles, but what happens to drinks served in restaurants, bars and homes where the consumer does not see the bottle and, therefore, does not see the label? so we have to come up with new ideas, for example leaflets accompanying purchases of alcoholic beverages and advice from doctors, as was mentioned in the report. these are important aspects. responsible communication, responsible sales and responsible marketing are also important aspects, and we have what is provided in the audiovisual services legislation. however, through the forum, we can develop a code of conduct to be complied with by all stakeholders. i should like to finish by saying that addressing alcoholic-related harm is a difficult challenge, precisely because we have to deal with one particular aspect, the excessive consumption and not the product itself. however, i believe we are moving in the right direction, before a writer. the commission is not 2001-2007 are six years in which the fight against terrorism was politically motivated. the only thing that has been seen in these six years is that every measure that has been taken has been politically responded to. what i miss is the approach: how does european policy on combating terrorism develop in the global context? what role do we play? what role do we want to play in the world? do we have a concept behind it? i have not yet seen any concept or document, either from the commission or the council or, moreover, from any of the member states, proposing a short, medium or longterm strategy to combat terrorism. we have put in place measures which have short-term effects, to curb financial flows. that was great! we have put in place measures to combat terrorism in the medium term by trying to combat terrorism through biometric data in identity documents - which i personally do not think is the right thing to do, but it was the political majority's intention. in the long term, i see no progress, no movement in the area of development aid, which can be understood as security policy. i also see no movement to respect the cultures that supposedly can generate terrorism, so that we don't go out into the world and try to pass our society on to others, but that we try to be globalized within each other, to live together sensibly in a globalized world. the question is therefore: what role will europe play? the responses since september 11, 2001 have been a variety of activism: in each case, governments have tried to calm their populations after attacks by taking action at short notice, whether it is the british vehemence in pushing through data retention immediately after the tragic attacks in london, or elsewhere - for example, in the federal republic of germany - when attempts are made to enforce online searches. it lacks the concept behind it. and fundamental rights interventions, similar to those in times of emergency laws, alone will not solve the problem. if we want to fight terrorism successfully, we must define europe's role in the world in this fight, and not pursue national actionism, which is then only executed in europe.
acting president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like first of all to apologize for the slight delay in my appearance in this parliament, which was due purely and simply to a miscalculation of the traffic on the distance from the hotel to this parliament. i would also like to congratulate commissioner frattini, who is here, and to try to answer the questions put by the members, hoping to provide all the clarifications that have been requested. the recent events in london and glasgow, as well as on the spanish-portuguese border and the attack in yemen, have undoubtedly confirmed that terrorism poses a significant threat to the security of europe and to the values of our democratic societies, in particular to the rights and freedoms of european citizens. we have no doubt that the member states must therefore continue to cooperate in order to strengthen and implement measures in the field of counter-terrorism, always with respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, which are the core values of our societies, the protection and promotion of which will contribute to the prevention of terrorism. terrorism must be fought, both at national and international level. international cooperation is an indispensable tool for effectively combating this scourge, both at national and multilateral level. we are aware that terrorism is a global threat and as such requires a global and concerted response, which necessarily involves increased flow and exchange of information, internal coordination of positions, coordination/partnership with third states, implementation of a global counter-terrorism strategy in which the united nations has a leading role, and close cooperation with a number of regional and international organisations involved in the fight against terrorism. the action taken by the european union has been stepped up since 11 september 2001, and subsequently since the horrific attacks in madrid in 2004 and london in 2005. in december 2005, the council adopted the european union counter-terrorism strategy, in which the union commits itself to combating terrorism worldwide in full respect of human rights and giving citizens the possibility to live in an area of freedom, security and justice. the european union's counter-terrorism strategy covers four lines of work: prevention, protection, prosecution and response. the presidency confirms that the council assesses the situation regarding the implementation of the eu counter-terrorism strategy and the strategy against the financing of terrorism every six months and the strategy against radicalisation and recruitment every year. the council also reviews the action plan to combat terrorism every six months and the action plan to combat radicalisation and recruitment annually. this monitoring process enables the council to identify measures that have not been adopted in the steps planned at eu level or that have not been properly implemented at member state level, and also allows it to deepen certain policies. the presidency has decided to speed up work on explosives, for example. the adoption of certain measures in the field of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters has been slowed down by the unanimity procedure required for such matters. the adoption and implementation of counter-terrorism measures will be accelerated by the ratification of the treaty, to be approved by the intergovernmental conference on the basis of the mandate approved by the european council at its last meeting in june. as regards the need for closer cooperation between law enforcement and security intelligence services, the security services of the member states are currently working closely and efficiently in the so-called anti-terrorist group. europol has developed very effective analysis files which have been increasingly fed by the law enforcement services of the member states. there is no doubt that more needs to be done. the european parliament maintains a close direct political dialogue with the council and the commission. on 16 may 2007, a meeting took place between the president of the council, the vice-president of the commission and the president of the libe commission to review the various counter-terrorism policies and to take stock of the implementation of the eu counter-terrorism strategy. these meetings, which are held every six months, are extremely useful in reaching consensus on policies to be developed in the field of the fight against terrorism. as regards the position of the european union counter-terrorism coordinator, the secretary-general/high representative informed the member states that he was considering, in close cooperation with the presidency, how best to ensure the coordination of counter-terrorism work in the council. as regards the relationship between the european union counter-terrorism coordinator and the situation centre, sitcen does not play any role in the elaboration of the european union's counter-terrorism policy, nor in the coordination of the council's counter-terrorism work, nor does it monitor the follow-up of the council's decisions. in the field of counter-terrorism, its competence is limited to presenting to the council strategic assessments of terrorist threats based on information received from national services. in addition, it supports the eu emergency and crisis coordination mechanism for providing assistance in coordinating a european union-wide response to major crises potentially including terrorist attacks. this is a mechanical function of disseminating information, providing meeting facilities and supporting the existing decision-making mechanisms of the institutions. it's not a coordination function. however, it was on the basis of the threat assessment carried out by sitcen that the council adopted sectoral policy recommendations in several areas, such as explosives, to prevent their illicit use by terrorists. the presidency has no doubt that its efforts to combat terrorism are supported by the european citizens, who have shown, in the recent attacks, not only their solidarity with the victims of these attacks but also their desire to see a european response. in drawing up such a counter-terrorism strategy, the presidency relies on the support of its partners who contribute to the high-level dialogues, with the european parliament, in particular, playing a key role. the council attaches paramount importance to the implementation of article 6 of the treaty on european union, as well as to all the other articles of the treaties. cooperation and dialogue with third countries is one of the pillars of the european union's counter-terrorism strategy. it is only this semester that troika dialogues are scheduled to take place with russia, the united states of america, algeria and morocco, thus signalling the interest in a deeper dialogue with these countries. in addition, the european union has counter-terrorism dialogues with other countries and international organisations. as regards our mediterranean partners, the regular ad hoc euromed terrorism experts meeting will also take place, which will allow for a broad debate with our mediterranean partners on a subject of vital interest in this region, and will aim at implementing priority areas of the euro-mediterranean code of conduct on counter-terrorism. with regard to the united states of america specifically, it should also be noted that the presidency has regular talks with the united states in various instances and at various levels on counter-terrorism, where topics such as radicalisation and terrorist recruitment, including the use of the internet by extremists, terrorist threat analysis, cooperation in international fora, public-private partnerships to combat terrorism, including explosives safety, critical infrastructure protection, terrorist financing, as well as other forms of cooperation between civil and law enforcement authorities are addressed. the portuguese presidency will also organise, together with the united states, a workshop on the application of financial sanctions in the fight against terrorism. the issue of respect for human rights in the fight against terrorism was also raised by both sides on several occasions, and the presidency considered it very important to continue this dialogue, which it considered to be key for both sides. i would conclude by recalling that the consolidation of the area of freedom, security and justice, on the basis of the hague programme and the action plan, is one of the main priorities of the joint programme for the 18 months of the german, portuguese and slovenian presidencies. the fight against terrorism is one of the major challenges in this field, and the three presidencies have set themselves the objective of intensifying cooperation in this area with a view to implementing the european union's counter-terrorism strategy. i would now like to answer oral question o-0053/07 with your permission, mr president. i would also like to inform this house that the council of the european union i now refer to the judgment of the court of first instance of the european communities of 12 december 2006, which has been referred to here. first, i would point out that judgment t 228/02 of 12 december 2006, the so-called wipo case, organisation of the mujahideen of the people of iran v council of the european union, does not allow the conclusion that the practice of terrorist lists adopted by the european union violates community law. the court did not rule against the adoption of lists of terrorists. the court merely considered that certain fundamental rights and guarantees, including the right of defence, the obligation to state reasons and the right to effective judicial protection, are in principle fully applicable in the context of the adoption of a community decision to freeze funds, in accordance with regulation (ec) no 2580/2001. secondly, it is public knowledge that the council has already carried out the necessary review of its procedures, in a systematic manner, with regard to the individuals and entities on the list to which regulation (ec) no 2580/2001 applies. the council adopted the following measures to implement judgment t 228/02: draws attention to the possibility of challenging the council's decision before the court of first instance of the european communities; informs that an application accompanied by supporting documentation can be submitted to the council for the consideration of the decision to include or maintain on the list, such request is assessed upon receipt; it provides all persons, groups and entities to whom it has been possible to make practical explanations of the grounds in other cases, the persons, groups and entities shall be informed by means of a notice published in the official journal of the european union; carry out an overall review of the list at least once every six months in accordance with the procedures described above, always taking into account the information received. the council also decided to set up a new working group called working partner on commum position 931 to deal with requests for inclusion and exclusion from the list and to prepare for the periodic review of the list by the vice-president of the commission. mr president, the commission continues to be fully committed to the implementation of the eu counter-terrorism strategy, the action plan, as the council just said, endorsed in 2005. our political goal remains to strike the right balance between the fundamental right to security of citizens, which is, first of all, the right to life, and the other fundamental rights of individuals, including privacy and procedural rights. all sources indicate that the threat of new terrorist attacks continues to be high. our member states’ authorities have been able to prevent a number of attacks, for which we must be very grateful. i am talking about spain, italy, belgium, the uk and germany. yesterday the danish authorities dismantled a group of young terrorists, also of danish nationality, ready to mount a bombing attack. minister espersen said it was the most serious terrorist case in denmark. this morning, we learn that suspected terrorists have been arrested in frankfurt, and the german minister of defence said an attack was imminent. do you believe that in all these cases no results have been achieved? do you not believe that stopping the final stage of a terrorist attack is not in itself a fantastic result for europe? my answer is – yes, it is. (applause)so there is no room for complacency or letting our guard down. i would first of all like to take this very good opportunity to inform you of a package of measures which are in preparation by my services, and which will be adopted by the commission this autumn in very close cooperation with the portuguese presidency. we are working on prevention and prosecution. this package will consist of a european action plan on the security of explosives, a proposal for an amendment of the framework decision on terrorism to deal with terrorist misuse of internet, and a proposal on european passenger name record (pnr) policy. in addition, the package will contain a report on evaluation of the implementation by the member states of the framework decision on terrorism. a few words on each of these elements: the european action plan on explosives is a follow-up to the 2005 commission communication on this topic, and aims to respond to repeated calls from the european council and the council of ministers of the interior to improve the explosives situation in europe. you will no doubt recall that the attacks in madrid were committed using commercially available explosives and detonators, which prompted the call for eu action in this area. i am glad that i can report to you that a lot of good work has been done by our services together with a wide range of stakeholders, including representatives of the private sector. i have received what i think will prove to be a ground-breaking report from a public-private expert group that i have established, which contains around 50 valuable concrete recommendations to improve security of explosives, precursors and detonators across the eu. these recommendations will form the basis for the european action plan which should be adopted, as i said, before november. the measures that will be proposed in it include, for example, the setting-up of a european explosives database at europol with links to all the responsible services in member states, in addition to an early warning system so that these services are informed very quickly, for example, when explosives have been stolen or a new terrorist modus operandi is discovered from credible intelligence information. this brings me to the internet and the way this tool, which has brought amazing advantages to our world, is being misused by terrorists. we all know that terrorists enjoy the benefits of the internet just as much as ordinary citizens, for instance to plan their attacks or to disseminate messages of concrete incitement to commit terrorist attacks. the benefits of e-learning have also not escaped the attention of terrorists. you can find on internet websites, for example, detailed information and instructions of all kinds of terrorist tactics, including the production of explosives. the proposal i mentioned just now will aim at ensuring that these forms of negative and criminal behaviour will be made punishable across the eu. another element of this package of measures relates to the idea of having a european policy on pnr. reflection on details of this proposal is still ongoing, but the commission’s main intention is to ensure that each member state collects pnr records, processes them and, where appropriate, exchanges them with others. up until now, pnr has been associated mostly with negotiation aimed at ensuring that european citizen data are processed correctly by our partners and allies, in particular the united states. i think the time has come to partially change focus and devote resources to the security of the european union. the union is at least as much a potential target of a terrorist attack as the united states and the use and analysis of pnr is an important law enforcement tool to protect our citizens, who deserve the same protection as the citizens of the united states. the final element of the package consists of the second report on the implementation of the framework decision on combating terrorism. the new report will also include information on the situation in the new member states, which was not available in 2004 – and you can understand why. this brings me to the more general question raised concerning an overall comprehensive evaluation of all counter-terrorist measures adopted until now. of course, i am in favour of the principle of evaluating the effectiveness of policies. as regards justice, freedom and security policies in particular you might be aware that work is ongoing on the development of global evaluation mechanisms. i am ready to cooperate, as i have been doing in the past with parliament, and in particular with the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, to carry out the evaluation of the existing measures, including the international and european agreements with our international partners. but let me make it clear that my aim is to strengthen, not to weaken, our ability to prevent and prosecute terrorism in a more effective way. as regards the exchange of information between member states and european institutions, i fully agree that this is an essential aspect of the fight against terrorism. as you know, i have been active in this area. over the past years, i have put forward a number of proposals on data protection in the third pillar, on the principle of availability and on data retention of electronic communications. unfortunately, except for data retention, it has not yet been possible to reach agreement on these proposals in the council, particularly on data protection in the third pillar. but i will continue to strive for their adoption and with the portuguese proposal we have an agreement in principle to try to get a final adoption of the framework decision on data protection in the third pillar by december. it is very often said that mutual trust is needed for effective cooperation, especially when combating terrorism. my view is that trust can be stimulated by us mainly in two ways. first, through ensuring that there is a clear and proper legal framework in place that provides confidence that information supplied will be treated in an appropriate manner and, secondly, through stimulating as many shared international experiences as possible, including joint training exercises so that people working in the field get to know and appreciate each other. concerning the situation centre (‘sitcen’), i should mention that it has certainly provided the council with a valuable strategic analysis of the terrorist threat, and i have established, thanks to cooperation with mr solana, a very good practical cooperation on this. nevertheless, i do not see a role for sitcen in the area of operational cooperation, certainly not as a coordinating tool for investigations, since its mandate is limited to dealing with non-personal information. this is rather a task for europol and eurojust. i believe these are organisations that should be better equipped to deal with such tasks. we should not forget that the large majority of our citizens – 84% in the latest eurobarometer – are strongly in favour of eu action to combat terrorists and organised crime. so, let us strengthen europol and eurojust based on that. naturally, any action we take must be in line with the fundamental rights acquis and with article 6 of the treaty. i intend to submit to the member states a questionnaire on anti-terrorist measures they have adopted, on their effectiveness and on how these relate to the human rights framework. i am ready to share with you data and results of this exercise. in conclusion, i believe that our counter-terrorist efforts clearly require joint action and the total dedication of the council, parliament and the commission. i am ready to respond once again positively to further possible invitations from this parliament and from the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, as i have been doing since my appointment at the commission. in writing. the commission's proposal to simplify and harmonise european legislation on the transport of dangerous goods is fully in line with the 'better regulation' approach. it was only on 31 august 2007 that i visited the traffic management centre of 7 road tunnels, including the longest tunnel in germany, and was made aware of the need for harmonisation, especially of the rules on dangerous goods transport in tunnels. not only the transport of goods in general, but also the transport of dangerous goods is growing rapidly. and it's happening globally, so even the growth can't be captured by any single mode of transport. it is therefore appropriate to include in the rules not only road and rail transport but also inland waterway transport. this will improve the chances of implementing the commodal approach in solving our transport problems. the fact that this act takes account of the specific recommendations of the united nations and at the same time respects the subsidiarity claim of the eu member states is particularly noteworthy for the understanding of our fellow citizens. by merging four 'old' directives and saving 2 000 pages of legal text, the directive is an example of how red tape is cut. member states will continue to be able to regulate or even refuse to regulate the national transport of certain dangerous goods, for reasons of national security or environmental protection, for example. as a result, citizens can expect this directive to contribute to improving both road safety and environmental safety.
in writing. i have voted in favour of the directive because it raises public awareness of the transport sector in particular. finally, transport logistics is one of the key factors for economic growth, competitiveness and quality of life in europe, and it serves to reduce environmental impact. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not affected by the crisis. i only agreed to the directive in the hope that the commission would take up the matter in the near future and settle it separately. this includes consideration of safety, environmental, transport and logistics aspects. the latest findings must be taken into account, as must the ability of the policy to set a strict framework for the use of such vehicles. for example, rules on the use of driver assistance systems such as emergency braking and lane keeping assistants, cruise controls with distance control, camera monitoring of the environment, or rules on steerable axles and the distribution of driving forces on several wheels. finally, the 60 tonnes gross tonnage limit is not automatically applicable to longliners. it should also be borne in mind that the longliners, with a total weight of 44 tonnes, are the ones that relieve the road, bring enormous benefits to the economy, traffic and the environment, and do not harm the railway, which cannot even cope with the increase in demand for transport capacity.

member of the commission. madam president, the report prepared by the rapporteur, ms valenciano martínez-orozco, and the resolution before parliament address a highly important but also increasingly complex instrument of the european union’s external human rights policy. commissioner ferrero-waldner (who regrets not to be able to attend this debate today) had accordingly instructed her services to lend every support to the rapporteur in her difficult task of scrutinising the functioning of the human rights dialogues and consultations with third countries. the report adds a further building block to parliament’s remarkable work in assessing the eu toolbox on human rights, through its regular annual reports, the agnoletto report on human rights clauses, the study of the european inter-university centre on the impact of parliament’s activities in the field of human rights, as well as the study on the guidelines on torture. the report also usefully complements the regular review of the human rights dialogues and consultations undertaken by the council and by the commission. the commission would like to compliment the rapporteur and parliament on its report and the detailed analysis and recommendations devoted to the european union’s human rights dialogues and consultations. the commission takes the view that, of all human rights instruments at our disposal, it is the dialogues that probably provide the best chance to secure positive, long-term results in the development of the respect for human rights worldwide, as long as we are prepared to invest sufficient time and energy in them. we firmly believe that the european union can obtain success in advancing the human rights record of third countries only through patient work of bridge-building and persuasion, and this not just in its bilateral relations but also in the framework of multilateral bodies, as developments in the human rights council demonstrate. the great variety and number of european union human rights dialogues and consultations with third countries – which, moreover, are steadily increasing – make any global evaluation very arduous. structured dialogues, such as with china; agreement-based dialogues like those with many neighbourhood countries; consultations with like-minded partners, such as with the us and canada, or local troika dialogues with a range of countries all differ in many respects, be it their periodicity, the policy level, the kind of interlocutors, the depth of the discussions or the fact that some are combined with civil society events and others are not. far from being a shortcoming of the instrument, the commission sees such variety as proof of the dynamism and potential of the dialogue instrument and an asset that should be preserved. the eu guidelines on human rights dialogues and the cotonou (acp-eu) agreement both stress the importance of flexibility to take into account the different country situations, their evolution over time and the dynamic relationships between any given third country and the european union. therefore, while keeping common base lines and targets for the dialogue, it would not be advisable to strictly align all their modalities. for this instrument to be effective it needs to be tailor-made and able to adapt to changing circumstances. it also needs to be borne in mind that the various dialogues and consultations are in different stages of maturity. the dialogue with china or the consultations with like-minded countries have developed more or less consolidated modalities over several years and therefore allow for rather intensive, deep discussions. in other cases, such as the dialogues with neighbourhood countries, we are still polishing the instrument and are in the phase of building up the necessary confidence to allow for genuinely meaningful exchanges. we are therefore confident that, also in these cases, issues such as the desirable participation of experts from line ministries, involvement of civil society or the consideration of individual cases will eventually become possible once the exercise finds its own solid ground. finally, you can rest assured that the recommendations directed at the commission will be examined carefully, and you can count on our commitment to improve the information to parliament in order to allow for increased transparency of human rights dialogues and consultations.

member of the commission. mr president, i am really very pleased to be here today to discuss with you the very important issues raised in the green paper on the review of the consumer acquis. i should like to start by thanking most sincerely ms patrie, all the shadow rapporteurs in the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and mrs wallis, who gave the opinion for the committee on legal affairs. it was excellent teamwork, with very close cooperation on this ambitious report. i am not just being courteous: it is sincere recognition of parliament’s hard work. the eight consumer protection directives under review focus on the contractual stage of the processes of sales or services provision. the eight directives in place deal, for instance, with consumer sales, distance contracts, doorstep-selling and unfair contract terms. however, they are all based on minimum harmonisation, leaving us with a patchwork of national rules built on top of the community’s standards. this regulatory fragmentation is confusing for consumers and costly for businesses. that is why, on 8 february 2007, the commission began a major consultation – a green paper on the review of the consumer acquis. the aim of the review is to simplify and adapt the existing rules by reducing regulatory fragmentation. this should, ultimately, improve consumer confidence in the internal market and allow businesses, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises, to trade more easily across the eu. through this process, we have the opportunity to contribute to a truly integrated eu retail market, providing consumers with lower prices and more choice and giving a measured stimulus to growth and jobs. i am glad that the commission and the european parliament agree on a common line in approaching this very important and challenging issue. your support will be an important reference for our follow-up work and for specific proposals. after the european parliament has adopted its report on the green paper, the outcome of the consultation will be published on the health and consumer protection directorate-general website. this will take place in october. however, i can already give you an outline of the results on some key issues. first of all, the commission welcomes parliament’s support for a mixed approach to the review, consisting of a combination of horizontal instrument-regulating aspects which some different directives have in common, and maintaining specific aspects in sectoral directives. i can already inform you that this mixed approach is supported by a large majority of respondents to the green paper. as regards harmonisation, the commission welcomes parliament’s endorsement of the principle of targeted full harmonisation, that is to say, full harmonisation of key aspects of consumer protection directives, which are needed in order to achieve the internal market for businesses and for consumers. this support for full harmonisation across the consumer acquis or targeted full harmonisation is shared by the majority of respondents to the green paper, in particular by businesses and member states. nevertheless, minimum rules will remain in several areas. the commission agrees with parliament that the mutual recognition clause should apply in these areas in order to make sure that additional requirements imposed by member states do not create unjustified internal market barriers. on more specific issues, such as harmonisation of withdrawal rights across the acquis, the definition of delivery of goods or the drawing up of a combined grey and black list of unfair contract terms at eu level, the majority of respondents to the green paper have expressed views which are largely in line with the report to be voted on today. in conclusion, i would like to thank you for your commitment to helping european citizens to enjoy all the benefits of the internal market. i look forward to working with you to fulfil our common goals and to achieve a citizens’ internal market.

in writing. the report advocates a ‘common european foreign policy on energy’. although so far there is not even a legal base for such a policy, it aims to push ahead with it even before it can be inserted in the new reform treaty. instead of solving the problem of expensive and polluting energy, the report wants to shape the eu as a hegemonic, global actor. such an expansive geopolitical approach of the eu would create more tension and conflicts worldwide. a strong anti-russian current is seen as a red thread in the text. almost every idea which could hinder the normal development of relations between russia and eu member states has been included. critics therefore speak of a touch of cold war. by the inclusion of a so-called ‘energy security clause’ in all agreements with producer and transit countries the eu will define its interest far beyond its borders. we are concerned about the foundation of an eu energy foreign policy that would be founded on geopolitical pressure, a background of military threat. the report calls for a close partnership with the usa on energy security, being aware that the usa is waging war in iraq to secure cheap energy resources.
in writing. the gruber report looks at immigration in parts only in terms of the utility of immigrant workers to capital. the report thus 'highlights the importance of building stable and legal employer-employee relations between enterprises and workers in order to improve the eu's productivity and competitiveness' and 'calls on the commission to take into account the impact that circular migration could have in this respect'. while the repressive measures against migrants and asylum seekers meet no resistance, 'any measure to increase the attractiveness of the union for highly qualified workers to meet the needs of the eu labour market, in order to ensure the prosperity of europe and the achievement of the lisbon objectives' should be supported. while the aim is to prevent the 'danger of the departure of top-level workers', 'return' is envisaged for migrants who can only enter fortress europe illegally. the approval of the strategic plan on legal immigration will focus on admission procedures which will allow for immediate response to changing demands in the labour market. immigration cannot be regulated on the basis of the criterion of its usefulness to eu capital. instead of immigration for eu companies, it must be about fundamental and human rights for migrants and asylum seekers. i am opposed to the idea of judging people on the basis of their usefulness.

in my view at least - not all of them, unfortunately, because the report stresses in some places that the completion of the internal market for services is lagging far behind the internal market for goods in the european union. i think that this is not really scientifically or factually provable, because we have the directive on the recognition of professional qualifications and other directives in the service sector in addition to the directive on services. secondly, the services sector in the internal market is a much more heterogeneous sector than the goods sector. it ranges from subordinate services to medical or legal services to mass services such as large banking and insurance services. i think it is dangerous to sum up all these services in the way that is done here in parliament. i think that - ‘twin-track’ approach – an activist policy agenda and an ambitious approach to the treaty reform were goals that supported each other. there was a lot of consensus in that debate, and i think there were three reasons for that. first of all, it reflects a degree of maturity in the european union, because europe today touches on so many areas of people’s lives, and this has created expectations. retreating into a lowest-common-denominator europe would be a big mistake. second, i think that the challenge of communicating europe with and to our citizens demanded a fresh approach, with a more profound awareness of how europe relates to their social needs, their economic aspirations and their underlying values. finally, this new approach was based not just on political instinct: it was union has been successfully developing a policy which recognises the fundamental link between economic success and social security. but globalisation is not static, as this summer’s turbulence in the first of all, i would like to thank mr chatzimarkakis and the committee members for their efforts. the commission proposal contains two items which are of political importance. first, to provide for the necessary follow-up on the relevant part of article 53b on the financial regulation, which stipulates that the transparency obligation and ex post publication of beneficiaries by the member states must be ensured by sector-specific legislation. second, to reinforce the mechanism by which financial discipline is safeguarded through a new reduction-suspension mechanism of agricultural aid, which is more structured and more transparent than the current mechanism already laid down in the regulation, and by introducing the possibility for the commission to make financial corrections for failing ex post controls. the commission is very much in favour of openness and transparency. one element of this is the right of the public to know what is happening with the community aid and to see who is receiving what amounts. article 53 of the financial regulation sets out that there should be an ex post publication of beneficiaries by member states. the follow-up to this general obligation is, as far as eaggf and eafrd spending is concerned, to be found in the commission’s proposal. the commission insists very much on the member states publishing this information, as, under shared management, they are the contact for the farming community and are therefore in a much better position than the commission to validate the information to be published. i am very grateful for you support on this issue. the commission will take inspiration from some of the amendments proposed when it adopts the implementing legislation, but it would not be in line with better regulation and simplification if information needs to be published, and publication will take place only within the context of the full respect of the privacy legislation applicable. as you know, there is already a reduction-suspension mechanism in regulation 1290/2005. in comparison with that mechanism, the proposed provision offers a new transparent and effective mechanism allowing a further simplification of the existing possibility to reduce or suspend payments to a member state in case of serious and persistent deficiencies in the national control systems. this new provision has the advantage that certain elements are determined in advance, so as to ensure a more efficient use of such an instrument. it goes without saying that the reduction mechanism already in place will continue to be applicable for other types of cases. however, amendments aimed at diluting the reduction mechanism are not acceptable to the commission. finally, i have noted quite a number of amendments aimed at member of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to thank the european parliament and in particular the rapporteurs, mrs belohorská and mrs klaß, for their extremely diligent work and the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, as well as mr ebner and the committee on agriculture and rural development and mrs corbey and the committee on industry, research and energy for their reports and the opinion they delivered at the first reading. over the last thirty years, european union policies and laws to protect public health and the environment have enabled us to make significant progress and to reduce the risks of pesticide use considerably. however, the legislation in force focuses on the authorisation and placing of products on the market and on the control of residues in food and feed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the use of pesticides is not restricted to the use of certain products. and yet this is the critical stage, which creates the greatest risks to human health and the environment. monitoring programmes in the member states show that pesticide residues are found in food and feed and in the environment at concentrations exceeding the limit values laid down in european legislation. it has also become clear that pesticides are a matter of serious concern to european citizens. we must therefore intensify our efforts to better protect european citizens and our environment. it is in this context, namely to address the risks posed by the use of pesticides to human health and the environment, that the thematic strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides and the accompanying framework directive fit in. the main elements of the commission's proposal for a framework directive are as follows: first, each member state will draw up national action plans setting out objectives, measures and timetables for reducing the risks and dependence of pesticides. secondly, professional users of pesticides - mainly farmers - as well as distributors and consultants, should have access to appropriate training, which will provide them with adequate knowledge of the risks of pesticide use and the application of alternative techniques. in the same way, a public awareness system should be set up to provide information on the risks of pesticide use. thirdly, professional pesticide spraying equipment should be subject to regular checks and proper maintenance. fourthly, aerial spraying will be prohibited, but member states will retain the possibility of derogating in a limited number of cases where aerial spraying is the only feasible solution. fifthly, specific measures will be taken to protect the general public and vulnerable groups of the population, as well as water systems and geographical areas such as natura 2000 sites. such specific measures may include, inter alia, the establishment of buffer zones and the prohibition or restriction of the use of pesticides. eighth and last, but equally important, we need to support low pesticide input farming techniques and create the necessary conditions for the implementation of integrated pest management - 'integrated best management' - which should become mandatory from 2014. other measures provided for in the thematic strategy have been incorporated or will soon be incorporated into other legislative acts. these are: proposal for a regulation on the placing of plant protection products on the market. the regulation will further restrict harmful active substances on the market, in particular through comparative evaluation and compliance with the principle of substitution. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. proposal for a regulation on the collection of statistical data on plant protection products. this is a key proposal, which establishes indicators to measure progress in reducing risk. this proposal is now being discussed in the committee responsible for the subject. proposal for a new directive laying down basic requirements for spraying equipment to be placed on the market. it will complement the existing provisions for the maintenance and regular inspection of spraying equipment. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to stress one important aspect of the proposed directive on the sustainable use of pesticides. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's environmental policy is properly implemented. this is a key measure in the commission proposal, which has been discussed in the various committees of parliament. it is not disputed that we need to reduce our dependence on pesticides and to turn to more environmentally friendly alternative techniques for plant protection or pest control. integrated management and control is the most effective way to achieve this objective and it is therefore particularly important that it be retained in our proposal and made mandatory in all member states from 2014.

principle in full or in part. the commission partially accepts the proposal that member states should set targets for reducing the use of the most dangerous pesticides in national action programmes. for the reduction of pesticide use at european union level, in addition to national targets, is not necessary and is therefore not supported by the commission. the general reduction in the quantity of pesticides does not necessarily imply a corresponding reduction in the risk, since the level of risk varies from one substance to another. action to reduce the risk must therefore be targeted and focused primarily on the most harmful substances. the commission can accept in principle the introduction of a minimum width for the buffer zones to be established in fields adjacent to watercourses, as this would bring additional environmental benefits. however, the imposition of 10 measures indiscriminately in all cases does not seem to be appropriate. the commission would prefer that member states should have some flexibility and determine the appropriate width of buffer zones, taking into account their geographical particularities. the commission may also accept some useful clarifications on other issues such as technical training and certification. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. firstly, the commission is convinced that the mandatory observance of common general principles of integrated pest control by professional users of pesticides is a key measure to reduce dependence on pesticides. it will bring significant environmental benefits throughout the european union and contribute to the development of a sustainable and competitive agricultural sector. i cannot therefore accept the deletion, by amendment no 86, of this extremely important measure contained in the european commission's proposal. secondly, the european commission agrees with the adoption of measures to protect the populations living near fields where aerial spraying is carried out. the committee also welcomed the commission's proposal to introduce a new system of taxation of the income of the self-employed. we must leave some room for manoeuvre for member states and local authorities to deal, if ever necessary and in exceptional and rare cases, with risks to public health or biodiversity which can only be addressed by the use of pesticides. thirdly, although the commission has committed itself to considering extending the scope of the directive to biocides, such a decision requires careful consideration, as well as the adaptation of certain aspects of the pesticide directive. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the use of cannot support the addition of a reference to article 152 (4) of the treaty, since the proposed directive clearly focuses on environmental protection, which already includes public health issues. draft opinion of the consultative committee on industry, research and energy. the commission has already made a number of proposals. mr davies, i think we need to remember once again very clearly why we need to discuss strict binding limits in the first place. it is because a voluntary agreement which was concluded between the commission and the automotive industry over ten years ago has been knowingly and willfully missed by the automotive industry. this was not an accident, this was not done to one's self, but it was brought about by decisions at the top of the group! i am therefore somewhat surprised, mr davies, that you have made it clear today, with your amendments - which i have only known about today, perhaps they have been around for a long time - that you are no longer interested in putting any real pressure on the innovative capacity and the innovative power of the automobile industry in europe, contrary to what has been decided in the committee on the environment. in my view, the only way to achieve europe's climate goals is to have the strict limit values - as originally proposed by the commission. i also think it is true - and you are right, mr dimas - that we can only guarantee the security of supply for transport in the long term if we immediately make cars more efficient, because we cannot stand by and watch valuable and hard-to-reach oil continue to be celebrated on our roads. the third point - and this is so important to the committee on industry for which i wrote the opinion - is that we must finally ensure that the knowledge and skills of engineers and designers in the automotive industry are put to use and that these good engineers are not further held back by bad management. i am firmly convinced that in the very near future only efficient, climate-friendly, affordable cars will be on sale, cars which are still classy, and those who today, by setting really harmless time limits for the limit values, mr davies, take the pressure off innovation, will be responsible for this if the european car industry is not competitive in the long term and if the car industry in europe loses jobs. it is quite clear that the world car market - at least if we believe our climate policy and our un climate policy - will change completely, and those who are on the brakes today on the limits are responsible for the fact that the automotive industry in europe is going down the drain and we are not taking our climate policy seriously at all.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the question of whether eu tax policies are actually helping to promote growth, employment and innovation is, unfortunately, a very narrow one: she's not doing it! the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. growth is not promoted by taxing earned income many times more than income from property ownership, and the gap between the two is even widening. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the taxation of small businesses is not disproportionately higher than that of speculative investments in stocks, bonds and financial derivatives. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in short, a socially balanced outlook and development of the eu is certainly not being promoted, but rather strangled, as long as those who are floating in money are being blessed with ever new tax gifts and are being fattened up ever further, while those who already have little are being pocketed ever more. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i know that on paper, of course, the design of national tax systems is still a matter for the member states, but the reality is different. in fact, the lack of eu-wide coordination - especially in the area of direct taxation - is leading to national tax systems becoming increasingly less politically oriented and more shaped by the icy logic of tax competition. this logic can be summed up in a simple formula: the more mobile a factor is, the greater its potential for extortion vis-à-vis the national tax authorities and, of course, the more extensive the tax relief it can enforce for itself. in order to avoid the total drain on government revenue, the sectors which are difficult or impossible to avoid taxation must be taxed even more heavily to compensate. this is why taxes are shifted from corporate profits to private income, here from capital income to labour income, which is just less mobile, within labour income from high paid work to the less well paid workers, who are just as much less mobile, and in general from income and wealth to consumption. the fact that this process has been going on for years and decades is very clearly demonstrated by the data on tax revenues and rates in the eu. not only the statutory but also the effective corporate tax rates in the eu have fallen by over 10 percentage points in the last decade. this is confirmed by all the studies on the subject that exist. in almost all eu countries, top tax rates have been reduced. in an increasing number of eu countries, the transition to dual taxation systems has led to a massive privileging of private capital income over labour income. and consumption taxes are rising more and more - on the one hand, because of so-called eco-taxes, which often, for lack of choice, have no environmental incentive at all, but simply drain households to the bone, and on the other hand, because vat rates are rising more and more and are approaching each other in more and more countries at the upper end of the agreed corridor. such a development is no coincidence. it is the direct consequence of unhindered tax competition in a single internal market. it should be noted that the downward trend in corporate taxation within the eu far outweighs that in the oecd as a whole. this means that tax rates have fallen significantly more than in the oecd as a whole. this too shows very clearly that the forces of globalisation, which are often and often invoked, are not at work here, but that these are home-made forces, made within the eu, and thus also forces which could very well be overcome on their own, if one wanted to. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to support them. only such minimum rates actually offer the chance of stopping the race to the bottom in corporate taxes at some point. my report included the call for a stronger taxation of wealth and financial transactions throughout the eu, the call for a significant reduction in working income in the lower and middle classes, and finally the call to reverse the fatal trend of increasingly shifting direct taxes to indirect taxes and to re-establish the opposite trend. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. unfortunately, the changes made in the report show very clearly the interests of the majority of the members of the economic committee, and particularly the liberal and conservative groups, because it is quite obvious who are the beneficiaries of the current tax regime in the eu. we have now tabled our main demands once again in the form of amendments. if they do not get a majority here, my group will vote against the report. a different tax policy in the eu, which reduces social contrasts rather than increasing them further and further - as the current tax policy does - would be very possible and urgently needed. but this would require that the mainstream politics in the european commission and indeed in the individual eu member states actually take the interests of the majority of europeans as their guiding principle, rather than acting as the enforcer of the interests of the top ten thousand, as has been the case so far. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we shall continue to exert pressure on this very point so that at some point the unspeakable euphemism acting president of the council. mr president, mr president of the european commission, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to begin my remarks today by recalling the memory of a friend of mine. the memory of mep fausto correia, who died a few days ago. he died young. his death was of course a great loss for the european parliament, but it was also a great loss for the portuguese socialist party. fausto
