disappearance was a personal loss for me, the loss of a longtime friend with whom i shared many moments of my life and who leaves me with great sorrow. ladies and gentlemen, when i presented the programme of the portuguese presidency to this house three months ago, i made it clear that the main challenge - the main priority - of the portuguese presidency would be to draw up and reach agreement on the new treaty, ending the six years of deadlock in the institutional debate in which the european union was immersed. it is therefore with great pleasure that i stand before the european parliament today to present to you the agreement reached by the intergovernmental conference on 18 october. the new treaty of lisbon was born of this agreement. the treaty will be signed on 13 december in the city which will henceforth give it the name by which it will be known. the portuguese presidency has begun the task of transforming the mandate given to us by the german presidency, the clarity and precision of which i wish to stress here as i have always done, but transforming this mandate into a new treaty. that was our mission. the agreement we have reached confirms the correctness of the method and timetable we defined at the beginning of our presidency. it was necessary - as i said to you here at the beginning of the presidency - to take advantage of the june council to try to conclude the treaty not in december, as some advocated, but in october, in the informal council. and we were right. the fact is that we have held the fastest intergovernmental conference in the history of the european union on the revision of the treaties. we started on july 23 and finished on october 18. when we make the history of this treaty, we will understand better the importance of this political decision not to leave for the end of the year the task that was within our power to finish earlier. europe needed a quick deal and got it. europe needed a sign of confidence and it got it. europe needed to look to the future and it did. we worked quickly with all the member states, which without exception showed a constructive spirit and a willingness to overcome the remaining difficulties. this has enabled us to present a full text of the treaty on 3 october, bringing us much closer to our objective. the questions that remained for the lisbon summit were limited, but politically difficult, to be sure. in this context, our strategy was to try to reach an agreement on the first day of the summit. we felt that this was not only possible but also very desirable, because we were sending an important signal to europe. the sign that the european union is able to decide quickly, even when decisions are involved which everyone recognizes as difficult. it was very important that we could, on the first day of the informal council, deal with institutional questions and, on the second day, immediately after that resolution, discuss globalisation and how europe should deal with global issues. the following issues were therefore agreed at lisbon, which allowed agreement on the treaty to be finalised: firstly, the ioannina clause, and in the agreement a two-tier solution was reached: a declaration, a declaration which is about the system of decision-making in the council by qualified majority and which makes explicit the ioannina safeguard mechanism itself; but another, a protocol which makes the modification or repeal of this mechanism conditional on consensus in the european council. as i have always said, the ioannina question, as i saw it in the last council agreement, required that this clause be legally binding but not in the treaty. this solution we have adopted, a declaration plus a protocol which ensures that this decision on ioannina is only changed by consensus, seems to us to be the solution which is most faithful to the spirit of the last agreement. in this way we have given guarantees as to ioannina's commitment without affecting the integrity of the qualified majority decisionmaking process. a political question concerning the number of advocates-general of the court of justice also had to be resolved. a statement was agreed that the council would give its approval to a possible request by the court of justice to increase the number of advocates-general from eight to eleven (therefore three more). in this case, poland will have a permanent advocate-general and will no longer participate in the rotation system, while the current rotation system will cover five advocates-general instead of the three it currently has. as regards the appointment of the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, we agreed on a declaration that the european parliament will be involved in the process of his appointment at the very beginning, in january 2009, through appropriate contacts. the conference also adopted a declaration clarifying the delimitation of competences between the union and the member states, as provided for in the treaties. and finally, the question of the composition of the european parliament. as you know, there has been an amendment to article 90a of the treaty on european union, which defines that the number of members of the european parliament cannot exceed 750 plus the president, that is to say 751, while maintaining the proportional degressivity of their representation. this amendment was accompanied by two declarations: one defining that the additional seat in the european parliament will be allocated to italy; the other ensuring that the european council will give its political agreement on the composition of the european parliament, on the basis of the parliament's own proposal. the council therefore accepted the criteria proposed by parliament and made an adjustment which it considered acceptable, with a view to adapting the current framework during the period 2009-2014. in addition to the issues i have mentioned, the portuguese presidency was also concerned to incorporate into the treaty those rules and exceptions which were part of the mandate, naturally respecting the positions of the member states which wished to obtain them, but always with the concern not to distort the essence of the community decisionmaking process and the overall coherence of the treaty. we have a new treaty. a new and a good treaty. a treaty that resolves the crisis of the past and puts europe on the road to the future. it is a treaty which has made significant progress, and i should like to highlight some of them. this treaty incorporates, without amendment, the extension of the european parliament's participation in the legislative process and also incorporates innovations in the budgetary procedure, thus reinforcing the democratic legitimacy of the union; other whereas this treaty improves the decision-making process, in particular by extending qualified majority voting to the area of freedom, security and justice; as regards the area of freedom, security and justice, this treaty lays down the legal basis for the development of more effective immigration and asylum policies, as well as for police and judicial coordination against terrorism and organised crime, which enhances the security of our citizens; this treaty clearly lists the areas in which member states have transferred powers to the union; this treaty strengthens the supervisory role of national parliaments. but among all the advances made by this treaty, there is one i would particularly like to emphasize: the treaty explicitly confers binding legal force on the charter of fundamental rights, which is to be proclaimed by the three institutions of the european union as early as 12 december. in addition, the union's accession to the european convention on human rights and the fact that a solution has been found to the question of the legal framework for european citizenship, as was requested by the representatives of this parliament. at the external level, the new institutional framework created by the treaty - in particular the merger of the posts of high representative and vice-president of the european commission for external relations - reflects europe's ambition in foreign policy, an ambition that will give europe a more prominent role on the international stage and the means for effective cooperation with our partners. ladies and gentlemen, it was a difficult and demanding negotiation, but europe has complied. europe has fulfilled and fulfilled the crucial objective, the objective of having a treaty that affirms european values, the objective of having a treaty that strengthens europe as a global economic actor and has fulfilled the crucial objective for europe of having the most effective institutional conditions to play its role. europe therefore emerges stronger from this summit. stronger to deal with global issues. stronger to take your place in the world. but it is stronger because it has given a signal of confidence to our economy and a signal of confidence to the citizens of europe. the treaty of lisbon now shows a europe that is prepared, a europe that is confident, and a europe that is self-assured. what the treaty of lisbon brings us back is a europe fit for the times. and let me thank the european parliament for that. i european union to have an increased capacity to act, you need strong, effective, democratic and accountable european institutions. the treaty of lisbon will reinforce the democratic nature of the european union. first, thanks to the efforts of the european parliament, there is now a clear definition of what european citizenship means. secondly, the reform treaty also gives legal force to the charter of fundamental rights, which will be a central part of the system of checks and balances in our union of law. together with president pöttering and prime minister socrates, we will proclaim the commission has already made a number of proposals. that was an interesting debate. we are dealing with a very different subject now. let us see how we come to a conclusion sooner or later. there is a saying, which i believe is heard throughout europe, that money does not make you happy, but it does make you calm. i would like to say that i am very pleased that the commission has taken this initiative. but if you have to get money from someone else, if you owe someone money from a sale, from damages or similar, then there is often reason not to be reassured but to be worried, for example, that the debtor is evading his obligations, that he is letting money or assets disappear, possibly even later than tonight. all the member states have procedures to prevent this, interim procedures, injunctions, arrests, provisional seizures - whatever you call it. it's very different everywhere, it's very complicated, and there's the language problem. if one were to use the crossborder procedure of the member state, it would often be that - as we say in germany - the rabbit was over the hill, that is to say, the debtor had the opportunity to make his assets disappear. the problem is now virulent across europe's borders. it is all the more important as we all want a single area of payments, cashless payments. this means that the possibility of assets disappearing across the border is growing. that is why the commission - and i want to say this explicitly - has been quite right to take the initiative. it has presented a very good green paper, which is very comprehensive and contains many details, some of which will certainly have to be clarified. that is the point of the hearing. the european parliament cannot answer everything at this stage, and neither can i. i would therefore like to make a few points in a very brief way. first of all, although it is obvious, it is only a provisional attachment, a provisional guarantee, not a final satisfaction. and besides, this is just about money, bank accounts, not about injunctions, foreclosures of other assets. the question would have been whether the objective could be achieved by harmonizing the 27 different systems in existence. that is certainly not a good idea, it would have to wait until christmas eve. it interferes with so many other things that it wouldn't be good. the commission is also proposing an autonomous, additional european regulation, preferably in the form of a regulation, which should be introduced alongside the national regulations, which will remain in force. i would like to mention brussels 1 in addition. the regulation we have here is not enough. the creditor must summarily make his claim credible, he must also make the risk credible. what is particularly important to us - and to me - is the protection of the debtor. the fact that we have a european regulation is precisely why i do not want to see any damage to a debtor or a third party, which would also affect europe. in certain circumstances, an unjustified attachment may also be destructive. i would just like to mention the points that the creditor may be liable for damage caused to the debtor, that he may be given a deadline to initiate the main proceedings, that he may have to provide security, that the debtor must be able to object, that a procedure is not chosen for this, which then takes forever, but roughly corresponds to the procedure before, that there is no over-collateralisation, and that the debtor must also remain the subsistence minimum. there's the issue of trust accounts. if there is any possibility of seizure there - i want to leave it open - then it must be secured in a very special way. the same applies to community accounts although they are not the same, they are not directly related because third parties are also protected and special protection measures are required for third parties. i would remind you that standard forms would be useful for the communication of banks, and i would like to say in this context and in conclusion once again: there is certainly still a need for comparative legal studies, detailed studies. i would like to express my gratitude to the commission for these extensive studies and studies, and to all my colleagues. we all worked very well together. i assume that this will be decided by a broad consensus.

our heartfelt condolences to the families and the finnish people. the groups have asked me to make a statement on the convention of 18 september 1997 on the prohibition of the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel mines and on their destruction (ottawa convention): in a few weeks' time, we will be celebrating the tenth anniversary of the signing of the convention on the prohibition of the use, stockpiling, production and transfer of anti-personnel mines and on their destruction. on 3 and 4 december 1997, 122 countries signed this historic treaty in ottawa. anti-personnel mines do not distinguish between civilian and military casualties. they are directed against people with the purpose of killing or maiming them. the ban on them by the ottawa convention is a victory for humanity. the agreement is also a success of the internationally networked civil society. in a process unprecedented in its kind, a coalition of ngos, together with committed governments and parliaments, managed to conclude an international treaty outside the usual diplomatic forums. the international campaign to ban landmines was awarded the nobel peace prize in 1997 for this achievement. the european parliament has supported the campaign against landmines from the outset. following the signing of the ottawa convention, the european parliament has been active in resolutions, hearings and opinions in favour of effective implementation. the successes of the international campaign are now evident. over three quarters of all states have ratified the ottawa convention. the use of antipersonnel mines has fallen dramatically, as has the number of countries producing land mines. despite this progress, landmines are still not completely eliminated in over 69 countries. it is clear that this objective cannot be achieved everywhere without additional financial resources. europe has made an important contribution to the implementation of the ottawa agreement in recent years. the european union has invested over one billion euros in the fight against landmines between 1997 and 2004. the european commission's anti-mines strategy is one of the most successful elements in the development of european external relations. this is not only an expression of our humanitarian commitments, but also a worthwhile investment in sustainable development and human security. the council of the european union is about to adopt a new joint action on landmines within the framework of the common foreign and security policy. we welcome the intention to work towards the universal ratification of the ottawa convention and an effective review conference in 2009. we look forward to working closely with the council and the commission in implementing the joint action. i hope that we will soon have the opportunity to discuss with the council and the commission their respective initiatives on landmines and mutual coordination. our common ultimate goal is a world without mines, and this requires a coherent common policy of the european union. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the rapidly growing air traffic needs to be integrated into the its system as soon as possible. the aim is to reduce the anthropogenic greenhouse effect by using this transport mode. from the point of view of transport policy, our legislative work is now about adjusting the framework conditions properly. these framework conditions must be such that, through a reasonable price per tonne of co2, the potential savings incentives are triggered without drastically restricting flight operations. for example, the initial allocation of allowances to airlines must be designed in such a way that their shortage can realistically be compensated for on the market, otherwise flights will have to be cancelled, and i do not know how much of this we and our society can take. even if 100% of the certificates were issued at the time of entry into the system - and none of us is asking for this - an annual growth of 5% in air transport would require equally high co2 emission savings. that's not a small effort. the greatest reduction potential lies in the realisation of the single european sky, and therefore depends on the political will of the member states. the airlines are therefore left with the task of renewing their fleet, provided that the auctioned amounts allow sufficient capital to be made available. this is unlikely to be the case with regional airlines.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr peter liese, for his excellent report and my colleague mr jarzembowski. i believe that the overall compromise is very viable. politics is often about symbols, and so we are sending a clear message here: this is the first legislative initiative after the spring summit, and we are beginning to actively implement climate action. the seven key points of the report - the start of emissions trading, the reference period, the number of permits, the use of revenues, the exemptions for small aircraft and the method of calculations - are, in my view, adequately and reliably assessed in the compromises. i do not want to make exceptions, but i certainly think that a special regulation for the outermost regions in an addendum is necessary to ensure that these regions are not disadvantaged. i think the proposal is very good and that competition is sufficiently appreciated here. we should not forget that even if the auction is 100% - in theory, as we have just heard - it is 2 billion euros, a figure that is quite manageable for airlines and which will probably also be reflected in pricing. but i see no problem here with the large number of flights. i hope that the eu will continue to lead on climate protection and that we can get all the other major competitors and their airlines to join this agreement.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, the comitology reform that was decided in july 2006 introduced a ‘regulatory procedure with scrutiny’, which gives a veto right to the european parliament on measures of general scope that amend a basic legal act adopted under codecision. in the framework of this reform, the three institutions concluded a joint statement in which they committed themselves to adapt 26 priority basic acts to this new procedure, and the commission adopted 26 priority alignment proposals at the end of last year. it is in our common interest to have these alignment instruments adopted as soon as possible. the commission is therefore very pleased to see that parliament is now ready to vote on several legislative resolutions, after having reached good and fair compromise solutions between the three institutions. other important dossiers will be on the agenda of another session of the european parliament later this month, and i am confident that we will be able to settle these dossiers as well. i want to thank the rapporteurs from the different committees for their very cooperative and constructive approach. consequently, the whole package of the 26 priority alignment proposals could be ready for adoption before the end of this year. this would be a very good result which will pave the way to the so-called ‘general alignment’. as you know, the commission made a commitment to review all existing codecision basic legal acts, in addition to these 26 priority acts, with a view to bringing them into line with the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny. the commission will respect this commitment and propose this general alignment of all non-priority acts. it concerns in total more or less 220 acts. this will take the form of four to five omnibus or package proposals, the first of which should arrive in the european parliament shortly in november. the next two omnibus proposals will follow within a couple of weeks and the final proposal just before the end of the year, or very early next year. a third aspect of revising parliament’s scrutiny rights is the revision of the agreement concluded in 2000 between the commission and parliament on comitology procedures. here i would like to thank parliament and, in particular, mr galeote and mr corbett for the excellent spirit of cooperation which prevailed endorses the outcome of the negotiations. i am confident that the agreement we reach will help our two institutions work more efficiently in the future.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to warmly thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs for the excellent work they have carried out regarding the adoption of international financial reporting standard (ifrs) 8 – operating segments, the new standard on segment information. after the international accounting standards board (iasb) issued the standard in november 2006, a debate ensued concerning the suitability of ifrs in the european context. this debate was useful. we had to make sure that the european union would not adopt a new accounting standard just for the sake of convergence with the equivalent us standard, but mainly because it improves the quality of financial information and is conducive to the european public good. before reaching a final decision, the commission and parliament agreed in may 2007 that the commission’s services would carry out an analysis of the potential consequences of adopting ifrs 8. they ran a public consultation during july and august and gathered the views of stakeholders on the cost/benefit implications and the overall impact of adopting ifrs 8. on the basis of almost 200 contributions, my services have prepared a report which was provided to parliament on 10 september 2007. the report’s main conclusion is that the benefits of adoption of ifrs 8 would outweigh its costs. further, many constituents stressed that a swift endorsement of ifrs 8 would remove uncertainty about the treatment of financial statements for the period ending in december 2007. let me stress that we did not ignore the concerns that had been raised regarding the introduction of the so-called ‘management approach’, which gives management more leeway compared with the existing standard on segment reporting. some constituents were concerned that ifrs 8 lacks strict requirements on detailed geographical information because it allegedly does not require sufficient detail on a country-by-country basis. discussions with constituents revealed, however, that ifrs 8 is rather expected to improve this kind of disclosure. further, it seems that particular concerns in this area, in our view – and in the view of the majority of respondents to our consultation – cannot be resolved through a financial reporting standard on segment information. this could be better done through a further development of a framework regarding corporate social responsibility aspects. we agreed that ifrs 8 should not be adopted solely for the sake of convergence, yet we believe that it is crucial to see the issue also in the broader context of the european union adopting a set of standards which are truly global. a couple of years ago we all agreed that europe should not opt for its own set of standards but rather support and promote the development of a high quality and global set of standards like ifrs. we are working on improving the governance of the iasb. on 7 november the european commission, the us securities and exchange commission and the japanese financial services agency made a joint statement announcing their agreement to seek certain changes to strengthen the institutional framework of the international accounting standards committee (iasc) foundation. these changes are intended to strengthen the accountability of the foundation’s trustees, in particular by replacing the current self-appointment process for the appointment of the trustees with a process in which public authorities are responsible for the final approval of trustees. the joint statement also recognised the importance of further strengthening the iasb’s due process, including by carrying out impact assessments. this agreement provides a strong basis to address the concerns expressed by this parliament. it also reflects the issues identified by the commission’s two monitoring reports to ecofin concerning the iasb’s governance. we will work with the iasc foundation and the international partners to develop more detailed proposals in the coming months. we will, of course, maintain a close dialogue with the european parliament throughout this process. i am confident that the outcome of this process will ensure that standards respond to european needs and are easily acceptable and applicable by all stakeholders in the eu and also globally. let me conclude. the swift adoption of ifrs 8 is important for two reasons. it improves the quality of financial information and it provides certainty to all market participants. the discussions of the last months have demonstrated that a stronger involvement of the european parliament in the endorsement process is necessary. the commission will also continue to work with the iasb and the iasc foundation and with our international partners to ensure that the process of developing international accounting standards is fully accountable, transparent and meets the needs of european stakeholders.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already done so. the ifrs 8 process is symptomatic of where we are today in the implementation, the endorsement process for ifrs in europe. i would like to say in advance, and very clearly, to those who may always accuse parliament of doing the opposite: the majority of the european parliament is for ifrs, is for a global standard and is for all of this going in a common right direction. we should also examine this process of ifrs in particular, whether it is right as it stands today, when the european parliament is presented with a standard by the commission at short notice, when the commission and industry are expected to implement it relatively quickly, when the pressure from industry is increasing and those responsible for justifying themselves to the citizens on the ground are not given a chance to form an opinion on this. the commission then set a corresponding stage, but we will have to speak bluntly about what has happened now. because what's happened now is that the implementation phase is being postponed. in order to prevent this from happening in the future, it is essential that legislative institutions such as the european parliament are informed in good time of the work being done. i welcome what was announced last week by the commission, with the ssi, with the japanese, with iosco. what was presented last week by the ifrs organisation, accordingly, is that 'giving oneself a governance' is a correct but long overdue step towards legitimation and governance, and we as the european parliament will be very careful to ensure that the democratic rules of the game are respected. this does not mean that we as a parliament have to be directly involved. but only if the process is right can we ensure that in future, in the further implementations, in each and every standard, and we will be asked in the future for each and every standard, we have an optimized process.

on behalf of the pse group. – as you know, the european union is currently defending airbus in a case before the wto brought by the united states on behalf of boeing. i believe it is important at this stage of the dispute for this body to build support for the european union’s position and against that of the united states. i should state at the outset that this entire dispute arose because boeing no longer wished to participate in a mutually-agreed international agreement between the united states and the european union – an agreement that allowed certain forms of government support to both airbus and boeing, the only two producers of large civil aircraft in the world. as my colleagues know, such agreements are the best foundation upon which relations among nations are based. it is incumbent on nations to abide by their obligations under these treaties. airbus has. the european union has. unfortunately, the united states has not. airbus and the european union have constantly abided by the spirit and intent of the 1992 bilateral aircraft agreement. for 11 years, competition between airbus and boeing flourished, resulting in important breakthroughs in commercial aviation technology and design that have led to safer, more efficient and more environmentally-sensitive air travel. but boeing decided it no longer wanted to abide by the obligations of this agreement. instead, with the assistance of the united states, they attacked airbus for exacting so-called ‘illegal subsidies’ – the very government assistance that boeing had originally agreed to in the 1992 agreement. as many of my colleagues are aware, airbus’s government loan funding is a targeted and non-trade-distorting use of a government’s limited research resources. it offers governments a fair return and brings to the market innovative products, which benefit everyone. simply stated, european government research and development funding is limited, repayable and has no impact on boeing’s ability to compete. meanwhile, because boeing produces both civil and military aircraft for the united states, technology used in its commercial aircraft today benefits greatly from us government awards to boeing military research and development contracts. for example, boeing’s current knowledge about composites, which is being used extensively in its new 787 dreamliner, stems – by its own admission – from its work on developing the v-22, the f-22, the b-2 and the joint strike fighter. this federal assistance is supplanted by us state and local government support to boeing in the form of tax breaks, favourable real estate and local infrastructure improvements intended to secure the company’s presence and job base in selected us cities. while boeing opposes the airbus repayable assistance programme, it has no problem with identical programmes benefiting boeing in japan. i highlight these points not to imply that the assistance received by boeing (repayable in japan but not in the us) is somehow worse than the repayable european loans received by airbus. i mention this assistance that boeing receives to illustrate the reality that both sides benefit from some form of government assistance, from nations wishing to retain their global leadership roles in aviation. while boeing has benefited from government support, it seeks to deny europe similar benefits. i believe we should urge the commission to direct airbus and boeing to develop a forward-looking arrangement that provides a stable environment for both sides to compete and develop state-of-the-art aircraft well into the future. maybe a six-month moratorium on the wto case would allow the two companies time to complete a new discipline. this is the opportunity that is now before us. we can dwell on the past or look forward to the future.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. our european interest in surviving in the age of globalisation means above all that we must seize our opportunities. we have too much public discussion of the effects that are negative. we discuss this when companies have to cut jobs or move them abroad. but we talk far too little about all the good things that come out of it. for example, if i look at my constituency, my home region, 74% of the industrial production in my constituency is now going abroad. we are definitely benefiting from globalization. unfortunately, in my home region too, people are being laid off by companies that are no longer profitable, but many more can be hired by other companies that have benefited from globalisation and have adapted to it, and we have a significant fall in unemployment. we don't talk about this very often. the european union is important in shaping globalisation. the 480 million europeans must stand together to defend their interests and values. we are already the most open economy in the world, but we need access to global markets. we need to pay more attention to reciprocity. non-tariff barriers to trade and other barriers are intolerable. we must be able to defend ourselves against unfair trade practices. we need trade defence instruments to do that. and for that we need a commissioner who does not represent the european union in an unbelieving and arrogant way, but who represents our interests in trade in an open, collegial and trusting manner. we need to protect intellectual property better, we need to promote more global rules and standards, we need to strengthen the wto and we need the transatlantic partnership. if we do this homework, and if the commission does this homework, then we can really use and shape globalisation to ensure that citizens as a whole continue to live in freedom and prosperity.
the commission has already done so. those who speak out for a more just world are not shy about pointing to globalization as a cause of economic hardship in their own countries. they therefore call for less market, more regulation and more government intervention. globalisation offers a real opportunity to become a win-win scenario, as it allows emerging economies and laggards to catch up with the global economy, and it offers us the opportunity to develop new markets for sophisticated, high-quality products, assets and services. but to seize these opportunities, we must do our homework: more efforts in education, training - especially for unemployed young people - and lifelong learning, more research and development, more investment in innovation and ecology, more creativity in shaping the value chains and processes of our economy, more free enterprise. without hindrance, globalisation leads to more open markets and more competition. all consumers benefit from this. we must resist the temptation to protect our economy. this protection would very quickly degenerate into pure protectionism. let us instead encourage the forces inherent in our economy to renew itself constantly. if we invest in the technologies of the future, we will win them too!

in writing. soil is one of the vital resources. as a non-producible commodity, it is of major importance for biodiversity, as a source of raw materials and also for storing and filtering nutrients and water. but land is not a transfrontier asset and cannot be taken for granted by the european union. the protection of our soils is in the interest of the landowners and therefore the responsibility of the member states. this application of the principle of subsidiarity must continue to be ensured. it is not justified to ignore all existing european legislation and the commitment of farmers to date and to adopt new rules in parallel with european directives, national regulations and cross compliance, which directly or indirectly concern soil protection. the eu has adopted a large number of soil-related directives and regulations, including the nitrates directive, the water framework directive, the emissions directive and the plant protection directive. the bureaucratic burden that could be placed on member states and the economy is in sharp contrast to the joint efforts to de-bureaucratize. in addition, the precautionary measures provided for in the directive cover all areas of agricultural law. i think that a soil protection directive at european level is unnecessary and not appropriate and i voted against this proposal.

been some talk of ratifying the treaty. it had to be so, because spain was a country that held a consultative referendum on the constitutional treaty, which then went through a process of renegotiation with a treaty nature, in the more classic sense of what the european concept represents. and i have been asked - i do not want to avoid any questions - why we do not put it to a member of the commission. mr president, on the basis of the agreed texts, member states will now have to establish marine strategies for their marine waters. such strategies will begin with an assessment of the status of marine waters and their existing impacts and pressures and will develop targets to find good environmental status. the member states will establish monitoring programmes and will then elaborate, as from 2015, programmes and measures necessary to achieve the objectives. this series of steps will be taken again every six years on a cyclical basis. a number of key elements have been included in the overall compromise package that is now proposed. most importantly, the objective of the directive is now clear and ambitious, as member states are required to take the necessary measures to achieve good environmental status in the marine environment by the year 2020 at the latest. the legislators have agreed on a definition of good environmental status, including a series of associated descriptors, which will have to be met. a revised timetable has now been agreed, which in fact is more demanding than what was included in the commission’s original proposal, but at the same time providing a sufficient time for taking appropriate action at each step. exceptions and derogations, including disproportionate costs, have been better qualified. member states will have to establish marine-protected areas to meet their objectives under this directive in accordance with the international commitments of the community and the member states. action will be required in the context of each marine region, and, therefore, to develop marine strategies will involve strong cooperation with and within regional sea conventions. the implementation of this i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the compromise on the air quality directive is first and foremost the result of successful teamwork. i should like to stress that at the outset. i would like to thank in particular my colleagues who have been actively involved in the drafting of this directive, in particular the rapporteurs, mrs anja weisgerber of the epp-ed group and mrs dorette corbey of the pse group, but also mrs satu hassi of the green group. i would also like to thank the commission for its valuable assistance and the portuguese presidency of the council, which, as an open and constructive negotiating partner, made a decisive contribution to the successful outcome. the compromise lays a solid foundation for the future eu air quality policy. the new directive balances ambitious targets and thresholds with the necessary flexibility for implementation in the member states. in addition, the focus is on exposure and the need to address the sources of pollution. let me first outline the main points of the compromise. the most important progress made in the revision of the air quality legislation is the regulation of the finest particles pm2,5. the smallest particles, which come exclusively from anthropogenic sources, are the ones which all experts consider to be the greatest risks to human health. pm2.5 - particles of fine dust less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter - which are not visible to the naked eye, can penetrate the lungs and cause serious respiratory illnesses in the long term. it is therefore overdue to put the smallest particles at the centre of european air quality policy. in the united states of america, a strict limit value for pm2.5 has been in place since 1997. the us is a decade ahead of the eu in this area of legislation. but with all due respect to american air quality policy, i would like to point out that we cannot simply copy what the americans have been doing for years. we have completely different conditions in europe, particularly in terms of population density and transport. the call by environmental groups for the immediate introduction of a strict limit value for pm2,5 is not realistic. the data situation in europe is not robust and the experience of measurements is insufficient not a good basis for a premature introduction of a limit value. the council and parliament agreed from the outset to regulate pm2,5 in two stages. the first is to set a target value from 2010 and the second is to set a limit value of 25 micrograms per cubic metre from 2015. the commission has always been in favour of a stricter value for pm2.5 despite the opposition of the council. it is therefore parliament's merit that we are today proposing to lower the limit value for pm2.5 to 20 micrograms per cubic metre in a second stage in 2020! in addition to a target and limit value for pm2,5, an exposure concentration obligation of 20 micrograms for member states shall be introduced in 2015. this is aimed at reducing background concentrations and will have a positive impact on the protection of human health, particularly in urban centres. the european parliament's proposal for reducing pm2.5 concentrations by 2020 has also been successful. it is differentiated by member state and more attention is paid to intermediate consumption. on pm10: the majority of parliament at first reading supported an ambitious annual limit for pm10 which, among other things, is more closely correlated with the current daily limit. the position of the council and the commission to leave the existing limit values untouched has been confirmed in the negotiations. with a three-year extension for pm10, from the entry into force of the new directive, municipalities that, due to their geographical location or meteorological conditions, have not been able to comply with the limit values despite all demonstrable efforts, will be granted an extension until 2012. while improving the quality of our ambient air will continue to be a major challenge for the eu in the future, i would like to highlight three points that i believe should be taken into account in the implementation of this directive and in the 2013 revision of the legislation. first, the pollution of our air has decreased dramatically in recent decades. a new study by the european environment agency shows that in the eu, the reduction of particulate matter emissions was around 50% between 1990 and 2004 - even before the introduction of pm10 limits. this has been achieved less by legislation than by technical progress. secondly, the conditions within the european union and between the member states vary greatly. i have already mentioned the meteorological and geographical conditions. but it is mainly the very different densities of settlement, transport and industry. this needs to be taken more into account in the implementation of future legislation. and thirdly, to further reduce air pollution, neither short-term actionism such as roadblocks and driving bans nor stricter limits that are only on paper will succeed. parliament welcomed the commission's statement on action at source, which will be published in the official journal in 2008 together with the new directive. the only way to reduce air pollution in the long term is at eu level, mainly by strengthening crossborder measures. the main focus should in future be on the policy on sources, which has been little considered so far, in particular private firing plants, shipping and agriculture.

member of the commission. madam president, firstly i would like to warmly thank the committee on legal affairs and the rapporteur, mr lehne, for the hard and excellent work he has carried out in the preparation of his report on the proposal to amend the design directive. i welcome the fact that this work has eventually allowed the committee to pave the way for liberalising the spare parts aftermarket in the whole community. currently, there is a situation of different, opposed regimes of design protection, where 10 member states have liberalised and 17 member states extend design protection to spare parts. this situation is entirely unsatisfactory for the internal market. in the automotive sector, which is the sector most affected, there is a single market for cars but no single market for their spare parts. this leads to distortion of prices and obstacles to trade. the proposed exclusion of design protection in the aftermarket for spare parts is the right and only effective way to achieve a single market in this area. the commission’s extended impact assessment analysing the options to solve the problem demonstrates this. the commission’s figures suggest that, currently, consumers are paying a 6% to 10% premium for these spare parts in member states which provide for design protection. with the liberalisation, consumers will benefit directly from the increased competition and the completion of the internal market. the independent distribution sector will be in a position to put a larger spectrum of parts on offer, including parts from original equipment suppliers, as well as the normally cheaper parts from independent producers. this will lead to more choice and lower prices for spare parts. liberalisation will also open business opportunities to independent spare parts producers, mostly smes, and create a european market of sufficient scale allowing new entrants to emerge. the essential purpose of design protection is to foster competition of forms through design innovation. this can, however, not apply to spare parts which have to be identical in design to the original parts if they are to serve a purpose. the consumer pays for the design when buying a new car or other product; he should not be forced to pay again each time he needs a spare part. the proposed repairs clause strikes a fair and correct balance between protecting innovation where appropriate and maintaining free trade and competition where necessary. european citizens and businesses today need a single market for spare parts which allows for more competition. with this directive we can provide the market with the right key to achieve this.
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. the commission has already made a number of proposals. we are coming today to the provisional end of a discussion that has lasted for seventeen years. i remember that we had to deal with this issue as far back as 1994, when i was first elected to this house. it was not brought to a conclusion at the time. we have only managed to avoid the subject during the conciliation procedure. the commission has put forward a new proposal a few years ago, which again took some time, but which is now finally being brought to an end, at least at first reading. what is now being proposed and is on the table is in principle what the commission is proposing, namely the liberalisation of the spare parts market, but with a transitional period of five years for the member states which have design protection for these areas. for 17 years, i have heard arguments for and against. most of them are not convincing. i would like to give a number of examples: firstly, the argument that there would be lower consumer prices if the repair clause were introduced. there's no empirical evidence to support that. quite the opposite! the comparison of spare parts prices in the uk liberalised and germany not liberalised shows the paradoxical result that spare parts prices in the uk are higher than in germany. it 's a simple game . the car companies have to put their design prices, their design costs, somewhere. if you don't put them in the spare parts department, you're gonna have to kill them on the new car price. so the cars are getting more expensive. this too must be paid for by the consumer. the same applies to insurance premiums. the insurance also covers part of the cost of buying new vehicles. if they become more expensive, it will not benefit the consumer. he always pays the piper in the end. the idea that the automotive industry would need this to protect itself against far eastern competitors that threaten its markets is also not very convincing in my view, because we will soon see the automotive industry finding ways to protect these parts in other ways: smart hoods and smart exterior mirrors through patent protection, and certain parts through trademark law, by simply putting certain logos on these parts, through regulations made under warranty agreements, and other approaches. the safety argument put forward is also not convincing, as our impact assessment has shown, because we know that safety can be guaranteed by type-examination. i am simply saying that i believe that all the arguments have in the end remained mere speculations and have not clearly answered the central question. in conclusion, i would like to make two main points which i accept: one is the copyright argument that intellectual property rights should be protected in an exemplary manner in europe. in fact, i believe that what we are about to decide here will probably send the wrong signal to china and india and that it is our duty as europeans to defend intellectual property rights. but i would also like to counter this by saying that we have a european single market and - as commissioner mcgreevy rightly said - that two thirds of the member states have liberalised, that is, they do not have protection, and one third do. if we want to create a single market in europe, we also need common legal rules. and it's not unusual for the majority principle to be followed. i have always considered that there was a compromise solution, which i had advocated with commissioner monti back in the 1990s. that was the idea of the compulsory licence. this means that anyone could have reproduced the parts and had to pay a corresponding license fee to the owner of the design rights. we have something very similar in the area of copyright, by the way. so no one can tell me that it's not possible. and there would have been an opportunity to protect design and create a market. unfortunately, there was no majority for this either in this house or in the council. what was left in the end was the consequence: we are liberalizing and, to protect those member states which need a certain amount of time to change, we are creating a transitional period. in the end, the dispute was left over for a period of five years or eight years. my group has decided, as the legal affairs committee has done, to vote for five years, and the socialist group, as i have heard, for eight years. the essence of the matter is that if parliament decides tomorrow whether to include five or eight years in the text, the signal to the council is that it should agree on a transitional period. i know from my talks with the slovenian presidency that the proposals that will come from there will be more long-term than short-term. i wish the slovenian presidency every success in its efforts. i think we should remember one thing for the second reading: if there is to be agreement in the council, we should make it a point in parliament not to complicate matters further in the second reading. the subject is not worth it, and it is high time to put an end to it. that is our contribution to bringing it to an end.
the committee also welcomed the commission's proposal to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the definition of the term 'competition'. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. after a long struggle, the legal affairs committee has voted in favour of full liberalisation of the secondary market for visible spare parts. the compromise reached in the legal affairs committee provides for a free market after a transitional period of five years, as we have just heard. i welcome this step, although personally i think the transitional period is too long rather than too short. the step is more than overdue. we have just heard from mr lehne that this subject has been under discussion for 17 years. as early as 2005, that is two and a half years ago, i had called for short-term liberalisation as rapporteur in the economic and monetary affairs committee. unfortunately, the original rapporteur on the committee responsible for legal affairs has repeatedly delayed the dossier. i do not know whether it was due to subjective doubts about the usefulness of the project or because he could not withstand the strong pressure of the car manufacturers in his own state. in any case, it is incomprehensible that we have a single market for new motor vehicles but not for spare parts. the liberalization of the secondary market will increase competition, tend to put pressure on prices and increase the supply to the consumer. this will not hinder innovation, on the contrary, it could even boost it, as car manufacturers will try to design their products in such a way that it becomes more difficult for independent suppliers to produce spare parts. i am of course in favour of the right to intellectual property and its protection, there is no question about that, but that right does not stand in the way of the liberalisation of the market. after all, there is only one case in which a car manufacturer has brought a complaint against another manufacturer for imitation of the design on the primary market, although some models did indeed bear very close resemblances to each other. small and medium-sized enterprises will also benefit from liberalisation through new market opportunities, which should have a positive impact on employment in the eu and replace some imports. the individual consumer is finally given the opportunity to choose freely between several suppliers. i'm sure he'll be happy to take that chance.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the liberalization of the market for visible car spare parts is welcome for three reasons. first, consumers will benefit from more choice and competition. secondly, perhaps a fall in prices is to be expected, but at least transparency in pricing, because design costs for a new car should be taken into account when buying the new car and not through a downstream monopoly on spare parts. thirdly, the labour market in the european union will benefit as european parts manufacturers will also be able to produce spare parts for imported vehicles in the eu. this was previously only possible for non-european manufacturers. i visited one of these companies near gütersloh during the 2004 election campaign. they'll be happy about this arrangement. i also welcome the fact that important elements of the commission's proposal, such as the reparation clause, are now included in the vote of the legal affairs committee. i have already supported this as rapporteur for my group in the committee on the internal market. i believe that this is another step towards the goal of a genuine single market. there are two major shortcomings, which have already been mentioned by the honourable members. the first is the delay in the report by the original rapporteur. mr radwan has not acted here as a representative of the european citizens, but as a representative of the bavarian motor works - bmw for short. that's not very nice. secondly, the delay in the five-year grace period is quite long. five years until liberalisation takes effect is a long time, it delays competition and the positive effects of liberalisation. i hear that the german government is planning to continue its blockade in the council. that's anti-competitive nonsense. unfortunately, this has become a trademark of the german government. i hope she'll back off in the council. the bottom line is that we have a compromise that we can live with and that we should accept. i can only echo the words of mr lehne, whom i would like to thank very much for his work here, that we should finish this now and not delay it any longer at second reading.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. the amendment to the design directive concerns whether or not a rightfully existing protection for the body design of a car should also extend to the corresponding visible spare parts, e.g. exterior mirrors or headlights. the consequence of such an expansion - in my opinion an exaggeration - of design protection would be the monopolization of a market of over 13 billion euros in favour of the car manufacturers. design protection for spare parts would exempt about 25% of the total spare parts market from the effect of the automotive block exemption regulation. the repair clause proposed by the eu commission ensures that the gmo, the basic law for the automotive sector, applies to the entire spare parts and repair market in the single market, as is now the case only in belgium, ireland, italy, spain and the uk. the transitional period of five years proposed by the epp group for the entry into force of the directive is sufficient and, in my view, more than generous. i would like to warn against further delays, also with regard to the council, because consumers have been waiting for a long time now, after these long discussions here in the house and between the member states, for lower repair costs and insurance premiums. we should not leave the question of what the inevitable consequence of further inaction would be to the ecj, but we should be the legislators who shape it. the council should also make an effort to reach a decision on this matter, which we shall be discussing here tomorrow.

for the institutions, because the charter guides their activity. they must also respect the rights and principles of the charter and promote its application, but it is also an instrument of action for citizens, because it shows that the union project is a citizens' project and shows that the union is at the service of citizens and that it protects and promotes their rights. the charter also rights and freedoms are universally respected. this charter will henceforth be at the service of the european union's external policy aimed at a world in which all these rights and freedoms are acting president of the council. in a globalised world where many argue that economic and financial rules are absolute, the fact that 27 european states within the union have reiterated this firm commitment to values and objectives of safeguarding and protecting fundamental rights is a significant contribution to the regulation of globalisation itself. fundamental rights are a common tradition of democratic states governed by the rule of law, a means of limiting power and a fundamental instrument for protecting the individual. by binding the institutions of the union and the states, the charter limits power and limits power in the name of the protection and interests of citizens and their organisations. and by enshrining this limitation of power, the limits of its application strictly observe the principle of subsidiarity and reinforce the eminently democratic nature of the union itself. the defence of fundamental rights is admittedly an essential value of european identity, it is part of our genetic code, it is an element that structures the whole european project and that allows europe to be defined as a union of values, and the unconditional affirmation of these values is also what the world expects from europe. that is the europe i want to belong to, a europe which defends these values. and we are fully aware, i and all the members, that the fight for fundamental rights is a daily task and probably an endless task, a task of states, a task of civil societies, a task of companies and trade unions, a task of individual citizens. that is why, in proclaiming the charter, we welcome the agreement reached on it and the recognition of its legal value on an equal footing with the union's own treaties. but more than a day of congratulations, the proclamation of this charter represents a commitment by the union's institutions to respect it and to apply it in their daily work. only in this way will we be equal to european history, only in this president of the commission. mr president of the european parliament, mr prime minister of portugal and mr president of the council of the european union, members of the european parliament, on the eve of the signing of the treaty of lisbon, the presidents of the three political institutions of the european union - the european parliament, the council and the commission - are signing the european charter of fundamental rights here in strasbourg. it is a great personal honour for me to take part in an event of such high significance. the proclamation of the charter of fundamental rights enshrines a culture of law in europe. in the european union, which is first and foremost a community of law, institutional changes require greater respect for fundamental rights. honourable members, today the three european institutions reaffirm their commitment the commitment they made in december 2000 when the charter was proclaimed for the first time. but, seven years later, we go a crucial step further. the charter of 2000 was not legally binding. with the signing of the treaty of lisbon tomorrow, and then ratification, the charter will be part of the primary law of the union and will have the same legal value as the treaties themselves. this progress will have very concrete benefits for european citizens. let me illustrate this point by looking briefly at the content of the charter. the 54 articles cover rights that until now had to be recognised by the court of justice on a case-by-case basis. now they are brought together. the charter, recognising the basic principles of human dignity, incorporates first of all the classic civil liberties already included in the european convention on human rights: freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, freedom of religion, equality before the law and the principle of non-discrimination. the charter also confirms economic and social rights. it includes the right to property and the freedom to conduct business, but at the same time the rights of workers and of the social partners, and it enshrines topics such as social security and social assistance. the charter also covers the new challenges facing society today. it therefore includes guarantees on data protection, on bioethics and on good administration, known as third-generation rights. these will be highly relevant in many of our areas of activity, be it in research policy, in the area of freedom, security and justice or in our permanent quest for good governance. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the charter encourages the european union to be anchored in a genuine culture of fundamental rights. by signing this charter of fundamental rights today, we, the presidents of the three political institutions of the european union, are above all committed to respecting these rights in our own action. at first sight, this commitment might seem easy to maintain but, in reality, it is a daily challenge to ensure the best possible respect for civil liberties in all the policies of the european union, whether it be in legislating on the internal market, managing immigration or trying to combat terrorism. the charter is the first legally binding document ever produced at international level which brings together not only political and civil rights but also economic and social rights in a single text, subject to the same mechanisms of judicial review. this is without doubt a major success of which the european union must be proud. it is, i think, particularly significant that this should be possible in this new enlarged europe, this europe which was divided by totalitarian and authoritarian regimes which did not respect human rights, but this europe we have today, which is a europe united around the values of freedom and solidarity. (applause from the centre) if we combine our efforts to stimulate this culture of human rights, we will make an essential contribution to a true europe of values, a europe of tangible and credible values in the eyes of its citizens. with this charter, europe is more determined to promote its values on a world scale. since the universal declaration of human rights, europe has always been at the forefront of the fight for fundamental rights. from today onwards, europe is even better equipped to win successfully this fight for freedom, for peace and for democracy. king of the hashemite kingdom of jordan. bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, mr president, members of parliament, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your warm welcome and, on behalf of the people of jordan, i am honoured to come before this distinguished institution again. my friends, a changing europe and a changing middle east are here today. a europe of expanding membership and a visionary mission: for cooperation across borders and growth without barriers. a middle east of new horizons and growing hope: for peace among neighbours, opportunities for our people and a future for our youth. these trends do not take place in isolation. the achievement of the hopes of our regions will advance stability and create new possibilities for security and prosperity worldwide. it is deeply in our interest to succeed. and a critical opportunity is before us. two weeks ago, with the support of the european union and nations from both our regions, israelis and palestinians met at annapolis. they pledged all-out negotiations toward a peace treaty in 2008 and immediate steps to implement their obligations under the road map. for the first time in years, we see movement towards a permanent settlement and an independent, sovereign, viable palestinian state. (applause) this progress is the work of many friends of peace, including leaders in europe and the arab states. we believed that, after years of worsening crisis, a change of strategy was required. we urged a new commitment to the two-state goal and a targeted process that could achieve it – with tight timelines, measurable requirements and milestones for action. second chances are rare, but i believe we have come to one. very real challenges lie ahead, but annapolis has created a new spark of hope. we can and must fan that spark into a blaze of confidence, action and tangible results. as our near neighbour, europe shares our interest in solving this, the central crisis of our age. all sides respect europe’s neutral role and model of regional progress and peace. for years, you have been our partner in the search for solutions. and you will be our partner, too, in the benefits of success: a vibrant zone of peace and prosperity throughout our shared hemisphere. these realities give europe an important and prominent role in the future of peace. i speak especially of the european union, and you, the voices of europe, here in the european parliament. and i have come here today to urge your active engagement, to seek your specific, practical skills and investment in the future, and to offer jordan’s own commitment in the days of work that lie ahead. my friends, there are major areas where action must begin now. the first is to support the negotiations and their goal: a final settlement creating an end to conflict, security for both palestine and israel, and at long last, a sovereign, independent and viable palestinian state. (applause)we must not underestimate the difficult days ahead. the issues are complex and decades old. real grievances must be faced – and left behind. on the positive side, israelis and palestinians understand their deep, shared stake in ending the conflict. and a great amount of work has already been done. from oslo, through the road map, through the geneva accords, and other initiatives, the parameters of the solutions are in focus. i believe the parties can get to the endgame. but for this to happen, it is vital that the international community be engaged. europe has a unique experience of the mechanisms and process of post-conflict recovery and reconciliation. this includes creating a security framework that can offer assurance to both sides. european peacekeeping forces have played a constructive role in lebanon. your commitment can help bring great trust to a palestinian-israeli settlement. on the ground, there is a need, not only for resources but for partnership – to boost economic opportunities, create confidence that the political process works, and help create the conditions that will sustain peace. both palestinians and israelis need to see tangible results, and quickly. that means security from violence and an end to occupation; but it also means better conditions of life. in the occupied territories, the humanitarian situation for palestinians remains dire. people need access to jobs and education, effective public services and more. such action will provide a major infusion of hope and be a powerful counter-argument to extremist predictions that nothing can change. next week, donor nations and institutions will meet in paris to make commitments and plan the way forward. european nations and the european union are already providing help, a commitment respected by people throughout the region. a second and related imperative is to understand and articulate the potential of peace. we must begin now to re-envision the future: a region where conflict has given way to cooperation, where a regional economy brings together the capabilities and resources of 22 countries – more than 300 million people, from the atlantic to the indian ocean – and where cross-border partnerships advance development, health, the environment and more. it is a future that empowers people to be full participants in global progress. and it will unleash a new scope of partnership with our european neighbours, in science, technology and trade. this promising future is why we must move swiftly on a comprehensive settlement, with action on the syrian and lebanese tracks. indeed, the entire arab world has recognized the importance of moving forward. the arab peace initiative was affirmed, unanimously, last spring. and it has received the support of muslim countries beyond the region. the opportunity is here, at long last, for a sovereign, independent, and viable palestinian state and full, normal relations between israel and 57 arab and muslim nations. this means acceptance; acceptance by key countries, with billions of citizens, representing almost a third of the membership of the united nations. and that opens a shared future of security, peace and new partnerships. achieving such a peace will also make a substantial impact on other issues. within the region, it will create new strategic space, allowing the resolution of other serious issues, from poverty to proliferation. aggressive forces will no longer be able to exploit the palestinian cause to serve their own ambitions and interests. (applause) resources and attention will be freed to advance the region’s potential through development and reform. we in jordan are ready to meet that future. we have pressed forward with our reform programme, despite regional instability. in the last decade, we have achieved significant gains: strong economic growth, rising per capita incomes, and a model education system. and europe has been an important partner, through private-sector investments, as well as official assistance. allow me to say that we deeply appreciate the support and friendship of this parliament and the european union. (applause)and we believe that in the days after peace, our partnership can only soar higher. my friends, today we can think of a larger neighbourhood, one that stretches from north of the baltic sea to south of the mediterranean, one that is shared by europe and the middle east. it is the basis of the euromed partnership, our region-to-region platform for cooperation and development. it is a relationship with great shared interests and unlimited potential. and it is up to us to develop our partnership to its fullest. today, young europeans are coming to adulthood who never knew a divided europe. their young counterparts, palestinian and israeli, have no such positive experience. they have grown up in a world of division and conflict. now, together, we have an opportunity to remove the barriers to their future, and leave the past behind. today, the european parliament represents significantly more member states than when i spoke before parliament only five years ago. that is the result of a region-wide commitment to increase the zone of partnership and progress. the middle east is tackling the same important task. now, together, we can help that work succeed. today, a renewed peace process has begun. we have seen such beginnings fail in the past. but this time, a unique confluence of events has created new openings for success. now, together, we can and we must, fulfil the promise of peace. (applause)my friends, we in jordan know that when an olive tree takes life, planting is only the first step. a hundred processes are then activated to create the cells and structures of life. roots emerge, growth occurs, and a core of strength ensures survival. from outside comes water and support to sustain life and create new fruit. in the arena of the middle east, a new olive branch has just been planted. now the real work must begin. it is in our hands to create the process and structures that will give peace roots, help it grow and sustain it into the future. i urge you to share in this effort. our partnership can create an historic transformation and a rich harvest – years of peace and prosperity that will benefit our peoples and our world.

i have to say, madam president, today's vote on the reform of the wine market is a very great success for the european parliament and the various wine regions and winegrowers. we have thus been able to establish that enrichment of wine with sucrose is still possible. the commission's plans to set out now the lifting of the ban on new plantings in 2014 have been rejected by parliament. here we have proposed a workable solution, by advocating that the decision on liberalisation be taken only after a study is available in 2012. we have also reached agreement on the labelling of the various wines, which takes due account of the different wine-labelling systems in europe. we have also succeeded in including the protection of the special bottle shapes in our region of france, the protection of the goat's bag, in the wine market regulation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the responsibility now lies with the council, and we as parliament have done our job very well.
in writing. the commission intends to take account of the specific characteristics of wine regions by creating a cmo with more responsibility and more scope for development. the european parliament has today put these ideas into practice. we are convinced of our proposals, which have been found by all members, across all member states. the wine industry in europe is part of our culture. here in europe is the home of wine growing worldwide. the wine industry is an economy, an income and a source of employment. it is not the commission's task to seek a market equilibrium by limiting our production or making it impossible by changing conditions. but it is their job to secure market share and to ensure that our products are properly represented worldwide. the aim must not be to limit the market but to conquer new markets. why should we change the winemaking methods where there are no sales problems?! it's part of an ancient culture and winemaking tradition. the european parliament has today reaffirmed its clear position in favour of more market measures, national budgets and regional flexibility, a socially compatible phasing-out of intervention measures and the maintenance of the existing oenological practices, i.e. sucrose and rtk, on an equal footing with each other through further rtk support. i hope that our proposals will be incorporated into the new common organization of the market in wine.
